ml-potentials-nucleation.domain: Machine-learned interatomic potentials and the simulation of first-order phase transitions (melting, freezing, nucleation, crystallization)
ml-potentials-nucleation.summary: First-order phase transitions are the hardest thing to get right in atomistic simulation. They demand two incompatible ingredients: quantum-mechanical accuracy in the energy differences between competing phases (often only a few meV per atom), and access to length and time scales — hundreds of thousands of atoms, hundreds of nanoseconds — far beyond density functional theory. Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) dissolved that tradeoff. The lineage begins with Joerg Behler and Michele Parrinello's 2007 high-dimensional neural network potential, which decomposed the total energy into atomic contributions expressed through symmetry-invariant descriptors, and with the Gaussian Approximation Potential of Albert P. Bartok, Mike C. Payne, Risi Kondor and Gabor Csanyi in 2010, which reframed the same problem as kernel regression. Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics (Linfeng Zhang, Jiequn Han, Han Wang, Roberto Car and Weinan E, 2018) made the approach scalable, and equivariant graph networks — NequIP (Simon Batzner, Boris Kozinsky and co-workers), Allegro, and MACE (Ilyes Batatia, Gabor Csanyi and co-workers) — made it dramatically more data-efficient. MACE-MP-0 extended this to a general-purpose foundation model. The payoff for phase transitions has been concrete: full ab initio-quality phase diagrams of water; homogeneous ice nucleation rates computed by seeding; the phase diagram and nucleation of gallium including the kinetic preference for metastable beta-Ga; silicon crystallization from deep metadynamics; crystallization kinetics of phase-change memory alloys; and evidence bearing on water's putative second critical point and hydrogen's liquid-liquid transition. Enhanced sampling — metadynamics (Alessandro Laio and Michele Parrinello, 2002), its well-tempered variant, multithermal-multibaric ensembles and OPES — supplies the rare-event machinery that makes nucleation observable at all.

items.claim: Joerg Behler and Michele Parrinello introduced the high-dimensional neural network potential, in which the total energy is decomposed into atomic contributions each predicted by an identical feed-forward network fed with symmetry-invariant functions of the local environment, demonstrating it on bulk silicon at a cost several orders of magnitude below DFT.
items.people: Jörg Behler, Michele Parrinello

items.claim: Albert P. Bartok, Mike C. Payne, Risi Kondor and Gabor Csanyi introduced Gaussian Approximation Potentials, applying Gaussian process regression to quantum-mechanical energies and forces so that the interatomic potential has no fixed functional form and can represent complex energy landscapes.
items.people: Albert P. Bartók, Mike C. Payne, Risi Kondor, Gábor Csányi
items.affiliation: Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge

items.claim: Albert P. Bartok, James R. Kermode, Noam Bernstein and Gabor Csanyi built a general-purpose Gaussian Approximation Potential for silicon that reproduces DFT reference results simultaneously for crystalline, liquid and amorphous bulk phases as well as point, line and planar defects — a prerequisite for treating melting and crystallization within one model.
items.people: Albert P. Bartók, James Kermode, Noam Bernstein, Gábor Csányi

items.claim: Linfeng Zhang, Jiequn Han, Han Wang, Roberto Car and Weinan E introduced Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics (DeePMD), a deep neural network many-body potential that preserves the natural symmetries of the problem and scales linearly with system size while reproducing the ab initio training data essentially exactly.
items.people: Linfeng Zhang, Jiequn Han, Han Wang, Roberto Car, Weinan E

items.claim: Linfeng Zhang, Han Wang, Roberto Car and Weinan E computed the phase diagram of a Deep Potential water model trained on the SCAN density functional from low temperature and pressure up to roughly 2400 K and 50 GPa, correctly predicting the molecular and ionic fluid phases and all stable ice polymorphs, ordered and disordered, with the exception of ices III and XV which are stable in experiment but metastable in the model.
items.people: Linfeng Zhang, Han Wang, Roberto Car, Weinan E

items.claim: Bingqing Cheng, Edgar A. Engel, Joerg Behler, Christoph Dellago and Michele Ceriotti used a neural network potential together with free-energy methods to compute the ab initio thermodynamics of liquid water and ice, obtaining melting properties and the relative stability of the two phases at first-principles accuracy including nuclear quantum effects.
items.people: Bingqing Cheng, Edgar A. Engel, Jörg Behler, Christoph Dellago, Michele Ceriotti
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116, 1110-1115

items.claim: Aleks Reinhardt and Bingqing Cheng computed the phase diagram of water at three hybrid density-functional levels of approximation, combining machine-learning potentials with advanced free-energy techniques and accounting for thermal fluctuations, nuclear quantum fluctuations and proton disorder; agreement with experiment is qualitative and best at pressures below roughly 8000 bar.
items.people: Aleks Reinhardt, Bingqing Cheng

items.claim: Bingqing Cheng, Guglielmo Mazzola, Chris J. Pickard and Michele Ceriotti used machine-learning interatomic potentials to overcome the system-size and timescale limits of ab initio molecular dynamics in dense hydrogen, finding evidence that the molecular-to-atomic transition in high-pressure liquid hydrogen is supercritical rather than a sharp first-order liquid-liquid transition over the range studied.
items.people: Bingqing Cheng, Guglielmo Mazzola, Chris J. Pickard, Michele Ceriotti

items.claim: Pablo G. Debenedetti, Francesco Sciortino and Gul H. Zerze presented computational evidence for a second, liquid-liquid critical point in deeply supercooled water in the TIP4P/2005 and TIP4P/Ice models, using histogram reweighting and large-system scattering calculations, with critical behaviour consistent with the three-dimensional Ising universality class.
items.people: Pablo G. Debenedetti, Francesco Sciortino, Gül H. Zerze

items.claim: Thomas E. Gartner III, Linfeng Zhang, Pablo M. Piaggi, Roberto Car, Athanassios Z. Panagiotopoulos and Pablo G. Debenedetti found signatures of a metastable liquid-liquid transition, with coexisting high-density and low-density liquid phases, in an ab initio deep neural network model of water trained on SCAN DFT data.
items.people: Thomas E. Gartner III, Linfeng Zhang, Pablo M. Piaggi, Roberto Car, Athanassios Z. Panagiotopoulos, Pablo G. Debenedetti
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 117, 26040-26046

items.claim: Pablo M. Piaggi, Jack Weis, Athanassios Z. Panagiotopoulos, Pablo G. Debenedetti and Roberto Car computed homogeneous ice nucleation rates at atmospheric pressure across a broad range of supercoolings using the seeding technique with a machine-learning model trained on DFT energies and forces, running systems of up to hundreds of thousands of atoms at ab initio accuracy.
items.people: Pablo M. Piaggi, Jack Weis, Athanassios Z. Panagiotopoulos, Pablo G. Debenedetti, Roberto Car
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 119, e2207294119

items.claim: Pablo M. Piaggi, Athanassios Z. Panagiotopoulos, Pablo G. Debenedetti and Roberto Car determined the phase equilibrium between liquid water and both hexagonal ice Ih and cubic ice Ic using a machine-learning potential trained on the SCAN functional, quantifying the small free-energy difference between the two ice polymorphs.
items.people: Pablo M. Piaggi, Athanassios Z. Panagiotopoulos, Pablo G. Debenedetti, Roberto Car
items.venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation 17, 3065-3077

items.claim: Sigbjorn Loland Bore and Francesco Paesani combined the MB-pol data-driven many-body water potential with enhanced-sampling algorithms to compute water's phase diagram, obtaining close agreement with experiment for the stability fields of the ice polymorphs.
items.people: Sigbjørn Løland Bore, Francesco Paesani
items.affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of California, San Diego

items.claim: Simon Batzner, Albert Musaelian, Lixin Sun, Mario Geiger, Jonathan P. Mailoa, Mordechai Kornbluth, Nicola Molinari, Tess E. Smidt and Boris Kozinsky introduced NequIP, an E(3)-equivariant graph neural network interatomic potential that matches or exceeds prior models while using up to three orders of magnitude less training data.
items.people: Simon Batzner, Albert Musaelian, Lixin Sun, Mario Geiger, Jonathan P. Mailoa, Mordechai Kornbluth, Nicola Molinari, Tess E. Smidt, Boris Kozinsky

items.claim: Albert Musaelian, Simon Batzner, Anders Johansson, Lixin Sun, Cameron J. Owen, Mordechai Kornbluth and Boris Kozinsky introduced Allegro, a strictly local equivariant deep neural network potential that represents many-body interactions through iterated tensor products of learned equivariant features without atom-centred message passing, enabling accurate simulations at very large scale.
items.people: Albert Musaelian, Simon Batzner, Anders Johansson, Lixin Sun, Cameron J. Owen, Mordechai Kornbluth, Boris Kozinsky

items.claim: Ilyes Batatia, David Peter Kovacs, Gregor N. C. Simm, Christoph Ortner and Gabor Csanyi introduced MACE, an equivariant message-passing architecture that carries higher body-order messages, overcoming the two-body limitation of conventional message-passing networks and yielding fast, accurate force fields.
items.people: Ilyes Batatia, Dávid Péter Kovács, Gregor N. C. Simm, Christoph Ortner, Gábor Csányi
items.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2022; arXiv:2206.07697

items.claim: Ilyes Batatia and a large collaboration released MACE-MP-0, a single general-purpose MACE model trained on roughly 150,000 inorganic crystal structures from the Materials Project, which runs stable molecular dynamics across solids, liquids, gases, reactions and interfaces out of the box and can be fine-tuned on a handful of application-specific points.
items.people: Ilyes Batatia, Philipp Benner, Yuan Chiang, Alin M. Elena, Dávid P. Kovács, Janosh Riebesell, Xavier R. Advincula, Mark Asta, Matthew Avaylon, William J. Baldwin, Fabian Berger, Noam Bernstein, Arghya Bhowmik, Filippo Bigi, Samuel M. Blau, and others

items.claim: Alessandro Laio and Michele Parrinello introduced metadynamics, a coarse-grained non-Markovian dynamics in which a history-dependent bias potential progressively fills the free-energy minima of selected collective variables, allowing escape from metastable states and reconstruction of multidimensional free-energy surfaces — the enabling technique for simulating nucleation as a rare event.
items.people: Alessandro Laio, Michele Parrinello
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 99, 12562-12566

items.claim: Alessandro Barducci, Giovanni Bussi and Michele Parrinello introduced well-tempered metadynamics, in which the deposited bias is rescaled so that the history-dependent potential converges smoothly to a tunable fraction of the free energy rather than diffusing indefinitely.
items.people: Alessandro Barducci, Giovanni Bussi, Michele Parrinello

items.claim: Pablo M. Piaggi, Omar Valsson and Michele Parrinello showed that enhancing fluctuations of entropy and enthalpy — used as collective variables — drives crystallization in atomistic simulations, providing a general order parameter pair for first-order freezing transitions.
items.people: Pablo M. Piaggi, Omar Valsson, Michele Parrinello

items.claim: Pablo M. Piaggi and Michele Parrinello introduced multithermal-multibaric molecular simulations derived from a variational principle, in which a single simulation samples uniformly in energy and volume across a chosen region of the temperature-pressure plane, so that static properties and phase boundaries can be extracted for the whole region at once.
items.people: Pablo M. Piaggi, Michele Parrinello

items.claim: Michele Invernizzi, Pablo M. Piaggi and Michele Parrinello presented a unified approach to enhanced sampling — the on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling (OPES) framework — that reformulates metadynamics-style and generalized-ensemble methods as targeted probability-distribution reweighting.
items.people: Michele Invernizzi, Pablo M. Piaggi, Michele Parrinello

items.claim: Luigi Bonati and Michele Parrinello trained a deep neural network potential on SCAN-functional data, seeded by metadynamics sampling with a classical potential, and used a collective variable derived from the Debye structure factor to drive silicon crystallization, recovering the free-energy surface at DFT accuracy and probing the early stages of nucleation in a material whose liquid is metallic and whose solid is semiconducting.
items.people: Luigi Bonati, Michele Parrinello

items.claim: Haiyang Niu, Luigi Bonati, Pablo M. Piaggi and Michele Parrinello trained a neural network potential on DFT data drawn from multithermal-multibaric simulations to compute the ab initio phase diagram of gallium, reproducing the equilibria among liquid Ga, alpha-Ga, beta-Ga and Ga-II, and showed that formation of the metastable beta-Ga phase is kinetically favoured over the thermodynamically stable alpha-Ga.
items.people: Haiyang Niu, Luigi Bonati, Pablo M. Piaggi, Michele Parrinello

items.claim: Haiyang Niu, Pablo M. Piaggi, Michele Invernizzi and Michele Parrinello simulated the crystallization of liquid silica with enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics, resolving the nucleation pathway of a network-forming glass former.
items.people: Haiyang Niu, Pablo M. Piaggi, Michele Invernizzi, Michele Parrinello
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115, 5348-5352

items.claim: Gabriele C. Sosso, Giacomo Miceli, Sebastiano Caravati, Joerg Behler and Marco Bernasconi built the first neural network interatomic potential for the phase-change memory material GeTe, reproducing DFT-quality descriptions of the liquid, crystalline and amorphous phases and opening large-scale simulation of technologically relevant crystallization.
items.people: Gabriele C. Sosso, Giacomo Miceli, Sebastiano Caravati, Jörg Behler, Marco Bernasconi

items.claim: Gabriele C. Sosso, Giacomo Miceli, Sebastiano Caravati, Federico Giberti, Joerg Behler and Marco Bernasconi used the neural network potential to run large-scale molecular dynamics of GeTe crystallization, quantifying the fast crystal growth that underlies phase-change memory operation.
items.people: Gabriele C. Sosso, Giacomo Miceli, Sebastiano Caravati, Federico Giberti, Jörg Behler, Marco Bernasconi
items.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters 4, 4241-4246

items.claim: Omar Abou El Kheir, Luigi Bonati, Michele Parrinello and Marco Bernasconi fitted a deep neural network potential to a large DFT database for Ge2Sb2Te5 and ran molecular dynamics on systems of over 10,000 atoms for more than 100 ns to resolve the crystallization kinetics of the compound across the range of temperatures relevant to memory devices.
items.people: Omar Abou El Kheir, Luigi Bonati, Michele Parrinello, Marco Bernasconi

items.claim: Volker L. Deringer, Noam Bernstein, Gabor Csanyi, Chiheb Ben Mahmoud, Michele Ceriotti, Mark Wilson, David A. Drabold and Stephen R. Elliott used a machine-learning potential to simulate transitions between disordered phases of silicon, predicting their electronic fingerprints and showing that pressure-induced crystallization of amorphous silicon proceeds through three distinct stages.
items.people: Volker L. Deringer, Noam Bernstein, Gábor Csányi, Chiheb Ben Mahmoud, Michele Ceriotti, Mark Wilson, David A. Drabold, Stephen R. Elliott

openQuestions: Does liquid water genuinely possess a second (liquid-liquid) critical point, or is the apparent transition an artefact of the finite-size, finite-time, and force-field choices used? Classical models (TIP4P/2005, TIP4P/Ice), ab initio deep neural network models, and MB-pol give broadly consistent signatures, but the experimental region remains inaccessible because crystallization intervenes.

How much of the residual disagreement between ML-computed and experimental phase diagrams is attributable to the underlying exchange-correlation functional (SCAN, hybrid functionals) rather than to the machine-learning fit? The deep-potential water phase diagram misplaces ices III and XV, and hybrid-functional diagrams degrade above roughly 8000 bar.

Nucleation rates computed by seeding depend on classical nucleation theory assumptions and on the choice of order parameter used to define cluster size. How large is the systematic error this introduces, and can rates be obtained without invoking classical nucleation theory at ab initio accuracy?

The supercritical interpretation of the molecular-to-atomic transition in dense liquid hydrogen has been contested in the subsequent literature. Resolving whether the transition is first-order requires disentangling ML-potential extrapolation error, nuclear quantum effects, and the accuracy of the underlying electronic structure method at extreme pressure.

Can universal foundation potentials such as MACE-MP-0 predict melting points and phase boundaries without system-specific fine-tuning? Training sets built from near-equilibrium crystal structures may systematically under-represent liquid and interfacial configurations, which are exactly what a first-order transition requires.

Nuclear quantum effects shift melting points and nucleation barriers appreciably in light-element systems, yet path-integral simulation multiplies cost. What is the cheapest treatment that preserves the accuracy of a first-order transition prediction?

Interfacial free energy between solid and liquid is the quantity that controls the nucleation barrier, and it is far more sensitive to potential quality than bulk free-energy differences. How well do current MLIPs reproduce it, and is anisotropy of the interfacial free energy captured?

Heterogeneous nucleation — on surfaces, impurities and pre-existing nuclei — dominates in nature but has been studied far less with MLIPs than homogeneous nucleation, in part because it requires accurate description of chemically distinct interfaces that are poorly represented in existing training sets.

verdicts.correction: The citation (authors, order, year, venue, article number, DOI) is correct, but the claim misattributes the introduction of OPES. The PRX paper's own abstract states that it adapts 'the recently developed on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling method [Invernizzi and Parrinello, J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 11.7 (2020)], which was originally introduced for metadynamics-like sampling.' Accurate replacement text: 'Michele Invernizzi, Pablo M. Piaggi and Michele Parrinello presented a unified perspective on enhanced sampling, focusing on the target probability distribution rather than the bias potential, and introduced a class of collective-variable-based bias potentials able to sample any expanded ensemble normally reached by replica exchange (OPES-expanded). Their practical implementation adapts the on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling (OPES) method, which had been introduced earlier that year by Michele Invernizzi and Michele Parrinello, "Rethinking Metadynamics: From Bias Potentials to Probability Distributions", Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters 11, 2731-2736 (2020).' URL for the PRX paper: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.10.041034 ; URL for the paper that actually introduced OPES: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.0c00497

verdicts.correction: Two defects. (1) The training-set figure is garbled: MACE-MP-0 was trained on the Materials Project Trajectory (MPtrj) dataset, which contains 1,580,395 DFT structures drawn from roughly 146,000 inorganic materials covering 89 elements. The ~150,000 figure is the number of MATERIALS, not structures; the number of training structures is ~1.6 million (an order of magnitude larger). The paper's own abstract says only 'a public dataset of moderate size' and gives no such count. (2) The work is no longer preprint-only. Accurate replacement text: 'Ilyes Batatia and a large collaboration released MACE-MP-0, a single general-purpose MACE model trained on the Materials Project Trajectory (MPtrj) dataset — about 1.6 million DFT structures drawn from roughly 146,000 inorganic materials — which runs stable molecular dynamics across solids, liquids, gases, chemical reactions and interfaces out of the box and can be fine-tuned on a handful of application-specific data points to reach ab initio accuracy.' Its abstract explicitly states that it provides a practical implementation 'by properly adapting the iterative scheme of the recently developed on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling method [Invernizzi and Parrinello, J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 11.7 (2020)], which was originally introduced for metadynamics-like sampling.' Accurate replacement text: 'Michele Invernizzi, Pablo M. Piaggi and Michele Parrinello presented a unified approach to enhanced sampling, recasting collective-variable bias methods (umbrella sampling, metadynamics) and tempering/expanded-ensemble methods such as replica exchange within one perspective focused on the target probability distribution, and implemented it by adapting the iterative scheme of the on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling (OPES) method.' Cite as: Michele Invernizzi, Pablo M. Piaggi, Michele Parrinello, 'Unified Approach to Enhanced Sampling', Physical Review X 10, 041034 (2020), https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.10.041034. OPES itself must be credited to: Michele Invernizzi and Michele Parrinello, 'Rethinking Metadynamics: From Bias Potentials to Probability Distributions', Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters 11, 2731-2736 (2020), https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.0c00497

verdicts.claim: Bonati & Parrinello (2018) trained a deep NN potential on SCAN data seeded by metadynamics with a classical potential, used a Debye-structure-factor collective variable to drive silicon crystallization, recovered the free-energy surface at DFT accuracy and probed early nucleation. PRL 121, 265701.

Niu, Bonati, Piaggi & Parrinello (2020) computed the ab initio phase diagram of gallium (liquid, alpha-Ga, beta-Ga, Ga-II) and showed metastable beta-Ga is kinetically favoured over alpha-Ga. Nature Communications 11, 2654.
Niu, Piaggi, Invernizzi & Parrinello (2018) simulated liquid silica crystallization with enhanced-sampling MD, resolving the nucleation pathway of a network-forming glass former. PNAS 115, 5348-5352.
Sosso, Miceli, Caravati, Behler & Bernasconi (2012) built the first neural network interatomic potential for GeTe, reproducing liquid, crystalline and amorphous phases. Physical Review B 85, 174103.

Sosso, Miceli, Caravati, Giberti, Behler & Bernasconi (2013) ran large-scale MD of GeTe crystallization, quantifying the fast crystal growth underlying phase-change memory. J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 4, 4241-4246.

Abou El Kheir, Bonati, Parrinello & Bernasconi (2024) fitted a deep NN potential to a large DFT database for Ge2Sb2Te5 and ran MD on >10,000 atoms for >100 ns to resolve crystallization kinetics. npj Computational Materials 10, 33; arXiv:2304.03109.

Deringer, Bernstein, Csányi, Ben Mahmoud, Ceriotti, Wilson, Drabold & Elliott (2021) simulated transitions between disordered silicon phases, predicted electronic fingerprints, and showed pressure-induced crystallization of amorphous silicon proceeds through three distinct stages. Nature 589, 59-64.

ml-phase-detection.domain: Supervised and unsupervised machine learning for identifying phases of matter
ml-phase-detection.summary: Between 2016 and 2019 condensed-matter physics acquired a new instrument: the pattern-recognition machinery of modern machine learning, pointed not at photographs but at Monte Carlo spin configurations, entanglement spectra, and experimental images. The founding move was supervised: Juan Carrasquilla and Roger G. Melko trained an ordinary feed-forward network on labelled Ising configurations and showed it recovered the critical temperature, then pushed the same architecture into Coulomb phases and the toric code, where no local order parameter exists. Almost simultaneously Evert P. L. van Nieuwenburg, Ye-Hua Liu and Sebastian D. Huber removed the need for labels with the "confusion" scheme, deliberately mislabelling data and reading the transition off a characteristic W-shaped performance curve. On the unsupervised side Lei Wang showed that plain principal component analysis of raw spin configurations reproduces the Ising order parameter, and Sebastian J. Wetzel extended the comparison through autoencoders and variational autoencoders. The field then split along two axes. One axis pushed toward harder physics: fermionic Hubbard models, sign-problematic simulations, many-body localization, Kosterlitz-Thouless vortices, Z2 spin liquids via quantum loop topography, and finally real laboratory data from quantum gas microscopes and ultracold-atom Floquet systems. The other axis pushed toward interpretability and rigour, because a network that classifies correctly may be reading the wrong feature: support vector machines with tensorial kernels that emit explicit order-parameter polynomials, kernel methods that reproduce Hamiltonian constraints, diffusion maps for topological order, anomaly detection for phases nobody labelled, and analytical predictors that replace the network entirely. Sceptical work — critical examinations of PCA, demonstrations that feature engineering rather than the network was doing the work — is as much a part of the record as the successes.

items.claim: Juan Carrasquilla and Roger G. Melko demonstrated that a standard feed-forward neural network, trained by supervised learning on raw Monte Carlo spin configurations of the two-dimensional square-lattice Ising model, can classify the ordered and disordered phases and locate the critical temperature without being given the Hamiltonian or any order parameter; a convolutional variant also distinguished the topological phase of the square-lattice Ising gauge theory, which has no conventional local order parameter.
items.people: Juan Carrasquilla, Roger G. Melko
items.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, Waterloo (Carrasquilla); Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo, and Perimeter Institute (Melko)
items.year: 2017 (Nature Physics); arXiv preprint posted 5 May 2016 as arXiv:1605.01735

items.claim: Evert P. L. van Nieuwenburg, Ye-Hua Liu and Sebastian D. Huber introduced the "learning by confusion" scheme, in which a neural network is trained repeatedly on data deliberately labelled with a proposed but generally wrong transition point; plotting classification accuracy against the proposed point yields a characteristic W shape whose central peak marks the true transition. The method was demonstrated on the topological transition of the Kitaev chain, the thermal transition of the classical Ising model, and the many-body-localization transition of a disordered quantum spin chain.
items.people: Evert P. L. van Nieuwenburg, Ye-Hua Liu, Sebastian D. Huber
items.affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zurich
items.year: 2017 (Nature Physics); arXiv preprint posted 6 October 2016 as arXiv:1610.02048

items.claim: Lei Wang showed that purely unsupervised learning identifies phases and phase transitions: principal component analysis applied to raw Ising spin configurations extracts a leading principal component proportional to the magnetization, and clustering in the low-dimensional feature space separates the phases, with further components carrying structure-factor information.
items.people: Lei Wang
items.affiliation: Beijing National Lab for Condensed Matter Physics and Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing
items.year: 2016 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted 1 June 2016 as arXiv:1606.00318

items.claim: Sebastian J. Wetzel systematically compared unsupervised methods — principal component analysis, manifold learning, clustering, and artificial-neural-network variational autoencoders — on Monte Carlo configurations of the two-dimensional Ising model and the three-dimensional XY model, finding that PCA and variational autoencoders recover latent variables corresponding to the known order parameters, and that the VAE reconstruction loss itself serves as a general-purpose indicator of a phase transition.
items.people: Sebastian J. Wetzel
items.affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik, Universität Heidelberg
items.year: 2017 (Physical Review E); arXiv preprint posted 7 March 2017 as arXiv:1703.02435

items.claim: Sebastian J. Wetzel and Manuel Scherzer addressed the interpretability problem by reconstructing the decision function of a trained neural network as an explicit simple function of its inputs when that decision function is sufficiently symmetric, thereby reading off the order parameter the network had implicitly discovered — demonstrated for the Ising model and for SU(2) lattice gauge theory.
items.people: Sebastian J. Wetzel, Manuel Scherzer
items.affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik, Universität Heidelberg
items.year: 2017 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted May 2017 as arXiv:1705.05582

items.claim: Kelvin Ch'ng, Juan Carrasquilla, Roger G. Melko and Ehsan Khatami trained a three-dimensional convolutional neural network on auxiliary-field configurations generated by determinant quantum Monte Carlo for the fermionic Hubbard model on a cubic lattice, and correctly predicted the finite-temperature antiferromagnetic phase diagram at half filling, extending the supervised approach from classical spins to strongly correlated fermions.
items.people: Kelvin Ch'ng, Juan Carrasquilla, Roger G. Melko, Ehsan Khatami
items.affiliation: San José State University (Ch'ng, Khatami); Perimeter Institute and University of Waterloo (Carrasquilla, Melko)
items.year: 2017 (Physical Review X); arXiv preprint posted 8 September 2016 as arXiv:1609.02552

items.claim: Peter Broecker, Juan Carrasquilla, Roger G. Melko and Simon Trebst showed that machine-learning classification of quantum Monte Carlo configurations remains effective for interacting fermion models afflicted by the sign problem, where conventional observables become statistically inaccessible.
items.people: Peter Broecker, Juan Carrasquilla, Roger G. Melko, Simon Trebst

items.claim: Yi Zhang and Eun-Ah Kim introduced quantum loop topography (QLT), a feature-engineering procedure that converts a many-body Hamiltonian or wave function into a multi-dimensional image by evaluating two-point operators forming closed loops at independent Monte Carlo steps, guided by the relevant response function (Hall conductivity). Fed to a fully connected network with a single hidden layer, QLT distinguished Chern insulators and fractional Chern insulators from trivial insulators, producing what the authors describe as the first machine-learned phase diagram containing a topological quantum phase transition.
items.people: Yi Zhang, Eun-Ah Kim
items.affiliation: Department of Physics, Cornell University, Ithaca, and Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics, University of California, Santa Barbara
items.year: 2017 (Physical Review Letters); arXiv preprint posted 4 November 2016 as arXiv:1611.01518

items.claim: Yi Zhang, Roger G. Melko and Eun-Ah Kim extended quantum loop topography to quasiparticle statistics, constructing loop observables sensitive to the mutual statistics of spinons and visons, and used a feed-forward network to locate the phase boundary between a Z2 quantum spin liquid and trivial phases without evaluating Wilson loops or topological entanglement entropy.
items.people: Yi Zhang, Roger G. Melko, Eun-Ah Kim
items.year: 2017 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted May 2017 as arXiv:1705.01947

items.claim: Joaquin F. Rodriguez-Nieva and Mathias S. Scheurer used diffusion maps — a nonlinear unsupervised manifold-learning technique — on bare spin configurations to cluster samples of the two-dimensional XY model by winding number and to capture the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, and applied the same method to the Ising gauge theory, achieving detection of topological order without manual feature engineering or labels.
items.people: Joaquin F. Rodriguez-Nieva, Mathias S. Scheurer
items.year: 2019 (Nature Physics); arXiv preprint posted 15 May 2018 as arXiv:1805.05961

items.claim: Jonas Greitemann, Ke Liu and Lode Pollet combined the theory of orientational tensors with support vector machines using a tensorial kernel (TK-SVM), producing a machine-learning method whose decision function is directly interpretable as an explicit multipolar order parameter, and used it to detect hidden multipolar (nematic) spin order.
items.people: Jonas Greitemann, Ke Liu, Lode Pollet
items.year: 2019 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted 23 April 2018 as arXiv:1804.08557

items.claim: Jonas Greitemann, Ke Liu, Ludovic D. C. Jaubert, Han Yan, Nic Shannon and Lode Pollet applied tensorial kernel support vector machines to frustrated magnets and showed the method identifies not only hidden order parameters but also the emergent local constraints (ground-state "ice rules") that characterize classical spin liquids.
items.people: Jonas Greitemann, Ke Liu, Ludovic D. C. Jaubert, Han Yan, Nic Shannon, Lode Pollet
items.year: 2019 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted 29 July 2019

items.claim: Pedro Ponte and Roger G. Melko showed that support vector machines can learn the explicit mathematical form of physical discriminators — order parameters and Hamiltonian constraints — for two-dimensional spin models including the ferromagnetic Ising model, a conserved-order-parameter Ising model, and the Ising gauge theory, making the learned classifier human-readable rather than a black box.
items.people: Pedro Ponte, Roger G. Melko
items.affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo, and Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics
items.year: 2017 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted 19 April 2017 as arXiv:1704.05848

items.claim: Wenjian Hu, Rajiv R. P. Singh and Richard T. Scalettar carried out a critical examination of unsupervised phase detection, applying principal component analysis and autoencoders to the square- and triangular-lattice Ising models, the Blume-Capel model, a highly degenerate biquadratic-exchange spin-one Ising model, and the two-dimensional XY model, and showing which transitions and crossovers PCA can and cannot distinguish.
items.people: Wenjian Hu, Rajiv R. P. Singh, Richard T. Scalettar
items.affiliation: University of California, Davis
items.year: 2017 (Physical Review E); arXiv preprint posted 1 April 2017 as arXiv:1704.00080

items.claim: Ce Wang and Hui Zhai applied principal component analysis to Monte Carlo configurations of the frustrated XY model on triangular and union-jack lattices, systems with two distinct order parameters and two transitions, and found the leading principal components track both orders and locate both transitions without human input.
items.people: Ce Wang, Hui Zhai
items.year: 2017 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted June 2017 as arXiv:1706.07977

items.claim: Matthew J. S. Beach, Anna Golubeva and Roger G. Melko examined whether neural networks classifying the two-dimensional XY model actually learn vortices, and found that substantial feature engineering of the raw spin states is required before that claim can be made: a single-layer network fails to classify the phases, a convolutional network succeeds, and a purpose-designed deep network can learn vortices without feature engineering. The work is a cautionary counterpoint to naive interpretations of supervised phase classification.
items.people: Matthew J. S. Beach, Anna Golubeva, Roger G. Melko
items.year: 2018 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted 26 October 2017 as arXiv:1710.09842

items.claim: Frank Schindler, Nicolas Regnault and Titus Neupert trained a multilayer perceptron with a single hidden layer on entanglement spectra of individual eigenstates of the random-field Heisenberg spin-1/2 chain, using labelled data from the deeply localized and deeply thermal regimes, and used it to locate the many-body-localization transition.
items.people: Frank Schindler, Nicolas Regnault, Titus Neupert
items.year: 2017 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted 5 April 2017 as arXiv:1704.01578

items.claim: Jordan Venderley, Vedika Khemani and Eun-Ah Kim showed that a single feed-forward network fed entanglement spectra from individual eigenstates can decode two distinct many-body-localized phases and a thermalizing phase, and that the network-based diagnostic gives a sharper phase boundary than entanglement entropy alone.
items.people: Jordan Venderley, Vedika Khemani, Eun-Ah Kim
items.year: 2018 (Physical Review Letters); arXiv preprint posted 31 October 2017 as arXiv:1711.00020

items.claim: Patrick Huembeli, Alexandre Dauphin and Peter Wittek applied adversarial domain adaptation — training on a known region of parameter space and adapting to unlabelled data elsewhere — to derive phase diagrams directly from ground states without ad hoc feature engineering, demonstrating it on the Ising model at finite temperature, the Bose-Hubbard model, and the disordered Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model.
items.people: Patrick Huembeli, Alexandre Dauphin, Peter Wittek
items.year: 2018 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted 23 October 2017 as arXiv:1710.08382

items.claim: Patrick Huembeli, Alexandre Dauphin, Peter Wittek and Christian Gogolin used interpretability tools on networks trained to detect the many-body-localization transition in order to extract the characteristic features the network relies on, automating the discovery of transition signatures rather than only the transition location.
items.people: Patrick Huembeli, Alexandre Dauphin, Peter Wittek, Christian Gogolin
items.year: 2019 (Physical Review B); arXiv preprint posted 1 June 2018 as arXiv:1806.00419

items.claim: Ye-Hua Liu and Evert P. L. van Nieuwenburg introduced discriminative cooperative networks (DCN), a pair of networks — a guesser that proposes labels and a learner that is trained on them — that cooperate to detect phase transitions from fully unlabelled data, generalizing the earlier confusion scheme.
items.people: Ye-Hua Liu, Evert P. L. van Nieuwenburg
items.year: 2018 (Physical Review Letters); arXiv preprint posted 25 June 2017 as arXiv:1706.08111

items.claim: Korbinian Kottmann, Patrick Huembeli, Maciej Lewenstein and Antonio Acín reframed unsupervised phase discovery as deep anomaly detection: a network trained to recognize data from one known region flags anomalous regions as candidate new phases. They mapped the phase diagram of the one-dimensional extended Bose-Hubbard model at integer filling using entanglement spectra, tensor-network central tensors, and experimentally accessible low-order correlation functions.
items.people: Korbinian Kottmann, Patrick Huembeli, Maciej Lewenstein, Antonio Acín
items.affiliation: ICFO - Institut de Ciencies Fotoniques, The Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology, Castelldefels (Barcelona)
items.year: 2020 (Physical Review Letters); arXiv preprint posted 22 March 2020 as arXiv:2003.09905

items.claim: Benno S. Rem, Niklas Käming, Matthias Tarnowski, Luca Asteria, Nick Fläschner, Christoph Becker, Klaus Sengstock and Christof Weitenberg applied neural networks directly to experimental ultracold-atom data, extracting the topological phase diagram of the Haldane model from raw density images and characterizing the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition — moving machine-learned phase identification from simulated configurations to laboratory measurements.
items.people: Benno S. Rem, Niklas Käming, Matthias Tarnowski, Luca Asteria, Nick Fläschner, Christoph Becker, Klaus Sengstock, Christof Weitenberg
items.affiliation: Institut für Laserphysik / Institute for Quantum Physics, Universität Hamburg
items.year: 2019 (Nature Physics); arXiv preprint posted 14 September 2018 as arXiv:1809.05519

items.claim: Annabelle Bohrdt, Christie S. Chiu, Geoffrey Ji, Muqing Xu, Daniel Greif, Markus Greiner, Eugene Demler, Fabian Grusdt and Michael Knap used machine learning to classify quantum-gas-microscope snapshots of the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model against two competing theories — a doped resonating-valence-bond spin liquid and geometric string theory with hidden spin order — and found that up to intermediate doping the classifier assigns experimental snapshots to the geometric-string description.
items.people: Annabelle Bohrdt, Christie S. Chiu, Geoffrey Ji, Muqing Xu, Daniel Greif, Markus Greiner, Eugene Demler, Fabian Grusdt, Michael Knap
items.year: 2019 (Nature Physics); arXiv preprint posted 29 November 2018 as arXiv:1811.12425

items.claim: Niklas Käming, Anna Dawid, Korbinian Kottmann, Maciej Lewenstein, Klaus Sengstock, Alexandre Dauphin and Christof Weitenberg combined anomaly detection with influence functions to map the topological phase diagram of the Haldane model from noisy finite-temperature experimental data in a fully unbiased way, without prior knowledge of an order parameter, and extended the approach to Floquet systems.
items.people: Niklas Käming, Anna Dawid, Korbinian Kottmann, Maciej Lewenstein, Klaus Sengstock, Alexandre Dauphin, Christof Weitenberg
items.year: 2021 (Machine Learning: Science and Technology); arXiv preprint posted January 2021 as arXiv:2101.05712

items.claim: Mathias S. Scheurer and Robert-Jan Slager devised an unsupervised algorithm that searches for adiabatic deformation paths between Hamiltonians and clusters them by topological equivalence class, giving a parametrization-independent, symmetry-class-agnostic route to band topology.
items.people: Mathias S. Scheurer, Robert-Jan Slager
items.year: 2020 (Physical Review Letters); arXiv preprint posted 6 January 2020 as arXiv:2001.01711

items.claim: Julian Arnold and Frank Schäfer derived the optimal analytical predictors that neural-network-based phase-detection schemes — including the confusion scheme and learning-by-prediction — converge to in the infinite-capacity limit, showing that in many benchmark cases the network can be replaced outright by a closed-form expression, which both speeds up detection and clarifies what these methods actually measure.
items.people: Julian Arnold, Frank Schäfer
items.year: 2022 (Physical Review X); arXiv preprint posted 14 February 2022

items.claim: Tomoki Ohtsuki and Tomi Ohtsuki applied deep convolutional neural networks to wave-function images of random two-dimensional electron systems and estimated the critical exponents and phase boundaries of the Anderson and quantum Hall transitions, one of the earliest deep-learning treatments of a disorder-driven quantum phase transition.
items.people: Tomoki Ohtsuki, Tomi Ohtsuki
items.venue: Journal of the Physical Society of Japan 85, 123706

items.claim: Giuseppe Carleo, Ignacio Cirac, Kyle Cranmer, Laurent Daudet, Maria Schuld, Naftali Tishby, Leslie Vogt-Maranto and Lenka Zdeborová wrote the standard review of the machine-learning/physics interface, covering statistical physics of learning, applications across particle physics, cosmology, many-body quantum matter, quantum computing and chemistry, and the cross-fertilization between the two fields; its many-body section is the canonical survey of phase-classification work.
items.people: Giuseppe Carleo, Ignacio Cirac, Kyle Cranmer, Laurent Daudet, Maria Schuld, Naftali Tishby, Leslie Vogt-Maranto, Lenka Zdeborová

items.claim: Juan Carrasquilla wrote a dedicated review of machine learning for quantum matter, covering algorithms that recognize conventional and topological states in both synthetic and experimental datasets, neural-network representations of quantum states, and applications to simulating and controlling quantum systems.
items.people: Juan Carrasquilla

openQuestions: The brief refers to a Nature Physics 2019 "Machine learning phases of matter" landscape article. I could not confirm that such an article exists. "Machine learning phases of matter" is the 2017 Carrasquilla-Melko paper (Nature Physics 13, 431). What Nature Physics volume 15 (2019) does contain is a cluster of machine-learning phase-identification papers — Rodriguez-Nieva & Scheurer (p. 790), Rem et al. (p. 917), Bohrdt et al. (p. 921) — and the accompanying editorial or News & Views could not be verified because nature.com redirects to an authentication endpoint. This citation should be checked against the physical issue before it goes into a book.

Institutional affiliations at time of publication were verified from title pages only for Carrasquilla & Melko, van Nieuwenburg/Liu/Huber, Lei Wang, and Zhang & Kim; several other entries carry an empty affiliation field rather than an unverified guess. If affiliations matter for the manuscript, each remaining title page should be pulled directly.

Exact page ranges are confirmed for most journal entries but not all: Rem et al. is cited here as Nature Physics 15, 917 (the arXiv journal-ref gives only the first page; one secondary source said 917-922, another 917-920). Verify against the publisher record.

The web-search budget for this session was exhausted partway through, so some worthwhile items were verified only through the arXiv API rather than cross-checked against a second independent source. Candidates researched but deliberately omitted from the item list — and worth adding if the chapter needs more breadth — include Torlai & Melko, Phys. Rev. B 94, 165134 (2016); Deng, Li & Das Sarma, Phys. Rev. B 96, 195145 (2017); van Nieuwenburg, Bairey & Refael, Phys. Rev. B 98, 060301 (2018); and Zhang, Mesaros, Fujita, Edkins, Hamidian, Ch'ng, Eisaki, Uchida, Davis, Khatami & Kim on electronic-quantum-matter imaging, Nature 570 (2019), DOI 10.1038/s41586-019-1319-8 (page numbers unverified).

A genuine open scientific question in this literature: when a supervised network classifies phases correctly, what feature is it actually using? Beach, Golubeva & Melko show that for the XY model the answer is often "whatever the human put into the feature engineering," and Arnold & Schäfer show that several unsupervised schemes reduce to closed-form estimators. How much of the field's apparent discovery power is genuine discovery versus rediscovery of built-in structure remains contested.

Whether machine-learned phase boundaries can deliver quantitatively reliable critical exponents and finite-size scaling — as opposed to approximate transition locations — is still unsettled; Ohtsuki & Ohtsuki attempted exponents directly, but the general reliability of the approach for critical phenomena is not established.

Reproducibility of the topological-order results (quantum loop topography, diffusion maps) on models beyond the handful of benchmark Hamiltonians used in the original papers is not comprehensively documented in the sources reviewed here.

collective-variables.domain: Machine learning of collective variables, reaction coordinates, and free energy landscapes for rare, discontinuous transitions
collective-variables.summary:
Molecular dynamics resolves atomic motion at femtosecond scale, but the transitions that matter — nucleation, melting, folding, unbinding, chemical reaction — are rare events separated by free energy barriers many times the thermal energy. Brute-force simulation almost never crosses them. Two broad families of remedies emerged. The first biases the dynamics along a low-dimensional collective variable: metadynamics (Alessandro Laio and Michele Parrinello, 2002), its well-tempered form, and its successor OPES, all implemented in the open-source PLUMED library. These methods work spectacularly when the collective variable is right and fail silently when it is wrong, which made the choice of variable the field's central bottleneck. The second family avoids biasing altogether by harvesting reactive trajectories: transition path sampling (Christoph Dellago, Peter Bolhuis, Félix Csajka, David Chandler, 1998), which needs no prior guess at the mechanism and defines the reaction coordinate a posteriori through the committor.

Machine learning entered at exactly this bottleneck. Time-lagged independent component analysis and Markov state models supplied a variational, data-driven definition of "slow"; VAMPnets (Andreas Mardt, Luca Pasquali, Hao Wu, Frank Noé, 2018) replaced the whole pipeline with one neural network. Parallel lines learn variables from labeled metastable states (Deep-LDA, Deep-TDA), from biased trajectories reweighted to equilibrium (Deep-TICA), from information-bottleneck objectives (RAVE, SPIB), or from spectral-gap maximization (SGOOP). A third strand bypasses dynamics entirely: Boltzmann generators (Frank Noé, Simon Olsson, Jonas Köhler, Hao Wu, 2019) train normalizing flows to draw one-shot equilibrium samples. Most recently, neural networks learn the committor itself, closing the loop between the 1998 path-sampling formulation and modern deep learning.

items.claim: Metadynamics, introduced by Alessandro Laio and Michele Parrinello in 2002, escapes free-energy minima by adding a history-dependent Gaussian bias potential along a small set of chosen collective variables, progressively filling the wells so the system is pushed over barriers it would otherwise never cross; the accumulated bias converges to the negative of the free energy surface.
items.people: Alessandro Laio, Michele Parrinello
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 99(20), 12562-12566

items.claim: Well-tempered metadynamics, introduced by Alessandro Barducci, Giovanni Bussi and Michele Parrinello in 2008, rescales the deposited Gaussian height according to the bias already accumulated, so the bias converges smoothly rather than oscillating, and a single tunable parameter controls how far up the free energy landscape the sampling is extended.
items.people: Alessandro Barducci, Giovanni Bussi, Michele Parrinello

items.claim: PLUMED 2, described by Gareth A. Tribello, Massimiliano Bonomi, Davide Branduardi, Carlo Camilloni and Giovanni Bussi in 2014, is the open-source C++ plugin library through which most enhanced-sampling methods and collective variables are applied to existing molecular dynamics engines; it is the standard vehicle by which machine-learned collective variables are deployed in production simulations.
items.people: Gareth A. Tribello, Massimiliano Bonomi, Davide Branduardi, Carlo Camilloni, Giovanni Bussi

items.claim: The PLUMED consortium's 2019 statement in Nature Methods established PLUMED-NEST, a public archive of complete input files for enhanced-sampling simulations, in direct response to the reproducibility problem created by the many free parameters of biased simulation.
items.people: The PLUMED consortium

items.claim: On-the-fly Probability Enhanced Sampling (OPES), introduced by Michele Invernizzi and Michele Parrinello in 2020, reformulates metadynamics as the direct reconstruction of a target probability distribution rather than of a bias potential, converging faster to a quasi-static bias and degrading far more gracefully when the collective variables are suboptimal or multidimensional.
items.people: Michele Invernizzi, Michele Parrinello
items.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters 11(7), 2731-2736

items.claim: Transition path sampling, introduced by Christoph Dellago, Peter G. Bolhuis, Felix S. Csajka and David Chandler in 1998, performs importance sampling in the space of dynamical trajectories rather than configurations, allowing rate constants to be computed without prior knowledge of the mechanism, the reaction coordinate, or the transition state.
items.people: Christoph Dellago, Peter G. Bolhuis, Felix S. Csajka, David Chandler

items.claim: The 2002 review by Peter G. Bolhuis, David Chandler, Christoph Dellago and Phillip L. Geissler, subtitled "throwing ropes over rough mountain passes, in the dark", set out the shooting-and-shifting Monte Carlo moves in trajectory space and the committor-based definition of the transition state ensemble that all later machine-learning work on reaction coordinates inherits.
items.people: Peter G. Bolhuis, David Chandler, Christoph Dellago, Phillip L. Geissler

items.claim: Ao Ma and Aaron R. Dinner in 2005 introduced the first automatic method for identifying reaction coordinates, combining a genetic algorithm with a neural network to select the subset of candidate coordinates that best predicts the committor from transition path sampling data - the direct ancestor of modern neural-network committor models.
items.people: Ao Ma, Aaron R. Dinner
items.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B 109(14), 6769-6779

items.claim: The 2011 paper by Jan-Hendrik Prinz, Hao Wu, Marco Sarich, Bettina Keller, Martin Senne, Martin Held, John D. Chodera, Christof Schuette and Frank Noe placed Markov state models on rigorous footing, bounding the approximation error of discretizing molecular dynamics into a transition matrix and showing that the error shrinks as the discretization resolves the slow eigenfunctions of the transfer operator.
items.people: Jan-Hendrik Prinz, Hao Wu, Marco Sarich, Bettina Keller, Martin Senne, Martin Held, John D. Chodera, Christof Schütte, Frank Noé

items.claim: Time-lagged independent component analysis was introduced to molecular kinetics in 2013 by Guillermo Perez-Hernandez, Fabian Paul, Toni Giorgino, Gianni De Fabritiis and Frank Noe as a variationally optimal linear method for finding the slowest-decorrelating order parameters, replacing intuition-based feature selection in Markov state model construction.
items.people: Guillermo Pérez-Hernández, Fabian Paul, Toni Giorgino, Gianni De Fabritiis, Frank Noé

items.claim: Christian R. Schwantes and Vijay S. Pande independently introduced time-structure based independent component analysis for Markov state model construction in 2013, and used it to reveal extensive non-native contacts in the folding of the protein NTL9.
items.people: Christian R. Schwantes, Vijay S. Pande
items.venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation 9(4), 2000-2009

items.claim: VAMPnets, introduced by Andreas Mardt, Luca Pasquali, Hao Wu and Frank Noe in 2018, replace the entire Markov state model pipeline - featurization, dimension reduction, clustering, transition matrix estimation - with a single neural network trained end-to-end on a variational score for Markov processes (VAMP), using a twin-lobe architecture that maps configurations at times t and t+tau into a soft assignment to metastable states.
items.people: Andreas Mardt, Luca Pasquali, Hao Wu, Frank Noé

items.claim: Christoph Wehmeyer and Frank Noe showed in 2018 that a time-lagged autoencoder - an encoder-decoder network trained to reconstruct the configuration at time t+tau from the configuration at time t - recovers low-dimensional embeddings capturing the slow dynamics, and analyzed how this objective relates to, and differs from, time-lagged independent component analysis.
items.people: Christoph Wehmeyer, Frank Noé

items.claim: SGOOP (Spectral Gap Optimization of Order Parameters), introduced by Pratyush Tiwary and B. J. Berne in 2016, selects a reaction coordinate by maximizing the spectral gap of the associated transfer operator - the separation between slow and fast eigenvalues - using a maximum-caliber estimate of the dynamics built from short biased trajectories.
items.people: Pratyush Tiwary, B. J. Berne
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113(11), 2839-2844

items.claim: RAVE (Reweighted Autoencoded Variational Bayes for Enhanced Sampling), introduced in 2018 by Joao Marcelo Lamim Ribeiro, Pablo Bravo, Yihang Wang and Pratyush Tiwary, alternates between training a variational autoencoder on reweighted trajectory data to learn a low-dimensional latent coordinate and running biased simulation along that coordinate, iterating until the learned variable and the free energy landscape are mutually consistent.
items.people: João Marcelo Lamim Ribeiro, Pablo Bravo, Yihang Wang, Pratyush Tiwary

items.claim: The State Predictive Information Bottleneck, introduced by Dedi Wang and Pratyush Tiwary in 2021, learns a minimal latent representation that predicts which metastable state the system will be in after a delay time; the authors showed that the learned representation is closely connected to the committor, and that tuning the delay time controls how finely metastable states are resolved.
items.people: Dedi Wang, Pratyush Tiwary

items.claim: Deep-LDA, introduced by Luigi Bonati, Valerio Rizzi and Michele Parrinello in 2020, builds a collective variable using only data from short unbiased simulations confined to the metastable basins: a neural network compresses a large set of physical descriptors, and Fisher's linear discriminant on the network output supplies the objective that maximizes separation between the states.
items.people: Luigi Bonati, Valerio Rizzi, Michele Parrinello

items.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters 11(8), 2998-3004; preprint arXiv:2002.06562

items.claim: Deep-TICA, introduced by Luigi Bonati, GiovanniMaria Piccini and Michele Parrinello in 2021, extracts transfer-operator eigenfunctions from trajectories that are already biased, reweighting them back to equilibrium statistics, so that the learned slow modes can be fed straight back into on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling; the method was demonstrated on conformational transitions, mini-protein folding, and materials crystallization.
items.people: Luigi Bonati, GiovanniMaria Piccini, Michele Parrinello

items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 118(44), e2113533118; preprint arXiv:2107.03943

items.claim: Deep-TDA, introduced by Enrico Trizio and Michele Parrinello in 2021, trains a neural network to map configurations onto a target one-dimensional distribution with pre-assigned, well-separated peaks for each metastable state, yielding a collective variable that produces a directly interpretable reaction profile from data confined to the basins.
items.people: Enrico Trizio, Michele Parrinello
items.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters 12(35), 8621-8626

items.claim: mlcolvar, released in 2023 by Luigi Bonati, Enrico Trizio, Andrea Rizzi and Michele Parrinello, is a PyTorch library that unifies the main families of machine-learned collective variables under one interface with a multi-task training framework, and exports trained models directly to PLUMED for use in biased simulation.
items.people: Luigi Bonati, Enrico Trizio, Andrea Rizzi, Michele Parrinello
items.venue: The Journal of Chemical Physics 159(1), 014801; preprint arXiv:2305.19980

items.claim: Boltzmann generators, introduced by Frank Noe, Simon Olsson, Jonas Koehler and Hao Wu in 2019, train an invertible neural network (a normalizing flow) to map a simple Gaussian latent distribution onto the Boltzmann distribution of a molecular system, so that independent equilibrium configurations - including configurations in distinct metastable states - can be drawn in one shot without simulating the transition between them, with exact reweighting correcting the residual bias.
items.people: Frank Noé, Simon Olsson, Jonas Köhler, Hao Wu

items.claim: Stochastic normalizing flows, introduced by Hao Wu, Jonas Koehler and Frank Noe in 2020, interleave deterministic invertible layers with stochastic Markov-chain sampling blocks; the authors showed that the stochastic blocks overcome the expressivity limits imposed by strict invertibility while non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (the Jarzynski/Crooks relations) still supplies exact importance weights.
items.people: Hao Wu, Jonas Köhler, Frank Noé
items.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020); preprint arXiv:2002.06707

items.claim: Qianxiao Li, Bo Lin and Weiqing Ren showed in 2019 that the committor function can be computed by training a neural network on the variational (Dirichlet-form) formulation of the backward Kolmogorov equation, with adaptive sampling supplying training points in the transition region where reactive trajectories are otherwise vanishingly rare.
items.people: Qianxiao Li, Bo Lin, Weiqing Ren
items.venue: The Journal of Chemical Physics 151(5), 054112; preprint arXiv:1906.06285

items.claim: Peilin Kang, Enrico Trizio and Michele Parrinello showed in 2024 that the committor can be computed self-consistently starting from information about the initial and final states alone: the current committor estimate is used to bias sampling toward the transition region, whose data then refine the committor, converging on the transition state ensemble without a pre-specified reaction coordinate.
items.people: Peilin Kang, Enrico Trizio, Michele Parrinello

items.claim: Hendrik Jung, Roberto Covino, A. Arjun, Christian Leitold, Christoph Dellago, Peter G. Bolhuis and Gerhard Hummer combined transition path sampling with deep learning in 2023 so that each newly shot trajectory updates a neural committor model, which in turn selects where to shoot next; symbolic regression then condenses the learned mechanism into human-readable physical observables, demonstrated on ion pairing, gas-hydrate crystal formation, polymer folding and membrane-protein assembly.
items.people: Hendrik Jung, Roberto Covino, A. Arjun, Christian Leitold, Christoph Dellago, Peter G. Bolhuis, Gerhard Hummer

items.claim: Luigi Bonati and Michele Parrinello combined a neural-network interatomic potential trained on density functional theory data with metadynamics in 2018 to simulate liquid silicon and its crystal nucleation from first principles, an early demonstration that machine-learned potentials and machine-assisted enhanced sampling can jointly reach a first-order phase transition inaccessible to either alone.
items.people: Luigi Bonati, Michele Parrinello

items.claim: The 2024 Annual Review of Physical Chemistry survey by Shams Mehdi, Zachary Smith, Lukas Herron, Ziyue Zou and Pratyush Tiwary organizes the field into three machine-learning strategies against the timescale problem - dimensionality reduction to collective variables, reinforcement-learning-style adaptive sampling, and generative flow-based direct sampling - and catalogs the open problems at their intersection.
items.people: Shams Mehdi, Zachary Smith, Lukas Herron, Ziyue Zou, Pratyush Tiwary
items.venue: Annual Review of Physical Chemistry 75, 347-370; preprint arXiv:2306.09111

openQuestions: Learned collective variables are trained on data from the basins the simulation has already visited, so they cannot represent a mechanism the sampling has never touched - how does one certify that a learned coordinate has not simply hidden an unexplored channel behind an apparently converged free energy profile?

Slowness and reactivity are not the same thing: transfer-operator eigenfunctions (TICA, VAMPnets, Deep-TICA) identify the slowest relaxing modes, while the committor identifies the coordinate that actually predicts the outcome of a transition. How far apart do these two answers drift for strongly first-order, discontinuous transitions such as nucleation?

Nucleation and other first-order transitions involve a growing cluster whose size is itself extensive and whose interface is diffuse - is a low-dimensional collective variable even the right object, or does the classical single-order-parameter picture break down in a way no neural network can repair?

Boltzmann generators demonstrably work on small systems, but the training cost and mode coverage of normalizing flows scale poorly with dimension; how far can transferable or coarse-grained flows push before exact reweighting stops rescuing the residual bias?

Neural committor methods depend on labeled endpoints - the definition of the two metastable states. For transitions where the product state is not known in advance (a new polymorph, an unexpected intermediate), the labeling that makes the method work is exactly the knowledge the simulation was meant to produce.

Reported successes are concentrated on a small set of benchmark systems (alanine dipeptide, chignolin, silicon, model potentials); the field lacks an agreed adversarial benchmark of genuinely hard discontinuous transitions on which methods can fail publicly.

Interpretability remains largely post hoc - symbolic regression on a trained network, or feature-importance analysis - rather than built into the objective, so it is difficult to know whether a learned variable encodes physics or an artifact of the descriptor set.

Lett. 121, 265701, 2018). Two overstatements: the collective variable was a hand-designed physical order parameter based on the Debye structure factor, not a machine-learned one, so 'machine-assisted enhanced sampling' misattributes the CV; and the work characterized the early stages of nucleation rather than simulating the full first-order transition. Accurate replacement text: 'Luigi Bonati and Michele Parrinello in 2018 trained a deep neural-network interatomic potential on DFT reference energies computed with the SCAN functional and combined it with metadynamics biased along a collective variable derived from the Debye structure factor. This recovered the free energy surface of silicon with DFT accuracy, gave thermodynamic properties near the melting point in good agreement with experiment, and revealed features of the nucleation mechanism in the early stages of crystallization — an early demonstration that a machine-learned potential can carry enhanced sampling to a first-order phase transition that ab initio molecular dynamics alone cannot reach.' nnqs-quantum.domain: Neural-network quantum states and quantum phase transitions
nnqs-quantum.summary: Neural-network quantum states (NQS) began as a single idea: parameterize the amplitude of a many-body wave function by a neural network and optimize it variationally, sidestepping the exponential wall of Hilbert space. Giuseppe Carleo and Matthias Troyer introduced the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) ansatz for spin systems in Science in 2017, benchmarking it on the transverse-field Ising and Heisenberg models — the transverse-field Ising chain, exactly solved by Pierre Pfeuty in 1970, remains the canonical testbed for quantum criticality. The field split quickly into two branches. In lattice spin and Hubbard physics, RBMs gave way to convolutional, group-equivariant, autoregressive, recurrent, and transformer architectures, with NetKet as the community software substrate. In quantum chemistry, PauliNet (Jan Hermann, Zeno Schätzle, Frank Noé) and FermiNet (David Pfau, James S. Spencer, Alexander G. de G. Matthews, W. M. C. Foulkes) applied deep networks directly to continuous-space electronic wave functions, later extended by Google DeepMind to excited states, while the separate DM21 functional attacked density functional theory's fractional-electron failures. The comparison baseline throughout is the density matrix renormalization group, introduced by Steven R. White in 1992, and its matrix-product-state descendants — which remain superior in one dimension and competitive in two. The 2024 V-score benchmark paper (Dian Wu, Riccardo Rossi, Filippo Vicentini, Giuseppe Carleo and a large consortium including White) is the field's first honest scorecard: it identifies where every method, NQS included, is still far from converged. In parallel, programmable quantum simulators — Rydberg arrays at Harvard/MIT (Mikhail Lukin, Markus Greiner), quantum gas microscopes, and superconducting processors at Google Quantum AI — now measure quantum phase transitions directly, providing experimental ground truth that classical variational methods must reproduce.

items.claim: Giuseppe Carleo and Matthias Troyer introduced the restricted Boltzmann machine as a variational ansatz for many-body quantum wave functions, optimizing it by stochastic reconfiguration to obtain ground states and unitary dynamics of the transverse-field Ising and antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models in one and two dimensions. The paper was first posted to arXiv (1606.02318) on 7 June 2016 and published in Science on 10 February 2017; it is the founding reference for neural-network quantum states.
items.people: Giuseppe Carleo, Matthias Troyer

items.claim: Dong-Ling Deng, Xiaopeng Li and Sankar Das Sarma showed that restricted Boltzmann machine states can encode volume-law entanglement with only a polynomial number of parameters, while RBM states with short-range connectivity obey an area law — establishing that the entanglement capacity of a neural-network ansatz is not limited the way matrix product states are.
items.people: Dong-Ling Deng, Xiaopeng Li, S. Das Sarma

items.claim: Yusuke Nomura, Andrew S. Darmawan, Youhei Yamaji and Masatoshi Imada combined a restricted Boltzmann machine with conventional variational Monte Carlo (pair-product/Gutzwiller-Jastrow reference states), substantially improving ground-state accuracy for the Heisenberg and Hubbard models on square lattices. This is the key early demonstration that NQS work best as a correlator on top of physics-informed reference wave functions.
items.people: Yusuke Nomura, Andrew S. Darmawan, Youhei Yamaji, Masatoshi Imada

items.claim: Giacomo Torlai, Guglielmo Mazzola, Juan Carrasquilla, Matthias Troyer, Roger Melko and Giuseppe Carleo used RBMs to perform quantum state tomography of highly entangled states in one and two dimensions, reconstructing quantities such as entanglement entropy from experimentally accessible measurement data. The arXiv preprint (1703.05334, 2017) carried the title 'Many-body quantum state tomography with neural networks'.
items.people: Giacomo Torlai, Guglielmo Mazzola, Juan Carrasquilla, Matthias Troyer, Roger Melko, Giuseppe Carleo

items.claim: Stefanie Czischek, Martin Gärttner and Thomas Gasenzer tested RBM wave functions against exact solutions, tDMRG and semi-classical methods for quenches near the Ising quantum critical point, finding that convergence slows badly when long-range correlations build up. This is an important early counterweight to NQS optimism: near criticality the ansatz is hardest to optimize.
items.people: Stefanie Czischek, Martin Gärttner, Thomas Gasenzer

items.claim: NetKet, the open-source machine-learning toolkit for many-body quantum systems, was released with a 19-author paper led by Giuseppe Carleo in SoftwareX in 2019 (arXiv:1904.00031). It implements neural-network quantum states as variational ansätze plus ground-state search, tomography and supervised learning on customizable lattices. Source: https://github.com/netket/netket

Davis, Stavros Efthymiou, Ivan Glasser, Sheng-Hsuan Lin, Marta Mauri, Guglielmo Mazzola, Christian B. Mendl, Evert van Nieuwenburg, Ossian O'Reilly, Hugo Théveniaut, Giacomo Torlai, Filippo Vicentini, Alexander Wietek

items.claim: NetKet 3, led by Filippo Vicentini with Giuseppe Carleo as senior author, rebuilt the library on JAX: arbitrary neural ansätze written in pure Python, just-in-time compilation, automatic differentiation, GPU/TPU support, discrete symmetry groups, chunking to thousands of degrees of freedom, and drivers for quantum dynamics. Published in SciPost Physics Codebases in 2022 (arXiv:2112.10526, 2021). Source: https://github.com/netket/netket

items.claim: Kenny Choo, Titus Neupert and Giuseppe Carleo applied a fully convolutional neural network ansatz to the frustrated spin-1/2 J1-J2 Heisenberg model on the square lattice — a sign-problem-afflicted benchmark inaccessible to quantum Monte Carlo — obtaining ground-state energies competitive with and sometimes better than the state of the art. Choo and Neupert were at the University of Zurich; Carleo at the Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute.
items.people: Kenny Choo, Titus Neupert, Giuseppe Carleo
items.affiliation: University of Zurich (Choo, Neupert); Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute (Carleo)

items.claim: Markus Schmitt and Markus Heyl simulated quantum many-body dynamics of the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model with artificial neural networks, reaching times comparable to or beyond tensor-network methods and observing collapse-and-revival oscillations of ferromagnetic order — directly relevant to Rydberg-atom quantum simulators.
items.people: Markus Schmitt, Markus Heyl

items.claim: Jan Hermann, Zeno Schätzle and Frank Noé introduced PauliNet, a deep-learning wave-function ansatz for the electronic Schrödinger equation with a multireference Hartree-Fock baseline, cusp conditions and antisymmetry built in, trained by variational quantum Monte Carlo. It reached near-exact energies for molecules with up to 30 electrons. Preprint arXiv:1909.08423 (2019); published in Nature Chemistry in 2020.
items.people: Jan Hermann, Zeno Schätzle, Frank Noé

items.claim: DeepQMC, the open-source successor framework to PauliNet, was published as a software suite unifying several deep-learning quantum Monte Carlo architectures under one JAX-based codebase. Source: https://github.com/deepqmc/deepqmc (arXiv:2307.14123).
items.people: Zeno Schätzle, P. Bernát Szabó, Matěj Mezera, Jan Hermann, Frank Noé

items.claim: David Pfau, James S. Spencer, Alexander G. de G. Matthews and W. M. C. Foulkes introduced FermiNet, a deep neural network that replaces the Slater determinant with permutation-equivariant many-electron orbitals, achieving chemical accuracy on small molecules without any basis set or reference wave function. Preprint arXiv:1909.02487 (2019, titled 'Ab-Initio Solution of the Many-Electron Schrödinger Equation with Deep Neural Networks'); published in Physical Review Research on 16 September 2020.
items.people: David Pfau, James S. Spencer, Alexander G. de G. Matthews, W. M. C. Foulkes

items.claim: David Pfau and colleagues at Google DeepMind extended neural-network variational Monte Carlo to excited states with a parameter-free method that requires no explicit orthogonalization, recasting the search for the lowest excited states as a ground-state problem in an expanded system. Combined with FermiNet and the Psiformer ansatz it recovered vertical excitation energies and oscillator strengths across a range of molecules. Preprint arXiv:2308.16848 (2023).
items.people: David Pfau, Simon Axelrod, Halvard Sutterud, Ingrid von Glehn, James S. Spencer
items.affiliation: Google DeepMind

items.claim: James Kirkpatrick and colleagues at DeepMind trained the DM21 exchange-correlation functional on molecular data plus fictitious systems with fractional charge and fractional spin, curing the delocalization and static-correlation errors that afflict conventional density functional theory. Note this is a DFT result, not a neural-network quantum state; it is the complementary DeepMind line of work.
items.people: James Kirkpatrick, Brendan McMorrow, David H. P. Turban, Alexander L. Gaunt, James S. Spencer, Alexander G. D. G. Matthews, Annette Obika, Louis Thiry, Meire Fortunato, David Pfau, Lara Román Castellanos, Stig Petersen, Alexander W. R. Nelson, Pushmeet Kohli, Paula Mori-Sánchez, Demis Hassabis, Aron J. Cohen
items.affiliation: DeepMind

items.claim: Javier Robledo Moreno, Giuseppe Carleo, Antoine Georges and James Stokes constructed 'hidden-fermion' neural network states — Slater determinants in an enlarged Hilbert space with a neural-network-parameterized constraint — proved the family universal, and matched leading variational methods on the two-dimensional Hubbard model. Preprint arXiv:2111.10420 (2021).
items.people: Javier Robledo Moreno, Giuseppe Carleo, Antoine Georges, James Stokes
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 119, e2122059119

items.claim: Christopher Roth, Attila Szabó and Allan H. MacDonald showed that very deep (4-16 layer) group-convolutional neural quantum states outperform state-of-the-art variational methods on highly frustrated magnets, including square- and triangular-lattice spin-liquid candidates. Preprint arXiv:2211.07749 (2022).
items.people: Christopher Roth, Attila Szabó, Allan H. MacDonald

items.claim: Ao Chen and Markus Heyl introduced a minimum-step stochastic-reconfiguration optimizer that removes the parameter-count bottleneck in training large neural quantum states, then used it on the frustrated J1-J2 model to produce evidence for a gapless quantum spin-liquid phase. Published in Nature Physics on 1 July 2024.
items.people: Ao Chen, Markus Heyl

items.claim: Dian Wu, Riccardo Rossi, Filippo Vicentini and Giuseppe Carleo, with a 30-author consortium that included Steven R. White, Masatoshi Imada, Federico Becca, Juan Carrasquilla and Antoine Georges, defined the V-score — a dimensionless accuracy metric built from the variational energy and its variance — and released a curated dataset of variational calculations across many-body Hamiltonians, exposing which models (notably frustrated and doped Hubbard-type systems) remain unsolved by every method including NQS. Preprint arXiv:2302.04919 (2023); published in Science on 18 October 2024.
