items.claim: Hannah Lange, Anka Van de Walle, Atiye Abedinnia and Annabelle Bohrdt published the standard review of neural quantum states, surveying architectures (RBM, CNN, autoregressive, RNN, transformer), optimization schemes and applications, including open systems and dynamics. Published 30 September 2024; preprint arXiv:2402.09402 (2024).
items.people: Hannah Lange, Anka Van de Walle, Atiye Abedinnia, Annabelle Bohrdt

items.claim: Steven R. White, then at the University of California, Irvine, introduced the density matrix renormalization group: truncate the Hilbert space by keeping the eigenvectors of the reduced density matrix with the largest weight rather than the lowest-energy states. Published 9 November 1992; extended in 'Density-matrix algorithms for quantum renormalization groups', Physical Review B 48, 10345-10356 (1993), doi 10.1103/PhysRevB.48.10345. DMRG and its matrix-product-state formulation remain the accuracy baseline against which every neural-network ansatz is measured.
items.people: Steven R. White
items.affiliation: Department of Physics, University of California, Irvine

items.claim: Ulrich Schollwöck's review recast DMRG in the language of matrix product states, which is the conceptual bridge between tensor networks and neural-network quantum states (an RBM is, in a precise sense, a different kind of tensor factorization). Submitted to arXiv August 2010 (1008.3477), published in Annals of Physics in 2011.
items.people: Ulrich Schollwöck

items.claim: Pierre Pfeuty gave the exact solution of the one-dimensional Ising model in a transverse field by Jordan-Wigner mapping to free fermions, establishing the critical point at transverse field equal to the exchange coupling. This is the canonical quantum phase transition and the standard first benchmark for every neural-network quantum state paper.
items.people: Pierre Pfeuty

items.claim: Juan Carrasquilla and Roger G. Melko showed that ordinary supervised neural networks — fully connected and convolutional — can classify phases and locate phase transitions in condensed-matter Hamiltonians directly from raw configurations, including states with no conventional local order parameter. Published in Nature Physics in 2017; this is the discriminative counterpart to the generative NQS programme.
items.people: Juan Carrasquilla, Roger G. Melko

items.claim: Evert P. L. van Nieuwenburg, Ye-Hua Liu and Sebastian D. Huber introduced 'learning by confusion': deliberately mislabel data at a trial critical point and read off the true transition from the W-shaped performance curve. Demonstrated on the Kitaev chain topological transition, the classical Ising transition and a many-body-localization transition, it requires no order parameter. All three authors were at the Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zurich. Preprint arXiv:1610.02048 (2016).
items.people: Evert P. L. van Nieuwenburg, Ye-Hua Liu, Sebastian D. Huber
items.affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zurich

items.claim: Markus Greiner, Olaf Mandel, Tilman Esslinger, Theodor W. Hänsch and Immanuel Bloch observed the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator quantum phase transition in a Bose-Einstein condensate loaded into a three-dimensional optical lattice, tuning the transition by lattice depth. Published 3 January 2002 at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität Munich; the founding experiment of quantum simulation of Hubbard physics.
items.people: Markus Greiner, Olaf Mandel, Tilman Esslinger, Theodor W. Hänsch, Immanuel Bloch
items.affiliation: Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München

items.claim: Markus Greiner's group at Harvard realized a cold-atom Fermi-Hubbard antiferromagnet on a roughly 80-site two-dimensional square lattice with a quantum gas microscope, observing antiferromagnetic correlations whose correlation length reached the system size. This is the experimental benchmark that classical Hubbard-model methods, including neural-network quantum states, are asked to reproduce.
items.people: Anton Mazurenko, Christie S. Chiu, Geoffrey Ji, Maxwell F. Parsons, Márton Kanász-Nagy, Richard Schmidt, Fabian Grusdt, Eugene Demler, Daniel Greif, Markus Greiner

items.claim: Alexander Keesling and co-workers in Mikhail D. Lukin's group used a programmable Rydberg-atom simulator to verify the quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism across an Ising-type quantum phase transition, measuring the growth of spatial correlations and the universal scaling of defect density with ramp rate. Preprint arXiv:1809.05540 (2018).
items.people: Alexander Keesling, Ahmed Omran, Harry Levine, Hannes Bernien, Hannes Pichler, Soonwon Choi, Rhine Samajdar, Sylvain Schwartz, Pietro Silvi, Subir Sachdev, Peter Zoller, Manuel Endres, Markus Greiner, Vladan Vuletić, Mikhail D. Lukin

items.claim: Sepehr Ebadi and colleagues at Harvard and MIT, with Mikhail D. Lukin and Markus Greiner as senior authors, mapped the phase diagram of a 256-atom programmable Rydberg quantum simulator, observing checkerboard, striated and star ordered phases and quantum phase transitions between them, with Subir Sachdev contributing the theory.
items.people: Sepehr Ebadi, Tout T. Wang, Harry Levine, Alexander Keesling, Giulia Semeghini, Ahmed Omran, Dolev Bluvstein, Rhine Samajdar, Hannes Pichler, Wen Wei Ho, Soonwon Choi, Subir Sachdev, Markus Greiner, Vladan Vuletić, Mikhail D. Lukin

items.claim: Giulia Semeghini and co-workers placed 219 atoms on the links of a kagome lattice and used Rydberg blockade to create a frustrated state with no local order, detecting the onset of a toric-code-type quantum spin liquid through topological string operators. Preprint arXiv:2104.04119 (2021).
items.people: Giulia Semeghini, Harry Levine, Alexander Keesling, Sepehr Ebadi, Tout T. Wang, Dolev Bluvstein, Ruben Verresen, Hannes Pichler, Marcin Kalinowski, Rhine Samajdar, Ahmed Omran, Subir Sachdev, Ashvin Vishwanath, Markus Greiner, Vladan Vuletić, Mikhail D. Lukin

items.claim: Google Quantum AI identified a phase transition in random circuit sampling controlled by the error rate per cycle, described by a weak-link model, and ran a 67-qubit, 32-cycle experiment in the computationally complex phase. Preprint arXiv:2304.11119 (2023, titled 'Phase transition in Random Circuit Sampling'); published in Nature in 2024.
items.people: Alexis Morvan, Benjamin Villalonga, Xiao Mi (Google Quantum AI and collaborators)
items.affiliation: Google Quantum AI

items.claim: Google Quantum AI's 69-qubit analogue-digital superconducting simulator, built with collaborators at Princeton, PSI and Geneva, revealed a coarsening-induced breakdown of Kibble-Zurek scaling in the XY model and signatures of the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, with cross-entropy benchmarking placing the evolution beyond classical simulation. Preprint arXiv:2405.17385 (2024); published in Nature on 6 February 2025.
items.people: Trond I. Andersen, Nikita Astrakhantsev, Amir H. Karamlou, Julia Berndtsson, Johannes Motruk, Aaron Szasz (Google Quantum AI and collaborators)
items.affiliation: Google Research / Google Quantum AI, with Princeton University, Paul Scherrer Institute and University of Geneva

openQuestions: Do neural-network quantum states have a genuine asymptotic advantage over tensor networks in two dimensions, or is the observed advantage confined to specific frustrated models where DMRG bond dimension is the binding constraint? The V-score dataset (Wu, Rossi, Vicentini, Carleo et al., Science 2024) frames the question but does not settle it.

NQS optimization degrades exactly where physics is most interesting — near quantum critical points, where correlations are long-ranged (Czischek, Gärttner and Gasenzer, Physical Review B 2018). Is this a fundamental expressivity limit of the ansatz, an optimization-landscape pathology of stochastic reconfiguration, or a sampling problem?

The fermion sign problem is transformed rather than removed by neural ansätze. Hidden-fermion and Slater-Jastrow-neural hybrids (Robledo Moreno, Carleo, Georges, Stokes, PNAS 2022) mitigate it for the Hubbard model, but no method yet reaches the doped-Hubbard accuracy needed to settle the superconducting ground state.

Lattice-spin NQS (NetKet lineage) and continuous-space electronic NQS (FermiNet, PauliNet, Psiformer) have almost disjoint architectures, software stacks and communities despite solving formally similar variational problems. Whether the continuous-space advances transfer back to lattice criticality is largely untested.

Scaling behaviour is unresolved: does adding depth and parameters to a neural quantum state buy accuracy predictably, the way scaling laws hold for language models, or does the variance of the local energy set a hard floor?

Programmable quantum simulators can now prepare states (Rydberg spin liquids, Fermi-Hubbard antiferromagnets) that classical variational methods struggle with. Which side is the ground truth when they disagree, and can NQS be trained directly on simulator measurement data rather than on a Hamiltonian?

Excited states, finite temperature and open-system dynamics remain far less developed than ground-state NQS. Pfau et al. (Science 2024) solved excited states for molecules; no comparably robust method exists for excitation spectra across a lattice quantum phase transition.

ml-as-physics.domain: Phase transitions inside machine learning: the statistical-physics theory of learning
ml-as-physics.summary: Machine learning is one of the few fields where the phase-transition metaphor is not a metaphor at all. When John J. Hopfield mapped associative memory onto a spin system in 1982, he made the tools of statistical mechanics literally applicable to a learning machine, and within three years Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund and Haim Sompolinsky had used replica theory to show that a Hopfield network of N neurons undergoes a genuine first-order transition at a critical load: below roughly 0.138N stored patterns memory works, above it the network collapses into a spin-glass state where retrieval is destroyed. Elizabeth Gardner then shifted the question from a fixed learning rule to the geometry of the solution space itself, computing the volume of weight configurations that satisfy a set of constraints and deriving the optimal capacity of a perceptron; the "Gardner volume" and its shrinking to zero at a critical constraint density is the template for nearly every later capacity calculation. Through the late 1980s and 1990s, Sompolinsky, Naftali Tishby, H. Sebastian Seung and Géza Györgyi extended this to generalization, showing that learning curves can display discontinuous, first-order jumps to perfect generalization when weights are discrete — the earliest rigorous ancestors of what is now called grokking. Geoffrey E. Hinton's Boltzmann machine imported the Boltzmann distribution directly into learning. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics to Hopfield and Hinton formally recognized this lineage. In the modern era the same framework reappears: algorithmic and information-theoretic thresholds in inference (Lenka Zdeborová, Florent Krzakala), the jamming transition separating under- from over-parametrized networks (Matthieu Wyart and collaborators), double descent, and the fierce ongoing argument over whether "emergent abilities" of large language models are real transitions or artifacts of discontinuous metrics.

items.claim: John J. Hopfield introduced a recurrent network of two-state neurons with symmetric connections whose dynamics descend a Lyapunov 'energy' function identical in form to that of an Ising spin system, so that stored memories are the energy minima; this paper made statistical mechanics directly applicable to neural computation and reported an empirical storage limit of about 0.15N patterns for N neurons.
items.people: John J. Hopfield
items.affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Biology, California Institute of Technology, and Bell Laboratories
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. 79, no. 8, pp. 2554-2558

items.claim: David H. Ackley, Geoffrey E. Hinton and Terrence J. Sejnowski defined the Boltzmann machine, a network of stochastic binary units whose equilibrium states follow the Boltzmann distribution, and derived a learning rule based on the difference between correlations in a clamped 'wake' phase and a free-running 'sleep' phase — importing simulated annealing and thermal equilibrium from statistical physics into machine learning.
items.people: David H. Ackley, Geoffrey E. Hinton, Terrence J. Sejnowski

items.claim: Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund and Haim Sompolinsky applied replica mean-field theory to the Hopfield model in the saturation limit where the number of stored patterns p grows proportionally to network size N (p = alpha*N), and showed that despite the model's spin-glass character, dynamically stable retrieval states almost fully correlated with individual stored patterns exist below a critical load — the first analytic proof that associative memory survives as a distinct thermodynamic phase.
items.people: Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund, Haim Sompolinsky
items.affiliation: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
items.venue: Physical Review Letters, vol. 55, no. 14, pp. 1530-1533

items.claim: In the full-length treatment of the Hopfield model near saturation, Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund and Haim Sompolinsky mapped the complete phase diagram in the load-temperature plane and located the critical storage capacity at zero temperature, above which retrieval states abruptly disappear and the network enters a spin-glass phase; below the critical load the network retrieves patterns with an error of less than about 1.5 percent. This critical value, conventionally quoted as alpha_c approximately 0.138, is the canonical 'memory cliff' of associative memory.
items.people: Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund, Haim Sompolinsky
items.affiliation: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
items.venue: Annals of Physics, vol. 173, no. 1, pp. 30-67

items.claim: Elizabeth Gardner reframed neural network capacity as a question about the geometry of weight space rather than about any particular learning rule, computing the typical fractional volume of the space of couplings that correctly stores a given set of random patterns as stable states. This volume shrinks continuously to zero at a critical pattern density, and the construction — now universally called the Gardner volume — became the standard method for computing capacity in learning systems.
items.people: Elizabeth Gardner
items.affiliation: University of Edinburgh
items.venue: Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General, vol. 21, no. 1, pp. 257-270

items.claim: Elizabeth Gardner and Bernard Derrida computed the maximum number of random patterns an optimal neural network can store as a function of the allowed fraction of bit errors and of a stability margin K, obtaining a critical line alpha_c(K) with alpha_c(0) = 2 — the celebrated result that an optimally trained perceptron can store two patterns per weight, twice the Hebbian-rule capacity.
items.people: Elizabeth Gardner, Bernard Derrida
items.affiliation: University of Edinburgh (Gardner)
items.venue: Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General, vol. 21, no. 1, pp. 271-284

items.claim: Elizabeth Gardner died in 1988, roughly nine months into a five-year fellowship at the University of Edinburgh, having produced her work on disordered systems and neural networks before the age of 30 while she was ill with cancer, which she chose to bear quietly. Her 1985 work on disordered systems contained the first description of what is now called the Gardner transition.
items.people: Elizabeth Gardner
items.affiliation: University of Edinburgh
items.venue: University of Edinburgh, Higgs Centre for Theoretical Physics — International Women's Day 2022 feature

items.claim: Haim Sompolinsky, Naftali Tishby and H. Sebastian Seung showed with equilibrium statistical mechanics that when the training error is a smooth function of continuously varying weights the generalization error decays asymptotically as the inverse of the number of examples, but that for networks with discrete weights the generalization error can undergo a discontinuous transition to perfect generalization — a first-order phase transition in learning itself.
items.people: Haim Sompolinsky, Naftali Tishby, Hyunjune Sebastian Seung
items.venue: Physical Review Letters, vol. 65, no. 13, pp. 1683-1686

items.claim: Géza Györgyi showed that a perceptron with binary synaptic weights learning from examples undergoes a first-order transition at a critical number of examples: below it the generalization error reaches a minimal positive value, and at the transition the network abruptly freezes into the state of the teacher perceptron with error identically zero. This is the cleanest early example of an all-or-nothing learning transition.
items.people: Géza Györgyi
items.venue: Physical Review A, vol. 41, no. 12, pp. 7097-7100

items.claim: H. Sebastian Seung, Haim Sompolinsky and Naftali Tishby gave the definitive statistical-mechanical treatment of learning from examples in feedforward networks, treating stochastic training as sampling from a Gibbs distribution over weights at an effective temperature. Smooth networks obey an inverse power-law learning curve; unrealizable rules can produce spin-glass phases with many degenerate minima; and nonsmooth networks display qualitatively different, sometimes discontinuous, learning curves.
items.people: Hyunjune Sebastian Seung, Haim Sompolinsky, Naftali Tishby
items.venue: Physical Review A, vol. 45, no. 8, pp. 6056-6091

items.claim: Timothy L. H. Watkin, Albrecht Rau and Michael Biehl wrote the standard review of the statistical mechanics of learning a rule, framing supervised learning as an inverse problem in a strongly interacting disordered system analogous to a spin glass and consolidating the replica-method learning-curve results of the preceding decade.
items.people: Timothy L. H. Watkin, Albrecht Rau, Michael Biehl
items.affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Oxford
items.venue: Reviews of Modern Physics, vol. 65, no. 2, pp. 499-556

items.claim: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2024 was awarded jointly to John J. Hopfield (Princeton University) and Geoffrey E. Hinton (University of Toronto) 'for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks'. The Nobel committee's own framing credits Hopfield with a network described in a manner equivalent to the energy of a physical spin system, and credits Hinton with using tools from statistical physics in 1983-1985 to create the Boltzmann machine. Hopfield was born in 1933 in Chicago and received his PhD from Cornell University in 1958; Hinton was born in 1947 in London and received his PhD from the University of Edinburgh in 1978.
items.people: John J. Hopfield, Geoffrey E. Hinton
items.affiliation: Princeton University (Hopfield); University of Toronto (Hinton)
items.venue: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Nobel Prize in Physics 2024

items.claim: Dmitry Krotov and John J. Hopfield introduced dense associative memory, replacing the quadratic Hopfield energy with a higher-order polynomial or rapidly growing interaction function, which raises storage capacity from linear in the number of neurons to superlinear (polynomial in the degree of the interaction). They established a duality between dense associative memory and feedforward networks with one hidden layer, and identified two operating regimes: a feature-matching regime and a prototype regime, with the crossover between them controlled by the sharpness of the energy function.
items.people: Dmitry Krotov, John J. Hopfield
items.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NeurIPS 2016), pp. 1172-1180; arXiv:1606.01164

items.claim: Pankaj Mehta and David J. Schwab constructed a formal mapping between Kadanoff's variational renormalization group and stacked Restricted Boltzmann Machines, arguing that successive layers of a deep network implement RG-style coarse-graining and that deep learning therefore extracts relevant features the way RG extracts relevant operators. The correspondence was illustrated on the Ising model.
items.people: Pankaj Mehta, David J. Schwab

items.claim: Maciej Koch-Janusz and Zohar Ringel challenged the assumption that ordinary RBM training performs renormalization, and instead built a neural network that maximizes real-space mutual information between coarse-grained blocks and their environment in order to identify the relevant degrees of freedom and iterate RG steps without prior knowledge of the system; the method recovers the Ising critical exponent in one and two dimensions.
items.people: Maciej Koch-Janusz, Zohar Ringel

items.claim: Ellen de Mello Koch, Robert de Mello Koch and Ling Cheng tested the RG/deep-learning correspondence empirically by comparing a single layer of an RBM trained on the Ising model to a single step of RG flow, and constructed observables that expose important differences between renormalization group flow and deep learning — a direct empirical check on the 'exact mapping' claim.
items.people: Ellen de Mello Koch, Robert de Mello Koch, Ling Cheng

items.claim: Aurélien Decelle, Florent Krzakala, Cristopher Moore and Lenka Zdeborová used the cavity method to obtain an asymptotically exact phase diagram for community detection in the stochastic block model, establishing a detectability/undetectability transition below which no algorithm can recover communities better than chance, and a separate easy/hard transition where belief propagation fails while the information-theoretic solution still exists. This is the canonical statistical-to-computational gap in inference.
items.people: Aurélien Decelle, Florent Krzakala, Cristopher Moore, Lenka Zdeborová
items.venue: Physical Review E, vol. 84, no. 6, art. 066106 (arXiv:1109.3041)

items.claim: Lenka Zdeborová and Florent Krzakala wrote the definitive review of the statistical physics of inference, systematizing the thresholds that separate regimes where inference is impossible, possible-but-computationally-hard, and easy — and connecting spin-glass concepts (clustering, condensation, replica symmetry breaking) to message-passing algorithms across signal processing, learning and community detection.
items.people: Lenka Zdeborová, Florent Krzakala
items.venue: Advances in Physics, vol. 65, no. 5, pp. 453-552 (arXiv:1511.02476, 2015)

items.claim: Jean Barbier, Florent Krzakala, Nicolas Macris, Léo Miolane and Lenka Zdeborová rigorously proved decades-old statistical-physics conjectures for the optimal estimation error in high-dimensional generalized linear models with random data matrices, and characterized exactly the parameter regions where the generalized approximate message-passing algorithm attains that optimum — thereby making the boundary between the 'hard' and 'easy' phases of learning a theorem rather than a conjecture.
items.people: Jean Barbier, Florent Krzakala, Nicolas Macris, Léo Miolane, Lenka Zdeborová
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. 116, no. 12, pp. 5451-5460 (arXiv:1708.03395, 2017)

items.claim: Lenka Zdeborová argued in a Nature Physics commentary that understanding deep learning is also a job for physicists, making the case that the tools built for disordered systems — replica calculations, message passing, phase diagrams — are the natural instruments for explaining why deep networks generalize.
items.people: Lenka Zdeborová

items.claim: Mikhail Belkin, Daniel Hsu, Siyuan Ma and Soumik Mandal identified the 'double descent' risk curve: as model capacity grows, test error first follows the classical U-shaped bias-variance curve, peaks sharply at the interpolation threshold where the model exactly fits the training data, and then descends again as capacity increases further, often to a lower error than the classical optimum. The peak sits precisely at the transition point between the underparametrized and overparametrized regimes.
items.people: Mikhail Belkin, Daniel Hsu, Siyuan Ma, Soumik Mandal
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. 116, no. 32, pp. 15849-15854 (arXiv:1812.11118, 2018)

items.claim: Preetum Nakkiran, Gal Kaplun, Yamini Bansal, Tristan Yang, Boaz Barak and Ilya Sutskever demonstrated double descent empirically across modern deep learning tasks and showed it occurs not only as a function of model size but also as a function of training epochs. They defined 'effective model complexity' to unify the two, and identified regimes in which increasing — even quadrupling — the number of training samples actively hurts test performance.
items.people: Preetum Nakkiran, Gal Kaplun, Yamini Bansal, Tristan Yang, Boaz Barak, Ilya Sutskever
items.venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2020; journal version Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment, vol. 2021, art. 124003 (arXiv:1912.02292, 2019)

items.claim: Mario Geiger, Stefano Spigler, Stéphane d'Ascoli, Levent Sagun, Marco Baity-Jesi, Giulio Biroli and Matthieu Wyart proposed that the loss landscape of a deep network is governed by a jamming transition analogous to that of repulsive particles: a sharp phase boundary in the number of parameters separates an underparametrized regime where the training data cannot be fitted from an overparametrized regime where it can, with characteristic critical behaviour in the Hessian spectrum near the transition. They also found that the capacity of fully connected networks to memorize random data is independent of depth.
items.people: Mario Geiger, Stefano Spigler, Stéphane d'Ascoli, Levent Sagun, Marco Baity-Jesi, Giulio Biroli, Matthieu Wyart

items.claim: Stefano Spigler, Mario Geiger, Stéphane d'Ascoli, Levent Sagun, Giulio Biroli and Matthieu Wyart showed that the jamming transition from under- to over-parametrization directly controls generalization: as network width grows, the test error decays, then rises to a cusp exactly at the transition, then slowly decays again. Classical overfitting is localized around the jamming point, and early stopping removes the cusp entirely — connecting the physics of jamming to the double-descent peak.
items.people: Stefano Spigler, Mario Geiger, Stéphane d'Ascoli, Levent Sagun, Giulio Biroli, Matthieu Wyart
items.venue: Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical, vol. 52, art. 474001 (arXiv:1810.09665, 2018)

items.claim: Alethea Power, Yuri Burda, Harri Edwards, Igor Babuschkin and Vedant Misra reported 'grokking': neural networks trained on small algorithmically generated datasets first memorize the training set with chance-level validation accuracy, and then, after a long plateau of continued training far past the point of overfitting, abruptly jump to near-perfect generalization. Smaller training sets require progressively more optimization before this jump occurs.
items.people: Alethea Power, Yuri Burda, Harri Edwards, Igor Babuschkin, Vedant Misra

items.claim: Neel Nanda, Lawrence Chan, Tom Lieberum, Jess Smith and Jacob Steinhardt reverse-engineered grokking in small transformers trained on modular addition, showing the network learns to compute discrete Fourier transforms and use trigonometric identities to turn addition into rotation on a circle. Defining progress measures from that mechanism, they split training into three continuous phases — memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup — demonstrating that the apparently abrupt transition in test accuracy is the visible surface of a smooth underlying reorganization.
items.people: Neel Nanda, Lawrence Chan, Tom Lieberum, Jess Smith, Jacob Steinhardt
items.venue: The Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2023), oral presentation (arXiv:2301.05217)

items.claim: Jason Wei and sixteen coauthors defined an 'emergent ability' of a large language model as one that is not present in smaller models but is present in larger ones, and therefore cannot be predicted by extrapolating the performance curve of smaller models. They catalogued dozens of tasks on which performance stays at random baseline until a critical model scale and then rises sharply.
items.people: Jason Wei, Yi Tay, Rishi Bommasani, Colin Raffel, Barret Zoph, Sebastian Borgeaud, Dani Yogatama, Maarten Bosma, Denny Zhou, Donald Metzler, Ed H. Chi, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Oriol Vinyals, Percy Liang, Jeff Dean, William Fedus
items.venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2022 (arXiv:2206.07682, submitted 15 June 2022)

items.claim: Rylan Schaeffer, Brando Miranda and Sanmi Koyejo argued that emergent abilities are an artifact of metric choice rather than a change in model behaviour: nonlinear or discontinuous metrics (such as exact-match accuracy) manufacture apparent sharp transitions, while linear or continuous metrics on the same models and outputs yield smooth, predictable improvement. They supported this with controlled experiments on GPT-3/InstructGPT, a meta-analysis of BIG-Bench tasks, and a demonstration that emergence can be induced at will in vision models by switching metrics.
items.people: Rylan Schaeffer, Brando Miranda, Sanmi Koyejo
items.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023) (arXiv:2304.15004, submitted 28 April 2023)

items.claim: The Schaeffer-Miranda-Koyejo rebuttal to emergent abilities received a NeurIPS 2023 outstanding paper award, which is why the 'mirage' framing became the standard counterweight to Wei et al. in subsequent discussion.
items.people: Rylan Schaeffer, Brando Miranda, Sanmi Koyejo

openQuestions: Is the sharpness of a learning transition an objective property of the system, or an artifact of the observable chosen to measure it? Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo show that metric choice manufactures discontinuities in LLM benchmarks, and Nanda et al. show that grokking's abrupt accuracy jump overlays a smooth internal reorganization — yet in the Hopfield model the transition at alpha_c is thermodynamically real and metric-independent. A book chapter needs to be explicit about which kind of transition each example is.

Does the finite-size scaling machinery of statistical physics actually apply to real deep networks? Sharp phase transitions are defined in the thermodynamic limit; real models have finite width and finite data. Whether the observed 'cusps' in double descent and jamming survive as true singularities, or are always rounded crossovers, is not settled.

Whether the 2024 Nobel Prize's framing — that Hopfield's network is 'described in a manner equivalent to the energy in the spin system found in physics' — is a claim about physics or about mathematical analogy. This has been contested publicly by physicists who question whether the prize was properly a physics prize.

How much of Elizabeth Gardner's programme was independently rediscovered rather than inherited. Modern capacity results for deep networks often reproduce Gardner-volume reasoning without citing it, and the historical question of transmission (versus parallel invention) is worth checking against primary sources.

The Mehta-Schwab RG/deep-learning correspondence remains unresolved: Koch-Janusz and Ringel argue that minimizing KL divergence in an RBM does not implement RG at all, and de Mello Koch et al. found concrete observables distinguishing the two. Whether any version of 'deep learning is renormalization' survives is still open.

Whether grokking, double descent, emergent abilities, and the jamming transition are four faces of one underlying transition or four unrelated phenomena that share a visual signature. Several papers claim a unification but none is yet accepted as definitive.

What the correct statistical-mechanical order parameter is for a transformer. The Hopfield model has overlap with stored patterns; the perceptron has the teacher-student overlap; no comparable quantity is agreed upon for modern architectures, which is the main obstacle to a genuine phase diagram for large language models.

verdicts.claim: Hopfield 1982, PNAS 79(8):2554-2558, DOI 10.1073/pnas.79.8.2554 — recurrent two-state neurons, Ising-like energy, empirical storage limit ~0.15N.
Ackley, Hinton, Sejnowski 1985, Cognitive Science 9(1):147-169, DOI 10.1207/s15516709cog0901_7 — Boltzmann machine; learning rule from clamped 'wake' phase minus free-running 'sleep' phase.
verdicts.correction: Bibliographic data fully confirmed via Crossref (title 'A Learning Algorithm for Boltzmann Machines'; authors, order, journal, volume, issue, pages, year all correct; DOI resolves). One factual anachronism: the 1985 paper uses the terms 'clamped' (phase+) and 'free-running'/'unclamped' (phase-) phases. The 'wake'/'sleep' vocabulary belongs to Hinton, Dayan, Frey and Neal's wake-sleep algorithm for the Helmholtz machine (Science, 1995), not to Ackley-Hinton-Sejnowski 1985. Replace with: '...and derived a learning rule based on the difference between unit correlations measured in a clamped phase and in a free-running phase.' URL unchanged: https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog0901_7

verdicts.claim: Amit, Gutfreund, Sompolinsky 1985, PRL 55(14):1530-1533 — replica mean-field theory of the Hopfield model at p = alpha*N; 'the first analytic proof that associative memory survives as a distinct thermodynamic phase.'
verdicts.correction: Citation fully confirmed via Crossref: 'Storing Infinite Numbers of Patterns in a Spin-Glass Model of Neural Networks', Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund, H. Sompolinsky, Phys. Rev. Lett. 55(14), 1530-1533 (1985); DOI resolves. The word 'proof' overstates the work: the replica method with a replica-symmetric ansatz is a non-rigorous (and, in the spin-glass regime, replica-symmetry-breaking-corrected) calculation, not a proof; rigorous versions came later (e.g. Talagrand, Bovier-Gayrard). Replace 'the first analytic proof that' with 'the first analytic demonstration that' or 'the first replica-theoretic calculation showing that'. URL unchanged: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.1530

verdicts.claim: Amit, Gutfreund, Sompolinsky 1987, Annals of Physics 173(1):30-67 — full phase diagram near saturation, alpha_c ≈ 0.138, retrieval error below ~1.5 percent.

Gardner 1988, J. Phys. A 21(1):257-270, DOI 10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/030 — 'The space of interactions in neural network models'; typical fractional volume of coupling space shrinking to zero at a critical pattern density (the Gardner volume).
Gardner and Derrida 1988, J. Phys. A 21(1):271-284 — alpha_c(K) with alpha_c(0) = 2, 'twice the Hebbian-rule capacity'.
verdicts.correction: Citation fully confirmed via Crossref: 'Optimal storage properties of neural network models', E. Gardner and B. Derrida, J. Phys. A 21(1), 271-284 (1988); DOI 10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/031 resolves. The comparison is factually wrong: alpha_c = 2 is roughly fourteen times, not twice, the Hebbian capacity. The Hebbian (Hopfield) rule stores alpha_c ≈ 0.138 patterns per neuron (Amit-Gutfreund-Sompolinsky), so 2 / 0.138 ≈ 14.5. (alpha_c = 2 coincides with Cover's 1965 counting result that a perceptron with N inputs can realise 2N random dichotomies; that is the correct comparison to draw, not a factor of two over Hebb.) Replace with: '...obtaining a critical line alpha_c(K) with alpha_c(0) = 2 — the celebrated result that an optimally trained perceptron can store two patterns per weight, more than an order of magnitude above the roughly 0.138 patterns per neuron achieved by the Hebbian rule.' URL unchanged: https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/031

verdicts.claim: Elizabeth Gardner died in 1988, nine months into a five-year fellowship at Edinburgh, work done before age 30, ill with cancer borne quietly; her 1985 work contained the first description of the Gardner transition. Source: Higgs Centre International Women's Day 2022 feature.

Sompolinsky, Tishby, Seung 1990, PRL 65(13):1683-1686 — smooth/continuous weights give generalization error decaying as 1/(number of examples); discrete weights can give a discontinuous transition to perfect generalization. URL https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10042332/
Györgyi 1990, Phys. Rev. A 41(12):7097-7100, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevA.41.7097 — first-order transition to perfect generalization in a binary-synapse perceptron.

Seung, Sompolinsky, Tishby 1992, Phys. Rev. A 45(8):6056-6091, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevA.45.6056 — Gibbs distribution over weights at an effective temperature; power-law learning curves for smooth networks, spin-glass phases for unrealizable rules, discontinuous curves for nonsmooth networks.
Watkin, Rau, Biehl 1993, Rev. Mod. Phys. 65(2):499-556 — standard review 'The statistical mechanics of learning a rule'. Affiliation given as 'Department of Physics, University of Oxford'.
verdicts.correction: Bibliographic data fully confirmed via Crossref (title, three authors in the given order, RMP 65(2), 499-556, 1993; DOI 10.1103/RevModPhys.65.499 resolves). The affiliation field is wrong as a blanket statement: Watkin and Rau were at the Department of Physics, University of Oxford, but Michael Biehl was at the Institut für Theoretische Physik, Universität Würzburg. Replace the affiliation with: 'Department of Physics, University of Oxford (Watkin, Rau); Institut für Theoretische Physik, Universität Würzburg (Biehl)'. (Note: I could not fetch the APS article page directly — it returned HTTP 403 — so the Würzburg attribution rests on Biehl's documented affiliation history rather than on the printed byline; verify against the PDF before print.) URL unchanged: https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.499

verdicts.claim: Nobel Prize in Physics 2024 to Hopfield (Princeton) and Hinton (Toronto) 'for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks'; committee framing on energy in a spin system and on Hinton's 1983-1985 statistical-physics tools; Hopfield born 1933 Chicago, PhD Cornell 1958; Hinton born 1947 London, PhD Edinburgh 1978.

Krotov and Hopfield 2016, NeurIPS 29, pp. 1172-1180, arXiv:1606.01164 — dense associative memory; capacity raised 'from linear in the number of neurons to superlinear (polynomial in the degree of the interaction)'; duality with one-hidden-layer feedforward networks; feature-matching vs prototype regimes controlled by the sharpness of the energy function.
verdicts.correction: Paper, authors, venue and page range confirmed (dblp lists NIPS 2016, pp. 1172-1180; arXiv:1606.01164 'Dense Associative Memory for Pattern Recognition', submitted 3 June 2016). The parenthetical is garbled: capacity is polynomial in N with an exponent set by the interaction degree, not 'polynomial in the degree of the interaction'. The paper gives K_max = alpha_n * N^(n-1) for a rectified-polynomial energy of power n. Replace with: '...which raises storage capacity from linear in the number of neurons N to polynomial, K_max ~ N^(n-1) for an interaction of power n.' The duality claim and the sharpness-controlled feature-to-prototype crossover are both confirmed against the paper text. URL unchanged: https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.01164

verdicts.claim: Mehta and Schwab 2014, arXiv:1410.3831 — formal (indeed 'exact') mapping between Kadanoff variational RG and stacked RBMs, illustrated on the Ising model.

Koch-Janusz and Ringel 2018, Nature Physics 14(6):578-582 (arXiv:1704.06279) — challenged the assumption that ordinary RBM training performs RG; real-space mutual-information network; 'recovers the Ising critical exponent in one and two dimensions.'
verdicts.correction: Citation confirmed via Crossref and arXiv (title 'Mutual information, neural networks and the renormalization group'; Nature Physics 14, 578-582, 2018). The challenge to RBM-as-RG is confirmed in the paper text, which states that prior work assumes training by Kullback-Leibler divergence and shows the RSMI filters for the dimer model are orthogonal to the KL-derived ones. The last sub-clause misstates the result. The abstract reads: 'We apply the algorithm to classical statistical physics problems in one and two dimensions. We demonstrate RG flow and extract the Ising critical exponent.' The one-and-two-dimensions scope attaches to the demonstrations, not to the exponent; and it is a single exponent, not exponents. Replace with: '...the method demonstrates RG flow on classical statistical-physics problems in one and two dimensions and extracts the Ising critical exponent.' foundations.domain: Physics foundations of phase transitions: classification, critical phenomena, the renormalization group, disordered systems, and nucleation theory
foundations.summary: Phase transition physics rests on two intertwined bodies of theory that a book must not conflate. The first is equilibrium classification and criticality. Josiah Willard Gibbs established the thermodynamic potential framework for heterogeneous equilibrium; Paul Ehrenfest in 1933 proposed classifying transitions by which derivative of the thermodynamic potential is singular, giving "first order" (latent heat, discontinuous first derivative) and higher orders. Modern usage keeps Ehrenfest's first-order category but replaces "second order" with "continuous," because real continuous transitions show power-law divergences rather than the finite jumps Ehrenfest assumed. Lev Landau supplied the order-parameter and symmetry-breaking language in 1937. Ernst Ising's 1925 model, Rudolf Peierls's 1936 argument, and Lars Onsager's 1944 exact solution of the two-dimensional Ising model showed that mean-field predictions fail: exponents are non-classical (Onsager's logarithmic specific heat; C. N. Yang's beta = 1/8). Benjamin Widom's scaling hypothesis, Leo Kadanoff's block-spin construction, and Kenneth Wilson's renormalization group explained universality — exponents depend only on dimensionality, symmetry, and interaction range. Wilson received the 1982 Nobel Prize; Michael E. Fisher was his key collaborator and expositor but never shared it. Beyond the standard picture lie the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless topological transition (2016 Nobel), quantum phase transitions at zero temperature (John Hertz, Subir Sachdev), percolation, and spin glasses, where Giorgio Parisi's replica symmetry breaking (2021 Nobel) revealed an infinite hierarchy of order parameters. Philip W. Anderson's "More Is Different" (1972) is the canonical statement of emergence. The second body is kinetics: classical nucleation theory (Volmer-Weber, Becker-Döring, Turnbull-Fisher), Ostwald's step rule, metastability and supercooling, and the Cahn-Hilliard treatment of spinodal decomposition, where no nucleation barrier exists at all.

items.claim: Josiah Willard Gibbs established the thermodynamic framework for phase equilibria and coexistence in "On the equilibrium of heterogeneous substances," the work that defines chemical potential, the phase rule, surface (interfacial) free energy, and the reversible work of forming a new phase — the thermodynamic ancestor of the nucleation barrier. The full memoir appeared in the Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences (vol. 3, 108-248 in 1876 and 343-524 in 1878); Gibbs published a long abstract in the American Journal of Science in 1878.

items.claim: Paul Ehrenfest proposed classifying phase transitions by the order of the lowest derivative of the thermodynamic potential that is discontinuous: a first-order transition has a discontinuity in the first derivative (hence latent heat and a jump in entropy and volume), a second-order transition has continuous first derivatives but a discontinuous second derivative (specific heat, compressibility, thermal expansion). The paper is "Phasenumwandlungen im ueblichen und erweiterten Sinn, classifiziert nach den entsprechenden Singularitaeten des thermodynamischen Potentiales," Proceedings of the Royal Academy of Sciences at Amsterdam 36, 153-157 (1933), issued simultaneously as Communications from the Kamerlingh Onnes Laboratory, Leiden, Supplement No. 75b. An English translation with historical commentary by Tilman Sauer appeared in 2016. Books must note that Ehrenfest's higher-order categories are now obsolete: continuous transitions generically show power-law divergences, not finite jumps, so modern usage is "first-order" versus "continuous."
items.people: Paul Ehrenfest; Tilman Sauer (translator and commentator)
items.affiliation: Leiden University (Ehrenfest)
items.venue: Proc. Royal Acad. Amsterdam 36, 153-157 (1933), Commun. Kamerlingh Onnes Lab. Leiden Suppl. 75b; translation in European Physical Journal Special Topics (2016), doi:10.1140/epjst/e2016-60344-y

items.claim: Lev Davidovich Landau introduced the order parameter and the expansion of the free energy in powers of it near a continuous transition, deriving mean-field critical exponents (beta = 1/2, gamma = 1, delta = 3, alpha = 0 with a jump in specific heat) and the rule that a continuous transition requires the low-symmetry phase's symmetry group to be a subgroup of the high-symmetry phase's. Originally published in Russian as "K teorii fazovykh perekhodov," Zhurnal Eksperimental'noi i Teoreticheskoi Fiziki 7, 19-32 (1937), with a German version in Physikalische Zeitschrift der Sowjetunion 11, 26 (1937). The standard English text is in Collected Papers of L. D. Landau, edited by D. ter Haar (Pergamon, 1965), pp. 193-216.
items.people: Lev Davidovich Landau
items.venue: Zh. Eksp. Teor. Fiz. 7, 19-32 (1937); English translation in Collected Papers of L. D. Landau (Pergamon, 1965), pp. 193-216

items.claim: Ernst Ising solved the one-dimensional version of the model his doctoral supervisor Wilhelm Lenz had proposed and found no phase transition at any nonzero temperature; Ising incorrectly extrapolated this conclusion to higher dimensions. The paper is "Beitrag zur Theorie des Ferromagnetismus," Zeitschrift fuer Physik 31, 253-258 (1925). A book should credit Lenz with the model and Ising with the one-dimensional solution, and should not repeat the myth that Ising proved there is no transition in two dimensions.
items.people: Ernst Ising
items.affiliation: University of Hamburg

items.claim: Rudolf Peierls gave the first argument that the two-dimensional Ising model does order at low temperature, by bounding the entropy versus energy cost of domain-wall contours — the "Peierls argument," still the standard textbook proof that a transition exists. Published as "On Ising's model of ferromagnetism," Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 32, 477-481 (1936).
items.people: Rudolf Peierls
items.venue: Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 32(3), 477-481

items.claim: Lars Onsager obtained the exact partition function of the two-dimensional square-lattice Ising model in zero field, demonstrating a genuine continuous phase transition with a logarithmically divergent specific heat (alpha = 0, log) and the exact critical temperature given by sinh(2J/kT_c) = 1, i.e. kT_c/J = 2/ln(1 + sqrt(2)) ~ 2.269. This was the first exact demonstration that a microscopic model produces non-mean-field critical behaviour, and it killed the assumption that critical exponents are classical. Published as "Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition," Physical Review 65, 117-149 (1 February 1944).
items.people: Lars Onsager
items.affiliation: Yale University

items.claim: Chen Ning Yang published the first derivation of the spontaneous magnetization of the two-dimensional Ising model, giving the order-parameter exponent beta = 1/8. Onsager had announced the result in 1948 without publishing a proof, so the exponent should be attributed to Yang's 1952 paper (with Onsager's priority acknowledged), not to the 1944 Onsager paper. Published as "The Spontaneous Magnetization of a Two-Dimensional Ising Model," Physical Review 85, 808-816 (1952).
items.people: Chen Ning Yang
items.affiliation: Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton

items.claim: Edward Armand Guggenheim showed that the liquid-gas coexistence curves of eight different substances (neon, argon, krypton, xenon, nitrogen, oxygen, carbon monoxide, methane) collapse onto a single curve when scaled by critical parameters, and that the curve is fitted by an exponent near 1/3 rather than the van der Waals mean-field value 1/2. This is the classic experimental evidence for universality and for non-classical exponents, predating the renormalization group by a quarter century. Published as "The Principle of Corresponding States," Journal of Chemical Physics 13(7), 253-261 (1945).
items.people: Edward Armand Guggenheim

items.claim: Benjamin Widom proposed the scaling hypothesis for the equation of state near a critical point — that the singular part of the free energy is a generalized homogeneous function of temperature and field — from which the scaling relations among critical exponents (including alpha + 2*beta + gamma = 2, later called the Rushbrooke relation, and gamma = beta*(delta - 1), the Widom relation) follow. Published as "Equation of State in the Neighborhood of the Critical Point," Journal of Chemical Physics 43(11), 3898-3905 (1965). Scaling here is phenomenological; it is Wilson's renormalization group that later explains why it holds.
items.people: Benjamin Widom

items.claim: Leo Philip Kadanoff introduced the block-spin construction: divide an Ising lattice into cells large compared with the lattice spacing but small compared with the correlation length, replace each cell by a single effective spin, and argue that the coarse-grained system is again an Ising model with rescaled coupling and field. This gave a physical rationale for Widom scaling and is the conceptual seed of the renormalization group. Published as "Scaling laws for Ising models near T_c," Physics Physique Fizika 2, 263-272 (1966) — note the unusual short-lived journal name, often miscited simply as "Physics."
items.people: Leo Philip Kadanoff
items.affiliation: University of Illinois, Urbana

items.claim: Kenneth Geddes Wilson turned Kadanoff's block-spin picture into a systematic calculational method by casting coarse-graining as a differential flow in the space of coupling constants, with critical points appearing as fixed points of the flow and critical exponents as eigenvalues of the linearized flow about the fixed point. Universality follows because distinct microscopic Hamiltonians flow to the same fixed point. Published as a pair of companion papers: "Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena. I. Renormalization Group and the Kadanoff Scaling Picture," Physical Review B 4, 3174-3183, and "II. Phase-Space Cell Analysis of Critical Behavior," Physical Review B 4, 3184-3205, both 1971.
items.people: Kenneth Geddes Wilson
items.affiliation: Cornell University

items.claim: Kenneth G. Wilson and Michael E. Fisher introduced the epsilon expansion, computing critical exponents in d = 4 - epsilon dimensions as a controlled perturbative series about the upper critical dimension four, where mean-field theory becomes exact. Setting epsilon = 1 gives usable three-dimensional exponents. Published as "Critical Exponents in 3.99 Dimensions," Physical Review Letters 28(4), 240-243, issue dated 24 January 1972.
items.people: Kenneth G. Wilson, Michael E. Fisher
items.affiliation: Cornell University

items.claim: Michael Ellis Fisher wrote the standard introductory review of the renormalization group approach to critical behaviour, covering the dependence of exponents on dimensionality d, on the number of order-parameter components n, and on the range and anisotropy of interactions — that is, the precise content of a universality class. Published as "The renormalization group in the theory of critical behavior," Reviews of Modern Physics 46, 597-616 (1 October 1974). Note a common citation error: Reviews of Modern Physics 47, 543 (1975) is the erratum, not the article.
items.people: Michael Ellis Fisher
items.affiliation: Cornell University

items.claim: The Nobel Prize in Physics 1982 was awarded to Kenneth G. Wilson alone, "for his theory for critical phenomena in connection with phase transitions." Wilson was a professor of physics at Cornell University, where he did the prizewinning work. Michael E. Fisher and Leo P. Kadanoff, whose work was essential to the development, did not share the prize — a point books frequently get wrong; the three were, however, jointly awarded the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1980.
items.people: Kenneth G. Wilson
items.affiliation: Cornell University
items.venue: Nobel Prize in Physics, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

items.claim: Norman David Mermin and Herbert Wagner proved that continuous symmetries cannot be spontaneously broken at any nonzero temperature in one- or two-dimensional systems with sufficiently short-range interactions, ruling out conventional long-range order in the 2D Heisenberg and XY models. This theorem is the obstacle that the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless mechanism circumvents, since BKT order is topological rather than conventional. Published as "Absence of Ferromagnetism or Antiferromagnetism in One- or Two-Dimensional Isotropic Heisenberg Models," Physical Review Letters 17(22), 1133-1136 (1966).
items.people: Norman David Mermin, Herbert Wagner

items.claim: Vadim Lvovich Berezinskii independently identified the destruction of long-range order by topological excitations in two-dimensional systems with continuous symmetry, publishing before Kosterlitz and Thouless. The paper is "Destruction of Long-range Order in One-dimensional and Two-dimensional Systems having a Continuous Symmetry Group. I. Classical Systems," Soviet Physics JETP 32(3), 493 (March 1971); Russian original ZhETF 59(3), 907 (1971). This is why the transition is properly called the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition; Berezinskii died in 1980 and was therefore ineligible for the 2016 Nobel Prize.
items.people: Vadim Lvovich Berezinskii
items.venue: Soviet Physics JETP 32(3), 493-500 (Russian original: Zhurnal Eksperimental'noi i Teoreticheskoi Fiziki 59(3), 907)

items.claim: John Michael Kosterlitz and David James Thouless defined topological order for two-dimensional systems that have no conventional long-range order, and described a transition driven by the unbinding of vortex-antivortex pairs: below the transition vortices are bound in neutral pairs, above it they are free, destroying superfluid stiffness. The transition is infinite-order in the Ehrenfest sense — the free energy is non-analytic but all derivatives are continuous, and the correlation length diverges exponentially rather than as a power law. Published as "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems," Journal of Physics C: Solid State Physics 6(7), 1181-1203 (1973). Kosterlitz supplied the renormalization-group treatment the following year in J. Phys. C 7, 1046-1060 (1974).
items.people: John Michael Kosterlitz, David James Thouless
items.affiliation: University of Birmingham
items.venue: Journal of Physics C: Solid State Physics 6(7), 1181-1203

items.claim: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2016 was awarded "for theoretical discoveries of topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter," with one half to David J. Thouless (University of Washington, Seattle) and the other half jointly to F. Duncan M. Haldane (Princeton University) and J. Michael Kosterlitz (Brown University). Books must get the split right: it was one-half / one-quarter / one-quarter, not an equal three-way division.
items.people: David J. Thouless, F. Duncan M. Haldane, J. Michael Kosterlitz
items.affiliation: University of Washington (Thouless); Princeton University (Haldane); Brown University (Kosterlitz)
items.venue: Nobel Prize in Physics, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

items.claim: John A. Hertz formulated the theory of zero-temperature (quantum) critical points by using Hubbard-Stratonovich functional integral transformations to build a quantum generalization of the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson functional in which the order-parameter field depends on imaginary time as well as space. This introduces the dynamical critical exponent z and the effective dimension d + z, so that quantum critical points in three dimensions can sit at or above the upper critical dimension. Published as "Quantum critical phenomena," Physical Review B 14(3), 1165-1184 (1 August 1976). The framework, extended by A. J. Millis in 1993, is standard as "Hertz-Millis theory."
items.people: John A. Hertz
items.affiliation: The James Franck Institute and Department of Physics, University of Chicago

items.claim: Subir Sachdev wrote the standard monograph on quantum phase transitions — transitions at absolute zero driven by a non-thermal control parameter such as pressure, magnetic field, or doping, where quantum rather than thermal fluctuations drive the change, and where the quantum critical point governs a fan-shaped finite-temperature region of anomalous behaviour. The book is Quantum Phase Transitions, Cambridge University Press; first edition 1999 (written while Sachdev was at Yale University), second edition 2011 (Harvard University), ISBN 978-0-521-51468-2. An accessible companion is Sachdev and Bernhard Keimer, "Quantum criticality," Physics Today 64(2), 29-35 (2011), doi:10.1063/1.3554314.
items.people: Subir Sachdev
items.affiliation: Harvard University (2nd edition); Yale University (1st edition)

items.claim: Simon Ralph Broadbent and John Michael Hammersley founded percolation theory, introducing the distinction between a random "medium" and a deterministic "fluid" and establishing the existence of a sharp critical probability p_c above which an infinite connected cluster appears. Percolation is the canonical purely geometric continuous phase transition, with its own critical exponents and universality classes and no Hamiltonian or temperature. Published as "Percolation processes. I. Crystals and mazes," Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 53(3), 629-641 (July 1957).
items.people: Simon Ralph Broadbent, John Michael Hammersley
items.venue: Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 53(3), 629-641

items.claim: Samuel Frederick Edwards and Philip Warren Anderson introduced the first theory of spin glasses, proposing that in dilute magnetic alloys the RKKY interaction oscillates in sign with distance so that there is no net ferro- or antiferromagnetic order, yet below a freezing temperature the spins lock into definite random directions. Their order parameter q — the time-averaged local magnetization squared, averaged over sites — is the Edwards-Anderson order parameter, and it explains the cusp observed experimentally in the susceptibility. Published as "Theory of spin glasses," Journal of Physics F: Metal Physics 5(5), 965-974 (May 1975); a second part appeared in J. Phys. F 6, 1927 (1976).
items.people: Samuel Frederick Edwards, Philip Warren Anderson
items.affiliation: Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge
items.venue: Journal of Physics F: Metal Physics 5(5), 965-974

items.claim: David Sherrington and Scott Kirkpatrick introduced the infinite-range (mean-field) spin glass: an Ising model in which every pair of spins is coupled by an independent Gaussian random interaction. Solving it by the replica trick with a replica-symmetric ansatz, they found both spin-glass and ferromagnetic phases — but the solution gives a negative entropy at zero temperature, an unphysical result that signalled the breakdown of replica symmetry and set the problem Parisi later solved. Published as "Solvable Model of a Spin-Glass," Physical Review Letters 35(26), 1792-1796 (1975).
items.people: David Sherrington, Scott Kirkpatrick

items.claim: Giorgio Parisi showed that the mean-field spin glass requires an infinite number of order parameters — a full function q(x) on the interval [0,1] rather than a single number — obtained by breaking the permutation symmetry among replicas in a nested, hierarchical (ultrametric) way. This is replica symmetry breaking, and it describes a rugged free-energy landscape with many pure states organized in a hierarchy. Published as "Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses," Physical Review Letters 43(23), 1754-1756 (received 22 June 1979, published 3 December 1979), with the explicit scheme in "A sequence of approximated solutions to the S-K model for spin glasses," Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General 13(4), L115-L121 (1980). The solution's correctness was proved rigorously by Michel Talagrand in 2006, building on Francesco Guerra's 2003 interpolation bound.
items.people: Giorgio Parisi
items.venue: Physical Review Letters 43(23), 1754-1756; Journal of Physics A 13(4), L115-L121

items.claim: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2021 was awarded "for groundbreaking contributions to our understanding of complex systems," divided with one half jointly to Syukuro Manabe and Klaus Hasselmann for physical modelling of Earth's climate, and the other half to Giorgio Parisi (Sapienza University of Rome) "for the discovery of the interplay of disorder and fluctuations in physical systems from atomic to planetary scales." Parisi's citation dates the key discovery to around 1980. Books should not describe this as a prize shared equally three ways, nor as a prize for spin glasses alone.
items.people: Giorgio Parisi, Syukuro Manabe, Klaus Hasselmann
items.affiliation: Sapienza University of Rome (Parisi)
items.venue: Nobel Prize in Physics, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

items.claim: Philip Warren Anderson argued that the reductionist hypothesis does not imply a constructionist one: at each level of complexity entirely new properties appear, and the science of one level is not simply applied science of the level below. Broken symmetry — exactly the phenomenon that defines a phase transition — is his central example of how new organizing principles emerge at larger scales. Published as "More Is Different: Broken symmetry and the nature of the hierarchical structure of science," Science 177(4047), 393-396, 4 August 1972. This is the canonical citation for emergence in phase-transition writing.
items.people: Philip Warren Anderson
items.affiliation: Bell Telephone Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey

items.claim: Max Volmer and Alfred Weber laid the foundation of classical nucleation theory, treating the formation of a nucleus in a supersaturated phase as a competition between a favourable bulk free-energy term proportional to volume and an unfavourable interfacial term proportional to surface area, producing a free-energy barrier at a critical nucleus size and a nucleation rate exponential in that barrier. Published as "Keimbildung in uebersaettigten Gebilden," Zeitschrift fuer Physikalische Chemie 119U(1), 277-301 (1926).
items.people: Max Volmer, Alfred Weber

items.claim: Richard Becker and Werner Doering gave the kinetic formulation of classical nucleation theory, treating nucleation as a birth-and-death process in cluster size space and deriving the steady-state nucleation rate including the Zeldovich non-equilibrium correction factor. The resulting Becker-Doering equations remain the standard kinetic model of nucleation. Published as "Kinetische Behandlung der Keimbildung in uebersaettigten Daempfen," Annalen der Physik 416(8), 719-752 (1935).
items.people: Richard Becker, Werner Doering (Döring)

items.claim: David Turnbull and John Chipman Fisher adapted classical nucleation theory to condensed systems, supplying the rate expression with an activation term for the transport of atoms across the nucleus-matrix interface — the form used for crystallization from melts and solutions, and the basis for Turnbull's later experiments showing that liquid metals can be supercooled to roughly 0.8 of their melting temperature before nucleating. Published as "Rate of Nucleation in Condensed Systems," Journal of Chemical Physics 17(1), 71-73 (1949).
items.people: David Turnbull, John Chipman Fisher

items.claim: Wilhelm Ostwald formulated the rule of stages (Ostwald's Stufenregel): a supersaturated or supercooled system does not necessarily transform directly into the thermodynamically most stable phase, but tends first to form the least stable phase whose free energy is nearest to that of the parent phase, then transforms stepwise toward stability. This is a kinetic, not a thermodynamic, principle, and it underlies polymorph selection in crystallization. Published as "Studien ueber die Bildung und Umwandlung fester Koerper. 1. Abhandlung: Uebersaettigung und Ueberkaltung," Zeitschrift fuer Physikalische Chemie 22U(1), 289-330 (1897).
items.people: Wilhelm Ostwald
items.affiliation: University of Leipzig

items.claim: John Werner Cahn and John Edward Hilliard introduced the square-gradient free-energy functional for a system of nonuniform composition, F = N_V * integral over V of [f_0(c) + kappa*(grad c)^2] dV, where f_0 is the homogeneous free energy per molecule and kappa the gradient-energy coefficient. This is the basis of all diffuse-interface and phase-field modelling of transitions. Published as "Free Energy of a Nonuniform System. I. Interfacial Free Energy," Journal of Chemical Physics 28(2), 258-267 (1958). Part III of the series, "Nucleation in a Two-Component Incompressible Fluid," J. Chem. Phys. 31(3), 688-699 (1959), doi:10.1063/1.1730447, derives the critical nucleus as a saddle point of this functional and shows the classical sharp-interface nucleus fails near the spinodal.
items.people: John Werner Cahn, John Edward Hilliard
items.affiliation: General Electric Research Laboratory, Schenectady, New York

items.claim: John Werner Cahn established the theory of spinodal decomposition: inside the spinodal region, where the second derivative of free energy with respect to composition is negative, a homogeneous solution is unstable to infinitesimal composition fluctuations, so phase separation proceeds by spontaneous continuous amplification of long-wavelength fluctuations with no nucleation barrier and no critical nucleus — in sharp contrast to nucleation and growth in the metastable region between the binodal and the spinodal. Cahn derived the fastest-growing wavelength that sets the characteristic microstructural scale, and showed that elastic energy from composition-dependent molar volume shifts the true limit of metastability away from the chemical spinodal. Published as "On spinodal decomposition," Acta Metallurgica 9(9), 795-801 (1961); the cubic-crystal extension is Acta Metallurgica 10(3), 179-183 (1962).
items.people: John Werner Cahn
items.affiliation: General Electric Research Laboratory, Schenectady, New York

openQuestions: Whether the three-dimensional Edwards-Anderson short-range spin glass actually exhibits Parisi's full replica symmetry breaking, or instead the two-state 'droplet' picture of Daniel S. Fisher and David A. Huse. This remains genuinely unsettled and a book should not present RSB in finite dimensions as established; Parisi's solution is proved only for the infinite-range Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model.

Whether an exact closed-form solution of the three-dimensional Ising model exists. None is known, and claims of one appear periodically and are not accepted. The best modern three-dimensional exponents come from the conformal bootstrap, not from an exact solution — a book should attribute the precise 3D Ising exponents to bootstrap and Monte Carlo work rather than implying Onsager's method generalizes.

Whether Hertz-Millis theory adequately describes metallic quantum critical points. The heavy-fermion and cuprate cases show apparent violations (local quantum criticality, strange-metal linear-in-T resistivity) that the order-parameter-only Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson framework does not capture, since fermionic excitations cannot always be integrated out safely.

The status of non-classical and two-step nucleation. A growing body of simulation and experiment suggests nucleation frequently proceeds through dense amorphous or prenucleation-cluster intermediates rather than the single spherical critical nucleus of classical nucleation theory. Classical nucleation theory routinely mispredicts absolute rates by many orders of magnitude, and a book should present its capillarity approximation as a useful idealization rather than a quantitative law.

Whether the metastable-to-unstable boundary (the spinodal) is a genuine sharp line or a mean-field artifact. In systems with short-range interactions the spinodal is smeared into a crossover; it is sharp only in the limit of infinite interaction range. Presenting 'nucleation and growth versus spinodal decomposition' as a crisp dichotomy overstates the case.

How to characterize infinite-order transitions within the Ehrenfest framework. The BKT transition has a non-analytic free energy with all derivatives continuous, which the Ehrenfest scheme cannot label; the same issue arises for topological transitions generally, and a book needs to be explicit that the first-order/continuous dichotomy is not exhaustive.

Whether Berezinskii should be named in the transition alongside Kosterlitz and Thouless. Usage is genuinely split between 'KT' and 'BKT' in the literature; the priority facts (Berezinskii 1971 versus Kosterlitz-Thouless 1973) are clear but the naming convention is not.

verdicts.claim: Gibbs, 'On the equilibrium of heterogeneous substances'; full memoir Trans. Connecticut Acad. Arts Sci. 3, 108-248 (1876) and 343-524 (1878); abstract in Am. J. Sci. ser. 3, vol. 16, no. 96, 441-458 (1878). URL https://doi.org/10.2475/ajs.s3-16.96.441

Ehrenfest 1933, 'Phasenumwandlungen im ueblichen und erweiterten Sinn...', Proc. Royal Acad. Amsterdam 36, 153-157, Commun. Kamerlingh Onnes Lab. Leiden Suppl. 75b; English translation and commentary by Tilman Sauer, EPJ Special Topics (2016), doi:10.1140/epjst/e2016-60344-y
verdicts.correction: The Ehrenfest original is exactly right (Proc. Royal Acad. Amsterdam 36, 153-157, 1933; Commun. Kamerlingh Onnes Lab. Leiden Suppl. 75b), and arXiv:1612.03062 resolves to Sauer's translation. But the Sauer translation year and volume are wrong. Correct text: 'An English translation with historical commentary by Tilman Sauer, "A look back at the Ehrenfest classification," European Physical Journal Special Topics 226, 539-549 (2017), doi:10.1140/epjst/e2016-60344-y (posted as arXiv:1612.03062 in December 2016).' Correct URL: https://doi.org/10.1140/epjst/e2016-60344-y (preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.03062). Separately, a caution on the editorial gloss: the dossier asserts books 'must note that Ehrenfest's higher-order categories are now obsolete.' Sauer's own commentary does not say this — it notes the He I / He II lambda-point logarithmic divergence forced modification but argues the framework 'remains important' and proved fruitful. Safer wording: Ehrenfest's higher-order categories do not describe real continuous transitions, which show power-law divergences rather than finite jumps, so modern usage is 'first-order' versus 'continuous.'

verdicts.correction: The author's name is fabricated. The co-author is John Crocker Fisher (born 19 December 1919, Ithaca NY; died 2 May 2018), Sc.D. MIT 1947, of General Electric Research Laboratory, who managed GE's physical metallurgy section. 'John Chipman' is an entirely different person — the MIT metallurgist and steelmaking chemist — and conflating the two would put a wrong name for a real man in print. Correct text: 'David Turnbull and John Crocker Fisher adapted classical nucleation theory to condensed systems... Published as "Rate of Nucleation in Condensed Systems," Journal of Chemical Physics 17(1), 71-73 (1949).' Everything else in the item checks out: the paper exists with that exact title, JCP volume 17, issue 1, pages 71-73, 1949, authors ordered Turnbull then Fisher, and the URL https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1747055 resolves to it. Note for the author: a stray erratum, JCP 17(4), 429 (1949), also exists, and some secondary databases circulate a wrong DOI (10.1063/1.1747279) and a wrong issue number (No. 4) for this paper — cite 10.1063/1.1747055 and issue 1. The supercooling figure (liquid metals to roughly 0.8 T_m) is accurate.
