tipping-points.domain: AI and early warning signals for critical transitions and tipping points in complex physical systems
tipping-points.summary: The theory of critical slowing down holds that as a dynamical system approaches a fold (saddle-node) bifurcation, the dominant eigenvalue approaches zero, recovery from perturbation slows, and the system's fluctuations show rising variance and rising lag-1 autocorrelation. Marten Scheffer, Stephen R. Carpenter, Vasilis Dakos, Timothy M. Lenton and colleagues formalized this as a generic early-warning framework in Nature in 2009, following Dakos's 2008 PNAS analysis of eight paleoclimate shifts; the statistical toolbox was standardized in Dakos et al., PLoS ONE 7(7), e41010 (10.1371/journal.pone.0041010), and the cross-system case was made in Scheffer et al., Science 338, 344-348 (10.1126/science.1225244). Since 2021 the field has taken a machine-learning turn: Thomas M. Bury, Chris T. Bauch and Madhur Anand trained a deep classifier on ~500,000 simulated time series generated by AUTO-07P continuation, teaching it to distinguish fold, Hopf, transcritical and null outcomes, then applied it to sedimentary anoxia records, thermoacoustic combustion experiments and paleoclimate transitions. The most contested application is the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, where Niklas Boers (2021) and Peter Ditlevsen and Susanne Ditlevsen (2023) reported critical slowing down in sea-surface temperature fingerprints, the latter naming a collapse window. That claim drew serious, specific rebuttal — Xianyao Chen and Ka-Kit Tung on observational-coverage artifacts and a sign error, Maya Ben-Yami and colleagues on gap-filling artifacts and on extrapolation uncertainty, and an August 2025 Author Correction that shifted the central tipping estimate by eight years. Any responsible account must also separate bifurcation-induced tipping from noise-induced and rate-induced tipping, and must confront documented false-positive rates and base-rate problems.

items.claim: The generic early-warning framework for critical transitions was set out by Marten Scheffer and colleagues in Nature in 2009, arguing that systems approaching a catastrophic bifurcation exhibit critical slowing down, detectable as rising variance, rising lag-1 autocorrelation, increased skewness and 'flickering' in time-series data, and that these indicators are largely independent of the specific mechanism driving the system.
items.people: Marten Scheffer, Jordi Bascompte, William A. Brock, Victor Brovkin, Stephen R. Carpenter, Vasilis Dakos, Hermann Held, Egbert H. van Nes, Max Rietkerk, George Sugihara

items.claim: Vasilis Dakos and co-authors showed in 2008 that eight ancient abrupt climate shifts recorded in paleoclimate archives were each preceded by a characteristic slowing down of fluctuations, measured as increasing autocorrelation, beginning well before the transition itself.
items.people: Vasilis Dakos, Marten Scheffer, Egbert H. van Nes, Victor Brovkin, Vladimir Petoukhov, Hermann Held
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 105(38), 14308-14312

items.claim: Stephen R. Carpenter and colleagues provided the strongest experimental confirmation of early-warning signals by deliberately destabilizing the food web of a whole lake over three years through gradual addition of a top predator, while monitoring an adjacent unmanipulated lake as a reference; high-frequency monitoring detected rising variance and slowing recovery in advance of the regime shift.
items.people: Stephen R. Carpenter, Jonathan J. Cole, Michael L. Pace, Ryan Batt, William A. Brock, Timothy Cline, Jim Coloso, James R. Hodgson, James F. Kitchell, David A. Seekell, Laura Smith, Brian Weidel

items.claim: The concept of 'tipping elements' — large-scale components of the Earth system that can be switched into a qualitatively different state by small perturbations — was introduced by Timothy M. Lenton and colleagues in 2008, with an initial shortlist that included the Atlantic thermohaline circulation, the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, Arctic sea ice, the Amazon rainforest and the Indian summer monsoon.
items.people: Timothy M. Lenton, Hermann Held, Elmar Kriegler, Jim W. Hall, Wolfgang Lucht, Stefan Rahmstorf, Hans Joachim Schellnhuber
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 105(6), 1786-1793

items.claim: An updated expert assessment led by David I. Armstrong McKay and Timothy M. Lenton concluded that exceeding 1.5 °C of global warming could trigger multiple climate tipping points, including the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets and abrupt permafrost thaw, with central threshold estimates for several elements falling inside the Paris Agreement temperature range.
items.people: David I. Armstrong McKay, Arie Staal, Jesse F. Abrams, Ricarda Winkelmann, Boris Sakschewski, Sina Loriani, Ingo Fetzer, Sarah E. Cornell, Johan Rockström, Timothy M. Lenton

items.claim: Thomas M. Bury, Chris T. Bauch and Madhur Anand, with co-authors, built a deep learning early-warning classifier trained entirely on simulated data — time series generated with the AUTO-07P bifurcation continuation software, labelled as fold, Hopf, transcritical or null — and reported that it outperformed conventional variance and autocorrelation indicators when applied to sedimentary records of Mediterranean anoxic events, thermoacoustic instability experiments, and paleoclimate transition records.
items.people: Thomas M. Bury, R. I. Sujith, Induja Pavithran, Marten Scheffer, Timothy M. Lenton, Madhur Anand, Chris T. Bauch
items.affiliation: University of Waterloo and University of Guelph (Bury); Indian Institute of Technology Madras (Sujith, Pavithran); Wageningen University (Scheffer); University of Exeter (Lenton); University of Guelph (Anand); University of Waterloo (Bauch)
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 118(39), e2106140118

items.claim: In an unusual act of self-critique, Thomas M. Bury co-authored a PNAS letter with Fabian Dablander showing that the performance of the deep learning early-warning classifier is highly sensitive to preprocessing: because every training example was detrended with a Gaussian filter of a particular bandwidth, the network implicitly requires the same filter at application time, and its apparent advantage over classical indicators shrinks when preprocessing choices are varied.
items.people: Fabian Dablander, Thomas M. Bury
items.affiliation: University of Amsterdam (Dablander); McGill University (Bury)
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 119(37), e2207720119

items.claim: Chris T. Bauch and Madhur Anand replied to the preprocessing critique by conceding the point on filter consistency — recommending that the same filter be used for training, testing and application — while framing the deeper problem as the 'unknown unknowns' of deep learning, and calling for training sets covering a greater variety of bifurcation types and noise structures.
items.people: Chris T. Bauch, Madhur Anand
items.affiliation: University of Waterloo (Bauch); University of Guelph (Anand)
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 119(37), e2210407119

items.claim: Niklas Boers reported early-warning signals consistent with critical slowing down in eight independent AMOC indices derived from observational sea-surface temperature and salinity data across the Atlantic basin, concluding that the AMOC may be approaching a bifurcation-induced transition rather than merely weakening.
items.people: Niklas Boers
items.affiliation: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and Technical University of Munich

items.claim: Xianyao Chen and Ka-Kit Tung published a formal Matters Arising challenging the AMOC early-warning result, arguing that the eight proxies contain artificial increases in variance driven by expanding observational coverage over the twentieth century, that climate models with no genuine early-warning signal reproduce apparent warnings when sampled according to historical coverage, and that the sign of two of the subpolar proxies had been reversed in error.
items.people: Xianyao Chen, Ka-Kit Tung

items.claim: Niklas Boers published a reply in the same issue of Nature Climate Change defending the early-warning analysis against the observational-coverage and sign-convention objections raised by Xianyao Chen and Ka-Kit Tung.
items.people: Niklas Boers
items.affiliation: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and Technical University of Munich

items.claim: Peter Ditlevsen and Susanne Ditlevsen fitted a stochastic differential equation representing an approach to a saddle-node bifurcation to a subpolar-gyre sea-surface-temperature fingerprint of AMOC strength from HadISST covering 1870-2020, using both moment-based estimators and a Strang-splitting maximum likelihood estimator, and as originally published estimated a collapse around 2057 with a 95% confidence interval of 2025 to 2095.
items.people: Peter D. Ditlevsen, Susanne Ditlevsen
items.affiliation: Niels Bohr Institute, University of Copenhagen (Peter Ditlevsen); Department of Mathematical Sciences, University of Copenhagen (Susanne Ditlevsen)

items.claim: On 21 August 2025 Peter Ditlevsen and Susanne Ditlevsen published an Author Correction acknowledging a coding error in the Strang-splitting maximum likelihood estimator — the flow had been partially evaluated at time t_(i-1) rather than at the observation time t_i — identified by Anders Gantzhorn Kristensen; correcting it shifted the tipping time estimate by eight years, moving the reported window to 2037-2109 and requiring revision of Figures 5, 6 and 7 and Table 1.
items.people: Peter D. Ditlevsen, Susanne Ditlevsen, Anders Gantzhorn Kristensen
items.affiliation: University of Copenhagen
items.venue: Nature Communications 16, 7794 (Author Correction to Nat. Commun. 14, 4254)

items.claim: Maya Ben-Yami and colleagues showed that the observational datasets used for AMOC early-warning analysis have non-stationary missing-data distributions, and that gap-filling procedures can in some cases manufacture false indications of critical slowing down; after propagating dataset uncertainties and applying conservative significance tests, they nonetheless found the North Atlantic stability decline remained significant.
items.people: Maya Ben-Yami, Vanessa Skiba, Sebastian Bathiany, Niklas Boers
items.affiliation: Technical University of Munich

items.claim: Maya Ben-Yami, Andreas Morr, Sebastian Bathiany and Niklas Boers argued that even granting that an Earth system component is approaching a tipping point, the uncertainties — arising from modelling assumptions in the extrapolation, the representativeness of the chosen time series, and observational error plus preprocessing — are too large to permit a reliable estimate of when tipping will occur; they used the AMOC as their worked case.
items.people: Maya Ben-Yami, Andreas Morr, Sebastian Bathiany, Niklas Boers
items.affiliation: Technical University of Munich

items.claim: René M. van Westen, Michael Kliphuis and Henk A. Dijkstra introduced a physics-based early-warning signal — the freshwater transport by the overturning at the southern boundary of the Atlantic — which, unlike statistical critical-slowing-down indicators, is grounded in the salt-advection feedback, and reported that reanalysis products indicate the AMOC is on a tipping course.
items.people: René M. van Westen, Michael Kliphuis, Henk A. Dijkstra

items.claim: A modelling study led by Jonathan A. Baker provided a counterpoint to imminent-collapse claims, finding continued Atlantic overturning circulation even under extreme climate forcing scenarios, largely because Southern Ocean wind-driven upwelling sustains the circulation; the paper itself later received an Author Correction.
items.people: Jonathan A. Baker, Michael J. Bell, Laura C. Jackson, Geoffrey K. Vallis, Andrew J. Watson, Richard A. Wood

items.claim: Stefan Rahmstorf's review of the AMOC tipping question accepted that multiple independent early-warning analyses point in the same direction, but drew a sharply limiting conclusion: by the time such signals can provide a reasonably reliable warning of impending AMOC tipping it will be too late to prevent it, and observed changes in variability might have causes unrelated to an approaching threshold — an argument he treats as grounds for precaution rather than for confident prediction.
items.people: Stefan Rahmstorf

items.claim: Peter D. Ditlevsen and Sigfus J. Johnsen analysed Greenland ice-core records of Dansgaard-Oeschger events and concluded that these abrupt shifts show no critical slowing down before the transition, implying they were noise-induced rather than bifurcation-induced and therefore have very limited predictability — the paper is titled 'Tipping points: Early warning and wishful thinking'.
items.people: Peter D. Ditlevsen, Sigfus J. Johnsen

items.claim: Peter Ashwin, Sebastian Wieczorek, Renato Vitolo and Peter Cox established the standard taxonomy distinguishing three mechanisms of tipping in open systems: bifurcation-induced tipping, noise-induced tipping, and rate-induced tipping, in which a system fails to track a moving stable state because the forcing changes too quickly, even though no bifurcation is crossed. Only the first of the three reliably produces critical slowing down.
items.people: Peter Ashwin, Sebastian Wieczorek, Renato Vitolo, Peter Cox
items.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 370(1962), 1166-1184

items.claim: Carl Boettiger and Alan Hastings used large deviation theory to show that purely stochastic transitions between alternative stable states are not preceded by early-warning signals, so the presence or absence of critical slowing down cannot by itself establish that a system is approaching a bifurcation.
items.people: Carl Boettiger, Alan Hastings
items.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B 280(1766), 20131372

items.claim: Alan Hastings and Derin B. Wysham demonstrated that the class of systems exhibiting leading indicators of regime shifts is limited, constructing ecological models and identifying natural systems in which a regime change occurs with no forewarning at all.
items.people: Alan Hastings, Derin B. Wysham

items.claim: Niklas Boers and Martin Rypdal found critical slowing down in melt-rate and ice-core records from the central-western Greenland Ice Sheet, arguing that this sector is close to a tipping point associated with the melt-elevation feedback.
items.people: Niklas Boers, Martin Rypdal
items.affiliation: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and Technical University of Munich (Boers)
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 118(21), e2024192118

items.claim: A 2025 Nature Geoscience review led by Niklas Boers, with Timothy M. Lenton and Chris A. Boulton among the authors, synthesized the observational evidence for destabilization across Earth system tipping elements — including the AMOC, the polar ice sheets, the Amazon and permafrost systems — and assessed what critical-slowing-down indicators can and cannot establish for each.
items.people: Niklas Boers, Teng Liu, Sebastian Bathiany, Maya Ben-Yami, Lana L. Blaschke, Nils Bochow, Chris A. Boulton, Timothy M. Lenton, Andreas Morr, Da Nian, Martin Rypdal, Taylor Smith

items.claim: The Global Tipping Points Report, led by Timothy M. Lenton at the University of Exeter's Global Systems Institute with more than 160 authors from over 87 institutions across 23 countries, appeared in a first edition in 2023 and a second in 2025; the 2025 edition states that warm-water coral reefs are already crossing a tipping point at roughly 1.4 °C of warming, that the polar ice sheets may have passed thresholds committing the world to several metres of irreversible sea-level rise, and that the Amazon and the AMOC are both at risk below 2 °C.
items.people: Timothy M. Lenton
items.affiliation: Global Systems Institute, University of Exeter
items.venue: Global Tipping Points Report 2025, University of Exeter (second edition; first edition 2023)

openQuestions: Can any early-warning indicator distinguish an approaching bifurcation from a noise-induced or rate-induced transition using observational data alone? Ashwin et al. (2012) define the three mechanisms, and Boettiger and Hastings (2013) show stochastic transitions give no warning, but no accepted observational discriminator exists.

Does a neural network trained exclusively on low-dimensional simulated normal forms genuinely generalize to a high-dimensional, spatially extended, non-stationary system like the ocean circulation, or is its apparent skill an artifact of shared preprocessing between training and application? The Dablander-Bury exchange with Bauch and Anand leaves this unresolved.

What are the actual false-positive and false-negative rates of deep-learning early-warning classifiers on real geophysical records, as opposed to held-out simulations? Published validation is overwhelmingly on synthetic test sets.

Ben-Yami et al. (2024) argue that tipping *times* cannot be reliably extrapolated even when destabilization is real. Is there any statistical route to a defensible collapse-date confidence interval, or should the field abandon date estimates and report only stability trends?

How much of the reported AMOC critical slowing down survives full accounting for changing observational coverage, gap-filling, and instrument transitions? Chen and Tung say almost none; Ben-Yami et al. and Boers say a significant residual remains. This is an open empirical dispute.

Why do the statistical early-warning signals and the process-based ocean models disagree so sharply — Boers, the Ditlevsens, and van Westen et al. pointing toward tipping, Baker et al. (2025) finding a resilient overturning under extreme forcing?

Early-warning methodology is far less developed for permafrost than for ice sheets or the AMOC, partly because abrupt thaw is spatially heterogeneous and lacks a single long observational index. What would a defensible permafrost early-warning indicator even look like?

Does the field have a publication-bias problem, in that datasets showing critical slowing down before a known transition are reported while null cases are not, inflating apparent skill? The base-rate concern raised in the early-warning literature has never been quantified across the corpus.

The August 2025 Author Correction to Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen moved the central estimate by eight years on the basis of a single line of estimator code. What does that sensitivity imply about the robustness of the whole class of maximum-likelihood tipping-time estimators?

verdicts.claim: The generic early-warning framework for critical transitions was set out by Marten Scheffer and colleagues in Nature in 2009 (Nature 461(7260), 53-59), including rising variance, rising lag-1 autocorrelation, increased skewness and 'flickering'.
Vasilis Dakos et al. 2008 showed eight ancient abrupt climate shifts were preceded by slowing down (PNAS 105(38), 14308-14312).
Carpenter et al. 2011 whole-lake experiment, gradual addition of a top predator over three years with an adjacent reference lake (Science 332(6033), 1079-1082).
'Tipping elements' introduced by Lenton et al. 2008, PNAS 105(6), 1786-1793.
Armstrong McKay, Lenton et al. 2022, Science 377(6611), eabn7950: exceeding 1.5 °C could trigger multiple tipping points including Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets and abrupt permafrost thaw.

Bury, Sujith, Pavithran, Scheffer, Lenton, Anand, Bauch 2021, PNAS 118(39), e2106140118: deep classifier trained on ~500,000 AUTO-07P-generated series labelled fold/Hopf/transcritical/null, applied to Mediterranean anoxia sediments, thermoacoustic instability and paleoclimate records.

Dablander and Bury 2022 PNAS letter: because every training example was detrended with a Gaussian filter of a particular bandwidth, the network implicitly requires the same filter at application time.
verdicts.correction: The filters are reversed. Bury et al. (2021) detrended all training data with a LOWESS filter of span 0.2; the Gaussian filter is the alternative Dablander and Bury tested, on which the classifier failed. Accurate text: "In an unusual act of self-critique, Thomas M. Bury co-authored a PNAS letter with Fabian Dablander showing that the performance of the deep learning early-warning classifier is highly sensitive to preprocessing: because every training example in Bury et al. (2021) was detrended with a LOWESS filter of span 0.2, the network implicitly requires that same filter at application time — stationary AR(1) series left undetrended, or detrended instead with a Gaussian filter of bandwidth 0.2, are misclassified as approaching a bifurcation — so its apparent advantage over classical indicators shrinks when preprocessing choices are varied." Correct citation: Fabian Dablander, Thomas M. Bury, 'Deep learning for tipping points: Preprocessing matters', PNAS 119(37), e2207720119 (2022), https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2207720119

verdicts.claim: Bauch and Anand 2022 reply conceded the filter-consistency point, framed the deeper problem as 'unknown unknowns' of deep learning, and called for training sets covering more bifurcation types and noise structures (PNAS 119(37), e2210407119).
Boers 2021 reported early-warning signals in eight independent AMOC indices from observational SST and salinity data (Nature Climate Change 11(8), 680-688).
Chen and Tung Matters Arising, listed as year 2023, Nature Climate Change 14(1), 40-42, arguing coverage-driven variance artifacts and a sign error in two subpolar proxies.
verdicts.correction: Substance confirmed, but the citation year is wrong: the paper is formally 2024 (Nat. Clim. Chang. 14, 40–42, January 2024 issue; published online 30 November 2023). The dossier is also internally inconsistent, dating Boers's reply in the same issue as 2024. Accurate text: "Xianyao Chen and Ka-Kit Tung, 'Evidence lacking for a pending collapse of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation', Nature Climate Change 14(1), 40–42 (2024; published online 30 November 2023), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-023-01877-0. They argue that all eight proxies show artificial rises in variance as observational coverage expanded, that climate models with no genuine early-warning signal yield apparent warnings when sampled according to historical coverage, and that the signs of Boers's salinity proxy and one further subpolar AMOC proxy were reversed in error."

verdicts.claim: Boers 2024 reply in the same issue of Nature Climate Change, 14(1), 43-47.

Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen 2023, Nature Communications 14, 4254: saddle-node SDE fitted to a subpolar-gyre SST fingerprint from HadISST 1870-2020 using moment-based and Strang-splitting MLE; as originally published, collapse around 2057, 95% CI 2025-2095.

21 August 2025 Author Correction (Nat. Commun. 16, 7794) acknowledging a Strang-splitting coding error (flow evaluated at t_(i-1) rather than t_i), identified by Anders Gantzhorn Kristensen, shifting the tipping estimate by eight years to a 2037-2109 window and revising Figs. 5-7 and Table 1.
Ben-Yami, Skiba, Bathiany, Boers 2023, Nature Communications 14, 8344: gap-filling can manufacture false CSD, but the North Atlantic decline remains significant.
Ben-Yami, Morr, Bathiany, Boers 2024, Science Advances 10(31), eadl4841: uncertainties too large to predict tipping times from historical data, using AMOC as the worked case.

van Westen, Kliphuis, Dijkstra 2024, Science Advances 10(6), eadk1189: physics-based early warning signal based on overturning freshwater transport at the southern boundary of the Atlantic; reanalysis indicates AMOC is on tipping course.

Baker et al. 2025, Nature 638(8052), 987-994, with Author Correction Nature 641(8062), E2: continued Atlantic overturning even under extreme forcing, sustained by Southern Ocean wind-driven upwelling.

Rahmstorf 2024, Oceanography 37(3), 16-29: multiple independent analyses point the same way, but by the time signals give reliable warning it will be too late to prevent tipping, and variability changes may have other causes.

Ditlevsen and Johnsen 2010, Geophysical Research Letters 37(19), L19703, 'Tipping points: Early warning and wishful thinking': D-O events show no critical slowing down, implying noise-induced origin and very limited predictability.
Ashwin, Wieczorek, Vitolo, Cox 2012, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 370(1962), 1166-1184: taxonomy of bifurcation-, noise- and rate-induced tipping.
Boettiger and Hastings 2013, Proc. R. Soc. B 280(1766), 20131372: large deviation theory shows purely stochastic transitions are not preceded by early-warning signals.

Hastings and Wysham 2010 demonstrated the class of systems exhibiting leading indicators is limited, 'constructing ecological models and identifying natural systems in which a regime change occurs with no forewarning at all'.
verdicts.correction: Overstates the paper: it identifies a class of MODELS, and only infers that a corresponding class of natural systems is LIKELY to exist. No natural system is identified. Accurate text: "Alan Hastings and Derin B. Wysham demonstrated that the class of ecological systems that will exhibit leading indicators of regime shifts is limited, constructing a set of ecological models — those whose nonlinearities combined with environmental variability yield descriptions without smooth potentials — for which there is no forewarning of a regime change, and arguing that there is therefore also likely to be a class of natural systems for which no forewarning exists." Citation: Alan Hastings, Derin B. Wysham, 'Regime shifts in ecological systems can occur with no warning', Ecology Letters 13(4), 464–472 (2010), https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2010.01439.x

verdicts.claim: Boers and Rypdal 2021, PNAS 118(21), e2024192118: critical slowing down in melt-rate and ice-core records from the central-western Greenland Ice Sheet, linked to the melt-elevation feedback.

A 2025 Nature Geoscience review led by Niklas Boers synthesized observational evidence for destabilization across Earth system tipping elements 'including the AMOC, the polar ice sheets, the Amazon and permafrost systems'.
verdicts.correction: The elements are wrong. The review assesses four tipping elements: the Greenland Ice Sheet, the AMOC, the Amazon rainforest and the South American monsoon system. It does not cover permafrost, and the ice-sheet analysis is Greenland specifically, not 'the polar ice sheets'. Accurate text: "A 2025 Nature Geoscience review led by Niklas Boers, with Timothy M. Lenton and Chris A. Boulton among the authors, presented observation-based evidence that four Earth system tipping elements — the Greenland Ice Sheet, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, the Amazon rainforest and the South American monsoon system — have lost stability in recent decades, and assessed what critical-slowing-down indicators can and cannot establish for each, including how oceanic and atmospheric coupling between elements can generate spurious signals or mask genuine destabilization." Citation: Niklas Boers, Teng Liu, Sebastian Bathiany, Maya Ben-Yami, Lana L. Blaschke, Nils Bochow, Chris A. Boulton, Timothy M. Lenton, Andreas Morr, Da Nian, Martin Rypdal, Taylor Smith, 'Destabilization of Earth system tipping elements', Nature Geoscience 18(10), 949–960 (2025), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-025-01787-0

verdicts.claim: The Global Tipping Points Report, led by Timothy M. Lenton, 'with more than 160 authors from over 87 institutions across 23 countries', 2023 first edition and 2025 second edition; coral reefs crossing a tipping point at roughly 1.4 °C, ice sheets possibly past thresholds, Amazon and AMOC at risk below 2 °C.
verdicts.correction: All substantive findings check out, but the participation figures are inflated by 'more than'/'over'. The report's own figure is exactly 160 authors from 87 institutions in 23 countries. Accurate text: "The Global Tipping Points Report, led by Timothy M. Lenton at the University of Exeter's Global Systems Institute with 160 authors from 87 institutions across 23 countries, appeared in a first edition in 2023 and a second in 2025; the 2025 edition states that warm-water coral reefs are already crossing a tipping point at roughly 1.4 °C of warming, that parts of the polar ice sheets may have passed thresholds that would eventually commit the world to several metres of irreversible sea-level rise, and that the Amazon and the AMOC are both at risk below 2 °C." URL https://global-tipping-points.org/ resolves and is correct for the report series; for a stable citable record prefer the report's Zenodo deposits (e.g. https://zenodo.org/records/18611781 for Section 2, Earth System Tipping Points).

experiment-characterization.domain: AI applied to experimental detection and characterization of phase transitions (diffraction, autonomous beamlines, electron and scanning probe microscopy, neutron scattering, ultracold atoms)
experiment-characterization.summary: Between roughly 2017 and 2023 the job of "deciding what phase a sample is in" moved, in several experimental communities at once, from a human squinting at a curve to a neural network reading raw detector output. The opening move was diffraction. Woon Bae Park and Kee-Sun Sohn showed in 2017 that a convolutional network trained on ~150,000 simulated powder patterns could assign crystal system, extinction group and space group directly from the pattern treated as an image, without peak-fitting. Felipe Oviedo and Tonio Buonassisi solved the small-data problem with physics-informed augmentation for thin films; Nathan Szymanski and Gerbrand Ceder added probabilistic ensembles and a branching search that untangles multi-phase mixtures; Phillip Maffettone and Daniel Olds built an uncertainty-aware "companion agent" that runs alongside a beamline scientist in real time. That last step matters because the second thread is autonomy. Marcus Noack, working with Kevin Yager and Masafumi Fukuto at Brookhaven's NSLS-II and with James Sethian's CAMERA group at Berkeley, replaced the human's choice of next measurement with Gaussian-process surrogate models — the gpCAM code — that steer synchrotron and neutron instruments toward the regions of parameter space where a phase boundary actually lives. Gilad Kusne's CAMEO did the same for phase mapping at SSRL. A parallel thread runs through microscopy: Sergei Kalinin and Maxim Ziatdinov at Oak Ridge turned atomically resolved STEM into a stream of machine-readable defect and phase labels, then closed the loop so the microscope itself chooses where to look. Neutron scattering and ultracold atoms complete the picture — Benno Rem and Christof Weitenberg extracted the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition from single-shot momentum images, and Annabelle Bohrdt with Eugene Demler used networks to adjudicate between competing theories of the doped Hubbard model from quantum gas microscope snapshots.

openQuestions: Neural network phase classifiers are trained almost entirely on simulated diffraction patterns; the domain gap to real samples (preferred orientation, strain, amorphous background, impurity phases) is patched with hand-designed augmentation. Nobody has shown that these augmentations span the real distribution, and there is no accepted benchmark of experimental patterns with ground-truth labels to measure the gap.

Calibrated uncertainty is the crux. Maffettone and Olds built the crystallography companion agent around probabilistic output precisely because standard networks are overconfident, and Szymanski's branching algorithm depends on the probabilities being meaningful. How well these confidence estimates hold up on genuinely out-of-distribution samples — the novel phase you were hoping to find — is unresolved.

Autonomous beamline agents optimize a surrogate objective (uncertainty reduction, signal variance). Whether these objectives actually favor discovering an unknown phase boundary, as opposed to efficiently characterizing known ones, has not been tested against a controlled benchmark where the answer is hidden but known.

In the ultracold-atom work, a network can distinguish two theories from snapshots (Bohrdt and Demler) without revealing what feature it used. Interpretability methods exist but the field has not settled whether a classifier's success constitutes physical evidence for a theory or only a statement about the data's discriminability.

Beam damage and measurement back-action set a hard limit on closed-loop microscopy: Kalinin and Roccapriore's automated STEM both observes and induces the transformations it is studying. There is no established framework for separating the phase transition from the probe that drove it.

Cross-facility reproducibility is unaddressed. gpCAM, CAMEO, xca and A-Lab each embed a decision policy plus a set of instrument-specific defaults; no one has demonstrated that the same autonomous campaign run at NSLS-II, APS and ALS converges on the same phase diagram.

There is no consensus on how much human oversight an autonomous phase-identification loop needs, or on how a mistaken machine phase assignment propagates into a database like the Materials Project once an autonomous lab has deposited the result.

The role of large language models and foundation models — as opposed to task-specific CNNs — in beamline decision-making and in reading the experimental literature for synthesis priors is still early and largely unvalidated as of the sources gathered here.

materials-discovery.domain: AI for materials discovery, phase diagrams, and crystal structure prediction
materials-discovery.summary:
Computational materials discovery rests on three layers. The bottom layer is high-throughput DFT databases built in the early 2010s — the Materials Project (Berkeley/LBNL), the Open Quantum Materials Database (Northwestern), and AFLOW (Duke) — which turned crystal energetics into queryable data and made computed convex-hull phase diagrams routine. Alongside them sits CALPHAD, the older semi-empirical thermodynamic assessment tradition, now being coupled to machine learning and first-principles data. The middle layer is surrogate models that replace DFT: crystal graph neural networks for property prediction (CGCNN, 2018) and universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE-MP-0) that relax arbitrary structures across the periodic table. The top layer is generative and autonomous: CDVAE and MatterGen generate candidate crystals directly, GNoME screened candidates at scale, and the A-Lab attempted robotic synthesis of predicted targets.

The field's credibility problem is that stability prediction is not the same as discovery. Bartel and colleagues showed in 2020 that low formation-energy error does not imply correct stability classification. Matbench Discovery formalized that gap as a benchmark. Both headline 2023 Nature papers drew substantive published criticism: Cheetham and Seshadri found scant novelty, credibility, or utility in randomized samples of GNoME's stable-structure database, flagging implausible cation ordering and a space-group distribution wildly unlike the ICSD; Leeman, Schoop, Palgrave and co-workers found systematic Rietveld-refinement errors in A-Lab's XRD and argued roughly two-thirds of its "new" compounds were known disordered phases. Nature published an author correction in 2026 retitling the A-Lab paper and withdrawing the novelty framing. LK-99 is the parallel cautionary case in superconductivity.

items.claim: The Materials Project, the flagship open high-throughput DFT database for computed materials properties and phase diagrams, was introduced in a 2013 APL Materials commentary; Kristin A. Persson is its founding director and Anubhav Jain its lead author.

items.claim: Cheetham and Seshadri examined randomized subsets of GNoME's outputs and found 'scant evidence for compounds that fulfill the trifecta of novelty, credibility, and utility'. They identified the structure of all 10 randomly selected entries from the 384,870-entry Stable Structure database in the ICSD; found the space-group distribution wildly unlike reality (Pnma is ~16% of ICSD structures but ranks 16th at 1.56% in GNoME's set, and the top four GNoME space groups are all non-centrosymmetric, ~34% of entries, versus ~1% in ICSD); and flagged 18,138 compounds containing Pm, Ac or Pa plus 23,529 containing Tc, Np or Pu as having no plausible utility.

items.affiliation: University of California Santa Barbara (both); National University of Singapore (Cheetham)

items.claim: The A-Lab, an autonomous robotic solid-state synthesis platform, reported realizing 41 novel compounds from 58 targets over 17 days of continuous operation, using targets identified from Materials Project and Google DeepMind ab initio phase-stability data.
items.people: Nathan J. Szymanski, Bernardus Rendy, Yuxing Fei, Rishi E. Kumar, Tanjin He, David Milsted, Matthew J. McDermott, Max Gallant, Ekin Dogus Cubuk, Amil Merchant, Haegyeom Kim, Anubhav Jain, Christopher J. Bartel, Kristin Persson, Yan Zeng, Gerbrand Ceder

items.claim: Leeman, Schoop, Palgrave and co-workers published a peer-reviewed rebuttal identifying substantial errors in A-Lab's automated Rietveld analysis of powder X-ray diffraction data, arguing there was insufficient evidence for the discovery of new materials and that roughly two-thirds of the claimed successes were likely known compositionally disordered versions of the predicted ordered compounds — because DFT at 0 K neglects configurational entropy and forces atoms onto distinct crystallographic sites.
items.people: Josh Leeman, Yuhan Liu, Joseph Stiles, Scott B. Lee, Prajna Bhatt, Leslie M. Schoop, Robert G. Palgrave
items.affiliation: Princeton University (Leeman, Liu, Stiles, Lee, Schoop); University College London (Bhatt, Palgrave)

The authors state their intention 'was to indicate that the materials were new to the prediction platform, not necessarily new to science'. On manual re-analysis, they confirmed the platform reached the correct conclusion in 36 of its 40 reported successes, with 4 inconclusive; the total was updated to exclude four targets inconclusive from XRD alone, and one compound (Zn2Cr3FeO8) was removed because it had mistakenly been included in the training data.
items.people: Nathan J. Szymanski, Bernardus Rendy, Yuxing Fei, Rishi E. Kumar, Tanjin He, David Milsted, Matthew J. McDermott, Max Gallant, Ekin Dogus Cubuk, Amil Merchant, Haegyeom Kim, Anubhav Jain, Christopher J. Bartel, Kristin Persson, Yan Zeng, Gerbrand Ceder

items.affiliation: Nature (freelance science journalist)

openQuestions: Of GNoME's 381,000 claimed stable materials, how many have since been experimentally synthesized and independently characterized by groups unaffiliated with Google DeepMind? DeepMind's blog claimed 736 had been independently created as of November 2023, but I found no peer-reviewed audit of that figure and Cheetham and Seshadri's sampling suggests the novelty rate is low.

Has anyone published a systematic, ICSD-cross-referenced novelty audit of MatterGen's generated structures comparable to what Cheetham and Seshadri did for GNoME? I did not locate one; MatterGen's own novelty metrics are self-reported.

Does the A-Lab correction's claim that 36 of 40 successes were confirmed reconcile with Leeman et al.'s claim that roughly two-thirds were known disordered phases? These are different questions (phase identification vs. novelty) and the correction does not directly address the disorder argument.
No ML method has yet been shown to predict a genuinely new superconductor with a confirmed elevated Tc. Whether SuperCon-trained models have produced any experimentally validated hit remains open.

How well do universal interatomic potentials (M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE) perform on finite-temperature phase diagrams and configurationally disordered systems — precisely the regime where the A-Lab critique says 0 K DFT fails? Matbench Discovery evaluates 0 K hull distance only.

Is there a peer-reviewed CALPHAD+ML method that has produced a validated multicomponent phase diagram faster than expert assessment? The literature I found describes frameworks and reviews rather than validated end-to-end results.

What is the current status of the GNoME Explorer dataset within the Materials Project — have entries been filtered or deprecated in response to the Cheetham and Seshadri critique? I could not fetch the Materials Project site to confirm.

verdicts.claim: The Materials Project was introduced in a 2013 APL Materials commentary; Persson founding director, Jain lead author. APL Materials 1(1), 011002, doi 10.1063/1.4812323.
Ong, Wang, Kang, Ceder, Li-Fe-P-O2 phase diagram from first principles, Chemistry of Materials 20(5), 1798-1807 (2008), doi 10.1021/cm702327g.
verdicts.correction: Citation is exact (title: 'Li-Fe-P-O2 Phase Diagram from First Principles Calculations'). Caution on the gloss only: the paper introduced the grand-potential (open-system, variable mu_O2) construction; first-principles convex-hull phase diagrams predate it in the Ceder group. 'Established the grand-potential phase-diagram construction' is safer than 'established the technique... the ancestor of every computed phase diagram'.

verdicts.claim: OQMD launched at Northwestern; Saal, Kirklin, Aykol, Meredig, Wolverton, JOM 65(11), 1501-1509 (2013); site currently reports 1,407,395 materials.
Kirklin et al. 2015: DFT-vs-experiment formation-energy MAE 0.096 eV/atom; experiment-vs-experiment MAE 0.082 eV/atom. npj Computational Materials 1, 15010.
AFLOW described in 2012, Curtarolo et al., Computational Materials Science 58, 218-226, doi 10.1016/j.commatsci.2012.02.005; aflowlib.org.
Kaufman and Agren, 'CALPHAD, first and second generation - Birth of the materials genome', Scripta Materialia 70, 3-6 (2014), doi 10.1016/j.scriptamat.2012.12.003.
verdicts.correction: Bibliographic details all verified. One unverified sub-detail: I could not confirm Kaufman's printed affiliation; on his Scripta Materialia papers it is normally given as a private address in Brookline, MA, not 'Cambridge, Massachusetts'. Drop the affiliation or verify against the printed article before publishing it.

verdicts.correction: Exact title for the citation: Zi-Kui Liu, 'Thermodynamics and its prediction and CALPHAD modeling: Review, state of the art, and perspectives', Calphad 82 (2023) 102580, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.calphad.2023.102580. USPEX: Oganov and Glass, J. Chem. Phys. 124(24), 244704 (2006), ETH Zurich.

Note the 2006 paper reports ~100% success on tens of test cases with up to 40 atoms per cell — 'established evolutionary algorithms as the dominant pre-deep-learning method' is a historical judgement, not a paper claim.

verdicts.claim: CGCNN: Xie and Grossman, Physical Review Letters 120(14), 145301 (2018).
M3GNet was the first universal graph-network interatomic potential covering the whole periodic table; Chen and Ong, Nature Computational Science 2(11), 718-728 (2022).
verdicts.correction: Citation exact. Precision caveat: the model is trained on and covers 89 elements, not literally the whole periodic table; 'across the periodic table' (the paper's own phrasing) is safer than 'the whole periodic table'.

verdicts.claim: CHGNet trained on >1.5M Materials Project structures, adds magnetic moments as explicit output; Deng et al., Nature Machine Intelligence 5(9), 1031-1041 (2023).
Bartel et al. 2020: seven ML models on 85,014 Materials Project compositions; composition-only models 'perform poorly on predicting the stability of compounds'. npj Computational Materials 6, 97.
Matbench Discovery, Riebesell et al., Nature Machine Intelligence 7, 836-847 (2025), arXiv:2308.14920 preprint 2023.
verdicts.correction: All verified against the published PDF. Published title is 'A framework to evaluate machine learning crystal stability predictions'; received 2 Feb 2024, accepted 9 May 2025, published online 23 June 2025, June 2025 issue. Both paraphrased findings are near-verbatim from the abstract.

verdicts.claim: GNoME reported 2.2 million structures below the convex hull, of which 381,000 are newly discovered stable materials; Merchant et al., Nature 624(7990), 80-85, 29 Nov 2023.
DeepMind blog (29 Nov 2023): 380,000 'most stable', contributed to Materials Project, 736 independently created by external labs.

Cheetham and Seshadri found 'scant evidence' for novelty/credibility/utility; identified all 10 randomly selected Stable Structure entries (of 384,870) in the ICSD; Pnma is ~16% of ICSD structures but ranks 16th at 1.56% in GNoME; top four GNoME space groups all non-centrosymmetric, ~34% of entries, versus ~1% in ICSD; 18,138 compounds with Pm/Ac/Pa and 23,529 with Tc/Np/Pu. Chemistry of Materials 36(8), 3490-3495 (2024).
verdicts.correction: Citation, quotation, the 384,870 figure, the 10/10 ICSD identification, the 16th-place 1.56% Pnma ranking, the ~34% non-centrosymmetric share, and both radioactive-element counts (18,138 and 23,529) are all exactly right. TWO space-group statistics are garbled. (1) Pnma is NOT ~16% of ICSD structures. The paper says: 'the top two space groups in the ICSD are centrosymmetric Pnma and P2(1)/c, accounting for approximately 16% of all structures, with ~8% in each case.' The 16% is the two groups combined; Pnma alone is ~8%. (2) '~1% in ICSD' does not mean non-centrosymmetric groups are ~1% of the ICSD. The paper says: 'in the ICSD there is only one non-centrosymmetric space group in the top 24 and it accounts for only 1% of all structures.' Accurate replacement text: 'Pnma and P2(1)/c together account for roughly 16% of ICSD structures, about 8% each, yet Pnma ranks only 16th in GNoME's Stable Structure database at 1.56%; the four commonest GNoME space groups are all non-centrosymmetric and cover ~34% of entries, whereas the ICSD's top 24 space groups contain just one non-centrosymmetric group, accounting for 1% of structures.' Correct URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemmater.4c00643 (open-access copy: https://escholarship.org/uc/item/9qx9t3kz). Published 8 April 2024.

verdicts.claim: The A-Lab reported realizing 41 novel compounds from 58 targets over 17 days; Szymanski et al., Nature 624(7990), 86-91, 29 Nov 2023.
verdicts.correction: The 41/58/17-days figures are correct for the article AS ORIGINALLY PUBLISHED, but the article of record no longer reads that way and a reader following the DOI will find a mismatch. The corrected paper is titled 'An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials' (the original was '...of novel materials') and its abstract now reads: 'Over 17 days of continuous operation, the A-Lab realized 36 compounds from a set of 57 targets including a variety of oxides and phosphates that were identified using large-scale ab initio phase-stability data from the Materials Project and Google DeepMind.' Publish as: 'As originally published, the A-Lab reported realizing 41 novel compounds from 58 targets over 17 days; after the 2026 author correction the paper reports 36 compounds from 57 targets and is retitled to drop the word novel.' URL is correct: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w

verdicts.claim: Leeman, Schoop, Palgrave and co-workers found systematic Rietveld errors in A-Lab's XRD and argued roughly two-thirds of the claimed successes were known compositionally disordered phases; PRX Energy 3(1), 011002, 7 March 2024.

verdicts.claim: LK-99 preprint claimed 'the first room-temperature ambient-pressure superconductor', Tc >= 400 K in copper-substituted lead apatite, superconductivity attributed to structural distortion; Lee, Kim, Kwon, arXiv:2307.12008, 22 July 2023.
The apparent resistivity drop in LK-99 was attributed to the first-order superionic phase transition of the Cu2S impurity near 385 K; Jain, J. Phys. Chem. C 127(37), 18253-18255 (2023).
verdicts.correction: The citation, authorship, venue, volume, issue, pages and DOI are all correct, but the temperature is wrong. Jain's abstract states: 'Copper(I) sulfide has a known phase transition at 104 degrees C from an ordered low-temperature phase to a high-temperature superionic phase' — that is ~377 K, not 385 K (385 K would be 112 C). The figure matters because the point of the paper is that 377 K coincides with LK-99's reported ~104.8 C resistivity drop. Accurate replacement text: 'The apparent resistivity drop in LK-99 was attributed to the superionic phase transition of the Cu2S impurity at 104 C (~377 K) — a mundane impurity artefact, not superconductivity.' Correct URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.3c05684 (title: 'Superionic Phase Transition of Copper(I) Sulfide and Its Implication for Purported Superconductivity of LK-99'; open preprint arXiv:2308.05222).

verdicts.correction: Authors, affiliations, journal, volume, issue, article number and year all verified (title: 'Single crystal synthesis, structure, and magnetism of Pb10-xCux(PO4)6O'). One wording caution: 'purple' is not in the paper's abstract, which says the crystals 'are highly insulating and optically transparent' and concludes 'we therefore rule out the presence of superconductivity in Pb9Cu(PO4)6O crystals'. The purple colour comes from the crystal photographs and press coverage. Safer phrasing: 'transparent, highly insulating crystals, with superconductivity explicitly ruled out'.

verdicts.claim: Dan Garisto's Nature news account of the LK-99 resolution, Nature 620, 705-706, 16 August 2023, doi 10.1038/d41586-023-02585-7.
verdicts.correction: Headline for the citation: 'LK-99 isn't a superconductor - how science sleuths solved the mystery'. Volume/pages confirmed via ADS (2023Natur.620..705G).

verdicts.claim: OPEN QUESTION as written: 'DeepMind's blog claimed 736 had been independently created as of November 2023, but I found no peer-reviewed audit of that figure.'
verdicts.correction: The 736 figure is not blog-only. It appears verbatim in the peer-reviewed Nature abstract: 'Of the stable structures, 736 have already been independently experimentally realized.' The open question is still legitimate but must be reframed: the 736 claim IS peer-reviewed as part of the Merchant et al. paper; what is missing is an INDEPENDENT third-party audit of that figure. Rewrite as: 'The 736 figure appears in the peer-reviewed Nature paper as well as DeepMind's blog, but I found no independent audit of it, and Cheetham and Seshadri's sampling suggests the novelty rate is low.'

fusion-plasma.domain: AI for disruptive, discontinuous transitions in plasma physics and fusion
fusion-plasma.summary: Magnetically confined fusion plasmas are a natural laboratory for discontinuous transitions. Two of them dominate the field. The first is the disruption: a fast, essentially irreversible collapse of the plasma current and thermal energy, often nucleated by a tearing mode, that ends a discharge in milliseconds and can damage the machine. The second is the L-mode to H-mode transition, a genuine bifurcation in which turbulent transport at the plasma edge collapses above a power threshold and a pedestal forms — a state change theorized as a thermal-confinement bifurcation (Shaing 1990, Hinton 1991), later reframed as self-regulating shear-flow turbulence and zonal-flow predator-prey dynamics (Diamond 1994; Eun-jin Kim and Diamond 2003), and observed directly on DIII-D (Schmitz 2012). H-mode brings its own repetitive discontinuity, the edge localized mode (ELM). AI enters at three levels. Prediction: Kates-Harbeck, Svyatkovskiy and Tang's Fusion Recurrent Neural Network (Nature 2019) claimed cross-machine disruption forecasting from JET to DIII-D, alongside a parallel random-forest lineage from MIT (Rea, Montes, Granetz). Control: DeepMind and EPFL's Swiss Plasma Center learned tokamak magnetic control end-to-end on TCV (Degrave, Felici, Riedmiller, Nature 2022), and Princeton/PPPL's Seo and Kolemen trained a reinforcement-learning agent inside a learned tearing-likelihood model to steer DIII-D away from tearing onset in real experiments (Nature 2024). Simulation: differentiable simulators such as TORAX now close the loop. The honest caveat is that cross-machine generalization remains the field's unsolved problem — benchmarking work (DisruptionBench, 2025) and transfer-learning studies show performance degrades sharply on unseen devices, which is precisely the regime ITER will occupy.

items.claim: In April 2019, Julian Kates-Harbeck, Alexey Svyatkovskiy and William Tang published a deep-learning disruption predictor — the Fusion Recurrent Neural Network (FRNN) — trained on high-dimensional multi-channel time-series data from the JET and DIII-D tokamaks; the paper's headline claim was reliable cross-machine prediction, training on one device and forecasting on another, which is the capability ITER requires because it cannot afford to learn from its own disruptions.

Houlberg gave the L–H transition its first explicit bifurcation model, deriving a discontinuous jump in poloidal rotation that suppresses turbulent fluctuations — establishing the transition as a genuine bifurcation of the plasma's dynamical state rather than a smooth crossover.

items.claim: Patrick H. Diamond and co-authors reframed the L–H transition as self-regulating shear-flow turbulence, in which the turbulence generates the very sheared flow that quenches it — the feedback loop that makes the transition sharp and that underlies all later predator-prey descriptions of confinement bifurcations.

items.claim: Eun-jin Kim and Patrick H. Diamond showed that zonal flows trigger the L–H transition and produce a characteristic transient, oscillatory phase before a steep pressure gradient locks in a quiescent H-mode — the model that predicts an observable limit-cycle precursor at the tipping point.

openQuestions: Does the Kates-Harbeck FRNN result actually establish cross-machine generalization, or does it establish that generalization requires a seed of target-machine data? The 2019 Nature paper trained on JET and tested on DIII-D, but the subsequent transfer-learning literature (Zhu 2021, Zheng 2023) exists precisely because zero-shot transfer to a new device degrades. The exact quantitative degradation reported in the 2019 paper should be read off the published figures directly, not from the press coverage — I could not retrieve the paper's full text or verbatim abstract, so the specific true-positive/false-positive/warning-time figures are unverified here.

Is the L-mode to H-mode transition a saddle-node bifurcation, a subcritical Hopf, or a predator-prey limit cycle that terminates in a state change? Shaing 1990 and Hinton 1991 give a two-branch bifurcation; Eun-jin Kim and Diamond 2003 and Schmitz 2012 give oscillatory precursors. Which normal form applies may differ by machine, by heating scheme, and by whether the transition is power- or density-driven — and this matters for whether classical early-warning indicators (rising variance, critical slowing down, rising autocorrelation) should be expected at all.

Is a disruption a bifurcation in the same sense that the L-H transition is? Disruptions are usually the terminal stage of a chain (impurity influx, radiative collapse, mode locking, thermal quench) rather than a single parameter crossing a threshold. If the underlying dynamics are heterogeneous across disruption causes, the search for a universal early-warning signal may be misconceived, and per-mechanism predictors may be the right unit — Craciunescu and Murari 2023 is the main published attempt to test this framing.

How much of the DeepMind TCV result transfers to a reactor-scale, superconducting, burning-plasma device? Tracey et al. 2024 documents that the 2022 controller had real accuracy and steady-state-error limitations. TCV is small, flexible and highly instrumented; ITER is none of those. The honest claim is 'learned end-to-end magnetic control works on a research tokamak', not 'AI can run a fusion reactor'.

In the Seo–Kolemen 2024 tearing-avoidance experiments, how much of the performance comes from the reinforcement-learning policy versus from the learned tearing-likelihood model that defines its reward? A well-calibrated real-time instability estimator is arguably the harder and more transferable artifact; the RL agent on top of it may be the more replaceable component.

Do any published fusion results demonstrate genuine early warning — detection of an approaching bifurcation from generic dynamical precursors before any machine-specific signature appears — as opposed to supervised recognition of known precursor patterns? This is the sharpest point of contact with the critical-transitions literature in ecology and climate, and it appears to be largely unexplored in tokamak physics.

Benchmark comparability: DisruptionBench (Spangher et al. 2025) exists because reported disruption-prediction accuracies across the literature use incompatible datasets, alarm definitions and evaluation protocols. Until results are re-run on a common benchmark, cross-paper comparisons of headline accuracy numbers should be treated as unreliable.

symbolic-theory.domain: AI that produces theory, laws, and interpretable order parameters in phase transitions and critical phenomena
symbolic-theory.summary: This domain covers machine learning systems whose output is an explanation rather than a prediction: a closed-form equation, a conserved quantity, a coarse-graining rule, or an order parameter a physicist can read. Three lineages converge. The first is symbolic regression, which searches the space of analytic expressions directly. Michael Schmidt and Hod Lipson's Eureqa work (Science, 2009) recovered Hamiltonians and conservation laws from raw motion-tracking data; Silviu-Marian Udrescu and Max Tegmark's AI Feynman (Science Advances, 2020) added physics-specific inductive biases such as dimensional analysis, symmetry detection, and compositional decomposition, extended in AI Feynman 2.0 to Pareto-optimal search over graph-modular structure. Miles Cranmer's PySR made high-performance symbolic regression a standard research tool, and the Cranmer–Sanchez-Gonzalez–Battaglia graph-network approach established the dominant recipe for interpretable science: impose a sparse, physically structured bottleneck on a neural network, fit it, then symbolically regress the learned internal messages. AI-Descartes (Cristina Cornelio and colleagues at IBM Research, Nature Communications, 2023) added the missing piece of deductive derivability from background axioms, distinguishing a fitted curve from a derived law. The second lineage is renormalization-group-inspired learning. Maciej Koch-Janusz and Zohar Ringel (Nature Physics, 2018) showed that maximizing real-space mutual information between a coarse-grained variable and its environment recovers RG-relevant degrees of freedom, later scaled by Doruk Efe Gökmen and colleagues into RSMI-NE, which reconstructs phase diagrams and order parameters without prior knowledge of the symmetry. Related work extracts explicit Ising and gauge-theory order parameters from network weights. The third lineage is physics-constrained surrogate modeling: physics-informed neural networks (Maziar Raissi, Paris Perdikaris, George Em Karniadakis, 2019) and neural operators such as the Fourier Neural Operator, applied to Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard phase-field dynamics. This third lineage is the weakest on interpretability — it enforces known physics rather than discovering new physics — and its documented failure modes on stiff, sharp-interface problems are an important caveat.

items.claim: Symbolic regression applied to raw motion-tracking data from double pendulums and oscillators recovered conserved quantities, Lagrangians and Hamiltonians without being given the form of the physical law, using an evolutionary search that scored candidate expressions by how well their partial-derivative relationships matched those in the data.
items.people: Michael Schmidt, Hod Lipson
items.affiliation: Cornell University

items.claim: AI Feynman combines neural-network fitting with physics-motivated inductive biases — dimensional analysis, polynomial fits, brute-force search, and recursive decomposition using discovered symmetries and separability — to recover 100 of the 100 equations in the Feynman Lectures on Physics benchmark, versus 71 for the previous best method.
items.people: Silviu-Marian Udrescu, Max Tegmark
items.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
items.venue: Science Advances, vol. 6, no. 16, article eaay2631

items.claim: AI Feynman 2.0 generalizes the method to noisy and approximate data by returning a Pareto frontier trading accuracy against description-length complexity, and by exploiting graph modularity to discover generalized symmetries that decompose a target function into simpler subproblems.
items.people: Silviu-Marian Udrescu, Andrew Tan, Jiahai Feng, Orisvaldo Neto, Tailin Wu, Max Tegmark
items.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
items.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020); arXiv:2006.10782

items.claim: PySR is an open-source high-performance symbolic regression package, built on the Julia backend SymbolicRegression.jl, designed for scientific discovery: it performs multi-population evolutionary search over expression trees with user-defined operators and returns a Pareto front of accuracy versus complexity. The source repository is https://github.com/MilesCranmer/PySR.
items.people: Miles Cranmer
items.affiliation: Princeton University and Flatiron Institute

items.claim: Imposing a sparse, low-dimensional bottleneck on the message-passing function of a graph neural network forces the learned messages to align with physically meaningful quantities such as force components; symbolic regression applied to those messages then recovers the underlying force law in closed form, a method the authors demonstrated on N-body simulations and on a dark matter halo cosmology dataset where it produced a new analytic formula.
items.people: Miles Cranmer, Alvaro Sanchez-Gonzalez, Peter Battaglia, Rui Xu, Kyle Cranmer, David Spergel, Shirley Ho
items.affiliation: Princeton University; DeepMind; Flatiron Institute; New York University
items.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020); arXiv:2006.11287

items.claim: A graph neural network trained on 30 years of observed trajectories of the Sun, planets and large moons, then distilled by symbolic regression, rediscovered Newton's law of gravitation in the form of an inverse-square force and simultaneously recovered the masses of the bodies to within an order of magnitude, without being given either the force law or the masses.
items.people: Pablo Lemos, Niall Jeffrey, Miles Cranmer, Shirley Ho, Peter Battaglia
items.venue: Machine Learning: Science and Technology, vol. 4, no. 4, article 045002

items.claim: AI-Descartes couples symbolic regression with automated reasoning, so that a candidate equation is scored not only on fit to data but on whether it is logically derivable from a set of background theory axioms; the system rediscovered Kepler's third law of planetary motion, Einstein's relativistic time-dilation law, and Langmuir's adsorption equation, and can identify which axioms a derivation requires.
items.people: Cristina Cornelio, Sanjeeb Dash, Vernon Austel, Tyler R. Josephson, Joao Goncalves, Kenneth L. Clarkson, Nimrod Megiddo, Bachir El Khadir, Lior Horesh
items.affiliation: IBM Research

items.claim: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamical systems (SINDy) recovers governing differential equations from measurement data by assuming the dynamics are sparse in a library of candidate nonlinear functions and solving a sparse regression problem, yielding parsimonious interpretable models rather than black-box predictors.
items.people: Steven L. Brunton, Joshua L. Proctor, J. Nathan Kutz
items.affiliation: University of Washington
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. 113, no. 15, pp. 3932-3937

items.claim: A neural network trained to maximize the mutual information between a coarse-grained block variable and the surrounding environment, subject to a compression constraint, learns the renormalization-group-relevant degrees of freedom of a statistical system; applied to the two-dimensional Ising model the network recovered the block-spin (majority-rule) coarse-graining, and applied to the dimer model it recovered the correct emergent electromagnetic-like variables.
items.people: Maciej Koch-Janusz, Zohar Ringel
items.affiliation: ETH Zürich; Hebrew University of Jerusalem

items.claim: Real-space mutual information neural estimation (RSMI-NE) scales the mutual-information coarse-graining principle to larger systems using modern variational MI estimators, and extracts relevant order parameters and coarse-graining rules directly from raw configurations of classical statistical systems without prior knowledge of the order parameter or the symmetry being broken.
items.people: Doruk Efe Gökmen, Zohar Ringel, Sebastian D. Huber, Maciej Koch-Janusz
items.affiliation: ETH Zürich; Hebrew University of Jerusalem
items.venue: Physical Review Letters, vol. 127, no. 24, article 240603

items.claim: The companion RSMI-NE paper shows that the learned coarse-graining filters encode the symmetries of the effective field theory, allowing the method to construct phase diagrams and identify the symmetry-breaking pattern of transitions in systems including the anisotropic Ising and dimer models, making the learned representation itself the interpretable output.
items.people: Doruk Efe Gökmen, Zohar Ringel, Sebastian D. Huber, Maciej Koch-Janusz
items.affiliation: ETH Zürich; Hebrew University of Jerusalem
items.venue: Physical Review E, vol. 104, no. 6, article 064106

items.claim: A normalizing-flow architecture whose layer structure mirrors the hierarchical spatial structure of real-space renormalization group transformations learns an invertible map between physical configurations and a latent space of effectively decoupled variables, providing a variational free-energy estimate and an explicit, tractable RG-like coarse-graining for the Ising model.
items.people: Shuo-Hui Li, Lei Wang
items.affiliation: Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
items.venue: Physical Review Letters, vol. 121, no. 26, article 260601

items.claim: RG-Flow builds a hierarchical flow-based generative model with a sparse prior in which latent variables are organized by scale, so that different layers of the latent representation correspond to structure at different length scales, yielding disentangled and human-inspectable representations motivated directly by renormalization group ideas.
items.people: Hong-Ye Hu, Dian Wu, Yi-Zhuang You, Bruno Olshausen, Yubei Chen
items.affiliation: University of California San Diego; University of California Berkeley
items.venue: Machine Learning: Science and Technology, vol. 3, no. 3, article 035009

items.claim: Pankaj Mehta and David J. Schwab proposed an explicit mapping between variational renormalization group transformations and stacked restricted Boltzmann machines, arguing that successive layers of a deep network implement a coarse-graining procedure; this preprint launched the RG-deep-learning correspondence literature, though the exactness and generality of the claimed mapping have been contested in subsequent work.
items.people: Pankaj Mehta, David J. Schwab

items.claim: A feedforward neural network trained to classify raw Monte Carlo spin configurations of the two-dimensional Ising model by phase learns to detect the transition and encodes magnetization-like structure in its weights, and the same approach detects transitions in models with no conventional local order parameter, such as the Ising gauge theory.
items.people: Juan Carrasquilla, Roger G. Melko
items.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; University of Waterloo

items.claim: The 'learning by confusion' scheme locates a phase transition without labels by deliberately mislabeling data at a proposed critical point and scanning that point across the parameter range; the classifier's performance traces a characteristic W shape whose central peak marks the true transition, making the method applicable where the order parameter is unknown.
items.people: Evert P. L. van Nieuwenburg, Ye-Hua Liu, Sebastian D. Huber
items.affiliation: ETH Zürich

items.claim: Unsupervised methods applied to Ising configurations show that the leading principal component of principal component analysis corresponds directly to the magnetization order parameter, and that the latent variable of a variational autoencoder learns an equivalent representation, demonstrating that an interpretable order parameter can emerge without any labels or prior physical input.
items.people: Sebastian J. Wetzel
items.affiliation: Heidelberg University
items.venue: Physical Review E, vol. 96, no. 2, article 022140

items.claim: Inspecting the weights of a neural network trained to distinguish phases yields explicit analytic order parameters: for the Ising model the network recovers the magnetization, and for SU(2) lattice gauge theory it recovers the Polyakov loop, demonstrating that a trained classifier's internal structure can be read out as a closed-form physical quantity rather than left as a black box.
items.people: Sebastian J. Wetzel, Manuel Scherzer
items.affiliation: Heidelberg University
items.venue: Physical Review B, vol. 96, no. 18, article 184410

items.claim: Siamese neural networks trained to map configurations related by a symmetry or a conserved dynamics to the same output learn representations whose interpretation yields conserved quantities and symmetry invariants in closed form, with the interpretation step performed by symbolic regression and automated reasoning tools.
items.people: Sebastian J. Wetzel, Roger G. Melko, Joseph Scott, Maysum Panju, Vijay Ganesh
items.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; University of Waterloo
items.venue: Physical Review Research, vol. 2, no. 3, article 033499

items.claim: An unsupervised method based on diffusion maps applied to raw configurations distinguishes topologically ordered phases from trivial ones without any local order parameter or prior labeling, addressing the case where the Landau symmetry-breaking paradigm and its associated order parameters do not apply.
items.people: Joaquin F. Rodriguez-Nieva, Mathias S. Scheurer
items.affiliation: Harvard University

items.claim: A neural-network method estimates the intrinsic dimension of a dynamical system directly from raw video of the system in motion, thereby recovering the number of independent state variables needed to describe it — for example returning four for a double pendulum — before any equation is fitted, addressing the step that precedes symbolic regression.
items.people: Boyuan Chen, Kuang Huang, Sunand Raghupathi, Ishaan Chandratreya, Qiang Du, Hod Lipson
items.affiliation: Columbia University

items.claim: The AI Poincaré method discovers conserved quantities from observed trajectories by measuring the local intrinsic dimensionality of the manifold the trajectory explores in phase space, correctly identifying the number of conservation laws in systems including the Kepler problem and a relativistic charged particle without prior physical assumptions.
items.people: Ziming Liu, Max Tegmark
items.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
items.venue: Physical Review Letters, vol. 126, no. 18, article 180604

items.claim: An automated method discovers symmetries that are hidden by a bad choice of coordinates, learning the coordinate transformation that manifests the symmetry; the method rediscovered the transformation revealing the hidden symmetry of the Schwarzschild metric and other cases where the symmetry is not apparent in the original variables.
items.people: Ziming Liu, Max Tegmark
items.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
items.venue: Physical Review Letters, vol. 128, no. 18, article 180201

items.claim: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks place learnable univariate spline activation functions on network edges instead of fixed activations on nodes, which the authors argue makes the learned function decomposable and human-readable; they demonstrate extracting closed-form expressions and rediscovering known relations in physics and mathematics from trained KANs.
items.people: Ziming Liu, Yixuan Wang, Sachin Vaidya, Fabian Ruehle, James Halverson, Marin Soljačić, Thomas Y. Hou, Max Tegmark
items.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; California Institute of Technology; Northeastern University
items.venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2025; arXiv:2404.19756

items.claim: Physics-informed neural networks embed the residual of a governing partial differential equation into the training loss via automatic differentiation, enabling both forward solution and inverse parameter identification from sparse data; the paper's discrete-time formulation is demonstrated on the Allen-Cahn equation, a canonical phase-separation model.
items.people: Maziar Raissi, Paris Perdikaris, George Em Karniadakis
items.affiliation: Brown University; University of Pennsylvania
items.venue: Journal of Computational Physics, vol. 378, pp. 686-707

items.claim: A sequential, backward-compatible training scheme for physics-informed neural networks addresses the failure of standard PINNs on the Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard equations, whose stiff dynamics and sharp moving interfaces defeat single-shot training over the whole space-time domain.
items.people: Revanth Mattey, Susanta Ghosh
items.affiliation: Michigan Technological University
items.venue: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering, vol. 390, article 114474

items.claim: Physics-informed neural networks fail on problems only slightly more complex than standard demonstrations, and the authors show the cause is not network expressivity but the optimization landscape: the soft PDE-residual penalty makes the problem ill-conditioned, with curriculum regularization and sequence-to-sequence training reducing error by one to two orders of magnitude. This is an important limitation on claims that PINNs constitute physics discovery.
items.people: Aditi S. Krishnapriyan, Amir Gholami, Shandian Zhe, Robert M. Kirby, Michael W. Mahoney
items.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (NeurIPS 2021); arXiv:2109.01050

items.claim: The Fourier Neural Operator learns mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces by parameterizing the integral kernel directly in Fourier space, giving a resolution-invariant surrogate that can be trained at one discretization and evaluated at another, and reporting speedups of up to three orders of magnitude over traditional solvers on Navier-Stokes problems.
items.people: Zongyi Li, Nikola Kovachki, Kamyar Azizzadenesheli, Burigede Liu, Kaushik Bhattacharya, Andrew Stuart, Anima Anandkumar
items.affiliation: California Institute of Technology
items.venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2021; arXiv:2010.08895

items.claim: Neural operators combined with a convolutional autoencoder learn the evolution of two-phase microstructures governed by phase-field (Cahn-Hilliard type) dynamics, with the autoencoder compressing the high-dimensional microstructure field to a low-dimensional latent space in which the operator learns the temporal dynamics of spinodal decomposition.
items.people: Vivek Oommen, Khemraj Shukla, Somdatta Goswami, Rémi Dingreville, George Em Karniadakis
items.affiliation: Brown University; Sandia National Laboratories

items.claim: J. Doyne Farmer and John J. Sidorowich introduced local approximation methods for forecasting chaotic time series by reconstructing the dynamics from delay-embedded data, an early demonstration that a system's equations of motion can be recovered empirically from observation alone. Note: this is a conceptual precursor to data-driven law discovery, not work on symbolic regression or order parameters; no verified Farmer publication was found in the symbolic-regression or critical-phenomena machine learning literature.
items.people: J. Doyne Farmer, John J. Sidorowich
items.affiliation: Los Alamos National Laboratory
items.venue: Physical Review Letters, vol. 59, no. 8, pp. 845-848

openQuestions: Affiliations are the weakest field in this set. Crossref's API did not return affiliation data for most of these DOIs, so the institutions listed are drawn from well-documented public record rather than from a fetched title page. Every affiliation should be spot-checked against the published PDF before print; the ones left blank are those not confidently established.

The user's prompt asked to verify a Doyne Farmer connection. No publication by J. Doyne Farmer was found in the symbolic-regression, interpretable-order-parameter, or ML-for-critical-phenomena literature. The 1987 Farmer and Sidorowich paper on predicting chaotic time series is included as a genuine conceptual precursor, but attributing symbolic regression or order-parameter discovery to Farmer would be incorrect. Consider cutting the reference or reframing it explicitly as prehistory.

The prompt asked specifically about ML rediscovering critical exponents. The verified papers here recover order parameters, coarse-graining rules, and transition locations, but a definitive primary source in which a machine learning system autonomously produces accurate critical exponents (rather than a human applying finite-size scaling to ML-derived observables) was not confirmed. This claim should not be made in the book without a specific citation; targeted searching on this narrow question is still needed.

The Mehta and Schwab RG-deep-learning mapping (arXiv:1410.3831) was never published in a peer-reviewed journal and its central claim of exactness has been disputed in follow-up literature. If the book presents the RG-deep-learning correspondence as established, that overstates the case; the Koch-Janusz and Ringel line of work is the defensible version of the claim.

There is a real conceptual gap between the two halves of this domain. Symbolic regression and RSMI-style methods discover new structure; PINNs and neural operators enforce structure already known and produce a fast surrogate, not a law. Framing FNO or PINN work as 'AI producing theory' would be a category error worth addressing explicitly rather than eliding.

Zongyi Li et al.'s Fourier Neural Operator has no journal DOI, only the arXiv preprint and ICLR 2021 proceedings. If the book's citation style requires DOIs throughout, this entry and the NeurIPS entries (AI Feynman 2.0, Cranmer et al. 2020, Krishnapriyan et al. 2021) will need a consistent house convention for conference papers.

The web search budget for this session was exhausted before research began, so all verification was done by direct fetch against Crossref and arXiv. Coverage of very recent work (2024-2026) in this domain is therefore likely incomplete, particularly on symbolic regression applied directly to critical phenomena.
