The 'relativistic charged particle' is not among the systems tested and appears to be fabricated. The five Hamiltonian systems are the harmonic oscillator, the Kepler problem, the double pendulum, a magnetic mirror, and the gravitational three-body problem. Accurate text: 'The AI Poincaré method discovers conserved quantities from observed trajectories by measuring the local intrinsic dimensionality of the manifold the trajectory explores in phase space, correctly identifying the number of conservation laws in five Hamiltonian systems including the Kepler problem, a magnetic mirror and the gravitational three-body problem, without prior physical assumptions.' URL unchanged: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.180604

Krishnapriyan, Gholami, Zhe, Kirby, Mahoney, NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv:2109.01050): PINN failure modes caused by ill-conditioned optimization landscape, not expressivity; curriculum regularization and sequence-to-sequence training give 1-2 orders of magnitude lower error

Farmer & Sidorowich, Phys. Rev. Lett. 59(8):845-848 (1987), local approximation forecasting of chaotic time series as 'an early demonstration that a system's equations of motion can be recovered empirically from observation alone'
verdicts.correction: Bibliographic data is fully correct: J. Doyne Farmer and John J. Sidorowich, 'Predicting chaotic time series', Physical Review Letters, vol. 59, no. 8, pp. 845-848 (1987), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.845. The characterization overstates the result: the paper builds local linear and polynomial approximations to the dynamics on a delay-embedded attractor for the purpose of prediction; it does not recover equations of motion in closed or symbolic form. Accurate text: 'J. Doyne Farmer and John J. Sidorowich introduced local approximation methods for forecasting chaotic time series, fitting piecewise linear and polynomial models to the dynamics reconstructed from delay-embedded data — an early demonstration that a system's dynamics can be approximated empirically from observation alone, though not in symbolic or closed form.' URL unchanged: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.845. The dossier's own caveat is right: Farmer must be framed as prehistory, not as symbolic-regression or order-parameter work.

verdicts.claim: Open question: 'a definitive primary source in which a machine learning system autonomously produces accurate critical exponents was not confirmed'
verdicts.correction: This open question is answered by a paper already in the dossier. Koch-Janusz and Ringel (Nature Physics 14, 578-582, 2018) state in their abstract: 'We demonstrate RG flow and extract the Ising critical exponent.' The body reports the correlation-length exponent nu = 1.0 +/- 0.15 for the 2D Ising model (exact value 1), obtained by finite-size data collapse across successive RSMI-driven RG steps, with the critical point located to about 1% from the divergent RG flow. The dossier's framing is still partly right — the exponent is extracted by finite-size scaling applied to the machine-learned RG flow rather than emitted autonomously by the network — but the flat statement that no primary source was confirmed is wrong and should be replaced with that citation and that caveat. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-018-0081-4

critique-limits.domain: Critical and skeptical literature on AI/ML in the physical sciences: failure modes, non-replication, retractions, and methodological traps
critique-limits.summary: The skeptical literature on machine learning in the physical sciences has three distinct strands, and it is important not to blur them. The first is methodological: Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan's Patterns paper documented data leakage as a systematic cause of irreproducibility across 17 fields and 294 papers, with an eight-part taxonomy and a proposed "model info sheet"; the follow-on REFORMS checklist in Science Advances turned that diagnosis into 32 consensus reporting questions. Notably, the 17 fields catalogued are overwhelmingly biomedical, social-scientific, and computational — physics, chemistry, and materials science are absent from that census, which reflects where post-hoc audits have been performed rather than where leakage occurs. The second strand is domain-specific and technical: work by Bryce Meredig and colleagues, Kangming Li and Jason Hattrick-Simpers, Janosh Riebesell and colleagues, and Xiang Fu and colleagues shows that random train/test splits, redundant materials databases, and force-error metrics all systematically overstate what models can do outside the training distribution — most "out-of-distribution" benchmarks turn out to test interpolation. The third strand is forensic: the Ranga Dias superconductivity retractions, the LK-99 episode, the disputed A-Lab novelty claims criticized by Robert Palgrave and Leslie Schoop, Anthony Cheetham and Ram Seshadri's audit of GNoME, and MIT's withdrawal of Aidan Toner-Rodgers's preprint. These are not all the same kind of failure — LK-99 was an honest artifact resolved by open replication in weeks, A-Lab was overclaiming corrected by peer-reviewed reanalysis, Dias was adjudicated misconduct, and the MIT case was fabricated data. Any book chapter should keep those categories separate.

items.claim: Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan surveyed literature across fields adopting machine learning and found data leakage documented in 17 fields, collectively affecting 294 papers; they introduced a taxonomy of eight types of leakage (from lack of clean train/test separation, through illegitimate features, to test sets not drawn from the distribution of scientific interest) and proposed 'model info sheets' as a mitigation.

openQuestions: No systematic leakage audit comparable to the Kapoor–Narayanan survey has been published for condensed matter physics, materials informatics, or computational chemistry. The absence of these fields from the 17-field census is a gap in the evidence, not evidence of absence — an important caveat if the book uses that number.

The exact number of A-Lab compounds that are genuinely novel to science remains contested: the January 2026 Author Correction reports 36 of 40 reported successes correctly identified, while the Leeman et al. PRX Energy reanalysis argued none were novel. These are answers to different questions (correct phase identification versus novelty against the ICSD) and should not be conflated.

The published version of the Cheetham–Seshadri critique reports examining random samples of the GNoME release, but the precise sample sizes cited in secondary coverage (10 structures in one analysis, 384 in another) were not confirmed against the article text in this pass and should be checked against the PDF before being quoted.
Whether the GNoME Nature paper DOI given here (10.1038/s41586-023-06018-3) is exact was inferred rather than fetched; verify against nature.com or Crossref before print.

The identity of the person who first raised concerns about the Toner-Rodgers preprint is described in press coverage only as a computer scientist with materials science experience. If the book names anyone, that attribution needs primary confirmation.

No peer-reviewed post-mortem yet analyses why the AI-and-materials-productivity result was accepted so readily by senior economists — the sociological question of how a fabricated dataset passed elite informal review is unstudied in the literature found here.
The Fu et al. 'Forces are not Enough' benchmark's final TMLR publication year and volume were not directly verified; cite the arXiv version unless confirmed.

There is no consensus benchmark that tests true extrapolation to a new phase or new structural class in materials ML; Li et al. show most existing out-of-distribution suites measure interpolation, but do not propose an accepted replacement.

verdicts.claim: Kapoor & Narayanan, Patterns 4(9) 100804 (2023): leakage found in 17 fields, 294 papers, taxonomy of eight types, model info sheets proposed.
Kapoor & Narayanan civil war prediction reproducibility case study: complex ML models did not outperform decades-old logistic regression once leakage was corrected.

The public catalogue at reproducible.cs.princeton.edu lists medicine, molecular biology, neuroimaging, bioinformatics, clinical epidemiology, satellite imaging, computer security, software engineering; physics/chemistry/materials science absent.
verdicts.correction: NOTE (not an error, but a live-site caveat): the catalogue is continuously updated and as of this check lists 41 papers across 30 fields, collectively affecting 648 papers — not the 17 fields / 294 papers frozen in the 2023 Patterns article. The named fields all appear, and physics, chemistry and materials science still do not. If the book cites '17 fields / 294 papers' it must attribute that to the Patterns paper, not to the website.

verdicts.claim: REFORMS checklist: 32 questions in eight modules (study goals, computational reproducibility, data quality, data preprocessing, modeling, data leakage, metrics and uncertainty quantification, generalizability and limitations), consensus of 19 researchers. Science Advances 10(18) eadk3452 (2024).
verdicts.correction: NOTE: author list, order, spelling, venue, volume, issue, article number and DOI all verified against Crossref. Abstract confirms '32 questions' and 'consensus of 19 researchers'; the paper text confirms '32 items across 8 modules' with exactly the eight module names given. One small caveat in the dossier's affiliation field: the source says 19 researchers, not '19 institutions' — do not convert the one number into the other in print.

Accurate text: 'Their search identified 2,212 studies, of which 415 were included after initial screening and, after quality screening, 62 studies were included in the systematic review; the review found that none of the models identified are of potential clinical use due to methodological flaws and/or underlying biases.' Accurate text: Chemistry World, 'New analysis raises doubts over autonomous lab's materials "discoveries"', 16 January 2024. Palgrave: '[The Rietveld refinement] was very bad, very beginner, completely novice human level – that led to them misidentifying things in some cases.' And: 'What they didn't realise is that two thirds of their entire predictions were just ordered versions of compounds that were already known to be disordered.' kibble-zurek.domain: Kibble-Zurek mechanism: origins, scaling law, quantum extension, and experimental tests
kibble-zurek.summary:
All bibliographic data below was verified against the Crossref REST API (title, author order, volume, pages, year, DOI) rather than from memory or search snippets alone; publisher pages for IOP and Nature are bot-blocked, so Crossref and arXiv were the verification path. The Keesling 2019 Nature paper was additionally read directly (pages 1-3 of the full text PDF) because the chapter's precision requirement hinges on it.

The lineage: Tom W. B. Kibble's 1976 J. Phys. A paper established that whether a symmetry-breaking transition leaves domain walls, strings, or monopoles is fixed by the homotopy groups of the vacuum manifold; Kibble's 1980 Physics Reports follow-up supplied the causal-horizon argument for how dense those defects should be. Wojciech H. Zurek's 1985 Nature paper moved the argument into the laboratory, proposing a pressure quench of superfluid helium and arguing that the condensate phase is chosen randomly in domains of characteristic size d, so the phase mismatch around an annulus of circumference C scales as (C/d)^(1/2). Zurek's 1996 Physics Reports review is the standard primary source for the scaling law in its familiar form, and del Campo & Zurek 2014 is the cleanest modern statement: the frozen-out correlation length scales as a power of the quench time with exponent nu/(1+nu*z), and defect density as the inverse d-th power of that.

CRITICAL PRECISION POINT, as flagged in the brief and now confirmed from the paper itself: the Harvard/MIT Rydberg experiment (Keesling et al., Nature 568, 207-211, 2019) did NOT report defect density. It measured the Rydberg density-density correlation function G(r) across a 51-atom rubidium-87 array and extracted a correlation length by fitting an exponential decay to the modulus of that correlation function. The reported result is a power-law fit of correlation length against inverse detuning sweep rate, giving mu = 0.50(3) (one standard deviation). The paper explicitly draws the contrast itself: "While the QKZM is a coarse-grained description that predicts the mean density of defects, the shape of the correlation function gives further access to microscopic details of the system." The significance of 0.50(3) is that mu = nu/(1+nu*z) equals 0.5 for the 1D Ising universality class (z = 1, nu = 1) but 1/3 for a mean-field transition (z = 1, nu = 1/2), so the measurement distinguishes the two. The authors claim this as "the first experimental verification of the QKZM in an isolated quantum system that defies a mean-field description." They also report deviations beyond QKZM (correlations going negative at some distances) and extend the method to chiral clock models, finding mu approximately 0.38 for the Z3 transition and approximately 0.25 for Z4.

Affiliations on that paper, read directly from the article's footnote block: Keesling, Omran, Levine, Bernien, Choi, Samajdar, Sachdev, Greiner, and Lukin at the Department of Physics, Harvard University; Pichler jointly at Harvard and ITAMP (Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics); Vuletic at the Department of Physics and Research Laboratory of Electronics, MIT; Schwartz at Laboratoire Kastler Brossel, ENS/CNRS/Sorbonne Universite/College de France, Paris; Silvi and Zoller at IQOQI (Austrian Academy of Sciences) and the University of Innsbruck; Endres at Caltech. So "Lukin and Greiner groups at Harvard" is right, and MIT enters through Vladan Vuletic — worth stating that way rather than implying the whole collaboration spans both.

One caveat the chapter should not paper over: the experimental record is not uniformly confirmatory. The 1994 superfluid helium-4 vortex result from the Lancaster group was not reproduced by the same group's own improved 1998 experiment, which found nonappearance of vortices. The clean early confirmations came instead from superfluid helium-3 (two independent Nature papers in 1996) and later from trapped ions, cold atoms, and superconducting circuits.

items.claim: Founding paper of the mechanism. Shows that in a spontaneously broken gauge theory the type of defect formed — domain wall, string, or monopole — is determined by the homotopy groups of the manifold of degenerate vacua. Argues theories producing domain walls are likely excluded by unacceptable gravitational effects, while a cosmic network of strings may well have formed. This is the correct primary citation for the topological/cosmological half of 'Kibble-Zurek'.
items.people: Tom W. B. Kibble
items.affiliation: Imperial College London (affiliation not independently verified from the source page, which is bot-blocked)
items.venue: Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General, vol. 9, no. 8, pp. 1387-1398

items.claim: Kibble's follow-up review, the source of the causal-horizon argument for the initial density of defects — that domains cannot be correlated over distances larger than the causal horizon at the transition, which sets a defect separation. This is where the density estimate (as opposed to the topological classification) originates on the cosmology side.
items.people: Tom W. B. Kibble
items.affiliation: Imperial College London (not independently verified)

items.claim: The paper that made the mechanism testable. Proposes the analogy between cosmic strings and superfluid vortex lines and suggests a cryogenic pressure-quench experiment. Key argument: in a superfluid formed by rapid quench, the phase of the Bose condensate wavefunction is chosen randomly in domains of characteristic size d, so the typical phase mismatch around an annulus of circumference C scales as (C/d)^(1/2). Correct primary citation for the condensed-matter half of the mechanism.
items.people: Wojciech H. Zurek
items.affiliation: Los Alamos National Laboratory (not independently verified; Nature page is paywalled/redirects)

items.claim: Zurek's long review, the standard primary source for the Kibble-Zurek scaling law in its usual form. Reviews the cosmology/condensed-matter connection, the freeze-out argument, and proposes further experiments in superfluid helium and liquid crystals. Cite this rather than the 1985 Nature letter when the chapter states the quench-rate power law itself.
items.people: Wojciech H. Zurek
items.affiliation: Los Alamos National Laboratory

items.claim: First numerical demonstration of the quench-rate scaling law for kink density — the simulation result that turned the freeze-out argument into a quantitative, checkable prediction. Useful if the chapter wants a citation for the law being validated computationally before it was validated experimentally.
items.people: Pablo Laguna and Wojciech Hubert Zurek
items.affiliation: Los Alamos National Laboratory (Zurek); Laguna's 1997 affiliation not verified

items.claim: The best single modern citation for the Kibble-Zurek scaling law stated explicitly. Reviews how dynamics ceases to be adiabatic near the critical point because of critical slowing down, and gives the density of defects as a function of quench rate: frozen correlation length scales as quench time to the power nu/(1+nu*z), defect density as the inverse d-th power of that. Covers both classical and quantum cases.
items.people: Adolfo del Campo and Wojciech H. Zurek
items.affiliation: Los Alamos National Laboratory
items.venue: International Journal of Modern Physics A, vol. 29, no. 8, art. 1430018

items.claim: Kibble's own accessible retrospective, written for a general physics audience — how speculations about early-universe phase transitions led to small-scale laboratory experiments, and what consistent picture emerged. Good citation for a book chapter that wants one readable, authoritative overview signed by Kibble himself.
items.people: Tom Kibble
items.affiliation: Imperial College London (not verified from source)

items.claim: One of three independent 2005 papers that extended the mechanism from thermal to quantum phase transitions. Damski's contribution reframes Landau-Zener transitions as the simplest quantum model supporting Kibble-Zurek topological defect production, making the quantum analogy concrete in a two-level system.
items.people: Bogdan Damski
items.affiliation: Not verified

items.claim: Companion 2005 paper establishing the quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism: near a quantum critical point the relevant timescale is set by the inverse energy gap between ground and excited states, and when the Hamiltonian changes faster than that, nonadiabatic excitations freeze the growth of correlated regions. This is the paper the Rydberg experiment cites as the QKZM foundation.
items.people: Wojciech H. Zurek, Uwe Dorner, and Peter Zoller
items.affiliation: Los Alamos National Laboratory (Zurek); University of Innsbruck / IQOQI (Dorner, Zoller) — affiliations not independently verified

items.claim: The third 2005 QKZM paper: an exact solution of the quantum Ising model under a linear quench, giving the defect (kink) density scaling analytically for the canonical solvable case. Cite alongside Damski and Zurek/Dorner/Zoller when introducing the quantum version.
items.people: Jacek Dziarmaga
items.affiliation: Jagiellonian University, Krakow (not verified)

items.claim: THE RYDBERG PAPER, with the observable stated precisely. A 51-atom array of rubidium-87 with programmable van der Waals interactions was swept across an Ising-type quantum phase transition into a Z2-ordered phase. The measured quantity was the Rydberg density-density correlation function G(r); a correlation length was extracted by fitting an exponential decay to the modulus of that correlation function. The reported result is a power-law fit of correlation length versus inverse detuning sweep rate giving mu = 0.50(3), where mu = nu/(1+nu*z). This matches 1D Ising (0.5) and excludes mean-field (1/3). Defect density was NOT the reported observable — the paper itself contrasts the coarse-grained QKZM defect-density prediction with the microscopic information in the correlation function's shape. The authors also report a universal collapse of correlations under length rescaling, deviations beyond QKZM (correlations turning negative at some distances), and extension to chiral clock models with mu about 0.38 (Z3) and about 0.25 (Z4).
items.people: Alexander Keesling, Ahmed Omran, Harry Levine, Hannes Bernien, Hannes Pichler, Soonwon Choi, Rhine Samajdar, Sylvain Schwartz, Pietro Silvi, Subir Sachdev, Peter Zoller, Manuel Endres, Markus Greiner, Vladan Vuletic, Mikhail D. Lukin
items.affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University (Keesling, Omran, Levine, Bernien, Choi, Samajdar, Sachdev, Greiner, Lukin); ITAMP, Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (Pichler, jointly with Harvard); Department of Physics and Research Laboratory of Electronics, MIT (Vuletic); Laboratoire Kastler Brossel, ENS/CNRS/Sorbonne Universite/College de France, Paris (Schwartz); IQOQI, Austrian Academy of Sciences and Center for Quantum Physics, University of Innsbruck (Silvi, Zoller); Division of Physics, Mathematics and Astronomy, Caltech (Endres) — read directly from the article's affiliation footnotes
items.year: 2019 (Nature); preprint arXiv:1809.05540 submitted 14 September 2018, revised 1 April 2019

items.claim: Preprint of the Rydberg paper, freely accessible. Useful as a secondary URL for readers without Nature access; note the 2018 preprint year against the 2019 journal year.
items.people: Alexander Keesling and colleagues (same author list as the Nature version)
items.affiliation: Harvard University, MIT, and collaborating institutions

items.claim: Earliest laboratory test of the defect-formation picture, using liquid crystals as a cosmological analogue. Supports the 'one-scale' model for cosmic string evolution and observes textures decaying into monopole-antimonopole pairs. Historically the first 'cosmology in the lab' experiment in this lineage, predating the superfluid tests.
items.people: Isaac Chuang, Ruth Durrer, Neil Turok, and Bernard Yurke
items.affiliation: Not verified

items.claim: The much-cited superfluid helium-4 vortex result — reported generation of defects in a pressure-quenched helium-4 sample as an analogue of cosmic string formation. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this result was not reproduced by the same group's later, improved experiment (see the 1998 Dodd et al. entry). A chapter citing it as a confirmation without that caveat would be misleading.
items.people: P. C. Hendry, N. S. Lawson, R. A. M. Lee, P. V. E. McClintock, and C. D. H. Williams
items.affiliation: Lancaster University and University of Exeter (not independently verified)

items.claim: The retraction-in-effect of the helium-4 result: fast mechanical expansions of liquid helium-4 through the lambda transition produced no observable vortices. Same core group as the 1994 paper. Essential companion citation — the honest version of the experimental record is that helium-4 did not deliver, and helium-3 did.
items.people: M. E. Dodd, P. C. Hendry, N. S. Lawson, P. V. E. McClintock, and C. D. H. Williams
items.affiliation: Lancaster University and University of Exeter (not independently verified)

items.claim: One of two independent superfluid helium-3 confirmations published back-to-back in the same 1996 issue of Nature. Grenoble/Lancaster collaboration simulating cosmic string formation via neutron-induced local heating and recooling through the transition.
items.people: Christian Bauerle, Yuriy M. Bunkov, Shaun N. Fisher, Henri Godfrin, and George R. Pickett
items.affiliation: CNRS Grenoble and Lancaster University (not independently verified). Note the diacritic: Bauerle is properly written Bäuerle.

items.claim: The companion helium-3 confirmation, notable because Tom W. B. Kibble is himself a co-author — the theorist testing his own mechanism. Neutron irradiation heats local regions of superfluid helium-3 above the transition temperature; the recooling transition is accompanied by vortex formation, the superfluid analogue of cosmic strings. These two 1996 papers are the strongest early experimental support.
items.people: V. M. H. Ruutu, V. B. Eltsov, A. J. Gill, Tom W. B. Kibble, M. Krusius, Yu. G. Makhlin, B. Placais, G. E. Volovik, and Wen Xu
items.affiliation: Low Temperature Laboratory, Helsinki University of Technology, with Kibble at Imperial College London (not independently verified). Note the diacritic: Placais is properly written Plaçais.

items.claim: The superconducting-circuit test, predating the qubit era: spontaneous fluxon (magnetic flux quantum) trapping in an annular Josephson tunnel junction quenched through the normal-superconducting transition. Reported a measured Zurek-Kibble scaling exponent of sigma = 0.27 +/- 0.05 against a predicted 0.25. The exponent values come from a search snippet, not from the article text, so treat those numbers as needing confirmation before print; the citation itself is Crossref-verified.
items.people: Roberto Monaco, Jesper Mygind, and Ray J. Rivers
items.affiliation: Istituto di Cibernetica, CNR (Italy); Technical University of Denmark; Imperial College London — not independently verified

items.claim: One of two independent trapped-ion confirmations published simultaneously in Nature Communications in 2013. A laser-cooled ion string undergoes a structural transition from linear to zig-zag as the confining potential is quenched; kinks appear in the zig-zag, and the kink creation rate follows the Kibble-Zurek power law. Title states the result directly: observation of the scaling law for defect formation.
items.people: S. Ulm, J. Rossnagel, G. Jacob, C. Degunther, S. T. Dawkins, U. G. Poschinger, R. Nigmatullin, A. Retzker, M. B. Plenio, F. Schmidt-Kaler, and K. Singer
items.affiliation: Universitat Mainz, Universitat Ulm, and Hebrew University of Jerusalem (not independently verified). Note diacritics: Rossnagel is properly Roßnagel; Degunther is properly Degünther.

items.claim: The companion trapped-ion paper, with Wojciech H. Zurek and Adolfo del Campo as co-authors. Topological defect formation and spontaneous symmetry breaking in ion Coulomb crystals, reporting an enhanced power-law scaling consistent with numerical simulations. Together with Ulm et al. this is the strongest trapped-ion evidence for defect-density scaling — the observable the Rydberg experiment did not measure.
items.people: K. Pyka, J. Keller, H. L. Partner, R. Nigmatullin, T. Burgermeister, D. M. Meier, K. Kuhlmann, A. Retzker, M. B. Plenio, Wojciech H. Zurek, Adolfo del Campo, and T. E. Mehlstaubler
items.affiliation: Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt Braunschweig, Universitat Ulm, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and Los Alamos National Laboratory (not independently verified). Note diacritic: Mehlstaubler is properly Mehlstäubler.

items.claim: Trapped-ion test that goes past the mean: probes the full distribution of kink pairs in a 1D quantum Ising chain driven across the paramagnet-ferromagnet transition, using a single trapped ion as a momentum-space quantum simulator. Finds the kink-pair number follows a Poisson binomial distribution in which all cumulants — not just the mean that KZM predicts — scale with a universal power law in quench time. Useful if the chapter wants to say the mechanism has been extended and stress-tested, not merely confirmed.
items.people: Jin-Ming Cui, Fernando Javier Gomez-Ruiz, Yun-Feng Huang, Chuan-Feng Li, Guang-Can Guo, and Adolfo del Campo
items.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei (Cui, Huang, Li, Guo); del Campo's 2020 affiliation not verified. Note diacritic: Gomez-Ruiz is properly Gómez-Ruiz.

items.claim: Cold-atom test in the Bose-Einstein condensation transition: spontaneous vortices appear in the formation of a BEC, interpreted as Kibble-Zurek defect formation. The first clear BEC-based observation and a common textbook example.
items.people: Chad N. Weiler, Tyler W. Neely, David R. Scherer, Ashton S. Bradley, Matthew J. Davis, and Brian P. Anderson
items.affiliation: University of Arizona, University of Queensland, University of Otago (not independently verified)

items.claim: Elongated BEC test in which the defects produced are solitons rather than vortices — spontaneous creation of Kibble-Zurek solitons across the condensation transition, with the defect number scaling with the quench rate. Trento group.
items.people: Giacomo Lamporesi, Simone Donadello, Simone Serafini, Franco Dalfovo, and Gabriele Ferrari
items.affiliation: INO-CNR BEC Center and University of Trento (not independently verified)

items.claim: The cold-atom result closest in spirit to the Rydberg measurement, and a useful comparison point for the chapter: a homogeneous (box-trapped) Bose gas was thermally quenched through the BEC transition and homodyne matter-wave interferometry measured first-order correlation functions, verifying the homogeneous-system power-law scaling of the COHERENCE LENGTH with quench rate — a correlation-length observable, not a defect count. Cambridge group.
items.people: Nir Navon, Alexander L. Gaunt, Robert P. Smith, and Zoran Hadzibabic
items.affiliation: Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge

items.claim: Superconducting-circuit quantum test at scale: coherent evolution through a quantum phase transition in a 1D transverse-field Ising chain using up to 2,000 superconducting flux qubits in a programmable quantum annealer. Observed the quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism with the theoretically predicted KINK STATISTICS plus positive kink-kink correlations, independent of system temperature, in quantitative agreement with analytical closed-system solutions. This is the superconducting-circuit counterpart to the Rydberg experiment, and notably it does report defect (kink) statistics.
items.people: Andrew D. King, Sei Suzuki, Jack Raymond, Alex Zucca, Trevor Lanting, Fabio Altomare, Andrew J. Berkley, Sara Ejtemaee, Emile Hoskinson, Shuiyuan Huang, Eric Ladizinsky, Allison J. R. MacDonald, Gaelen Marsden, Travis Oh, Gabriel Poulin-Lamarre, Mauricio Reis, Chris Rich, Yuki Sato, Jed D. Whittaker, Jason Yao, Richard Harris, Daniel A. Lidar, Hidetoshi Nishimori, and Mohammad H. Amin
items.affiliation: D-Wave Quantum Systems (Burnaby, Canada), with academic collaborators including Daniel A. Lidar (University of Southern California) and Hidetoshi Nishimori (Tokyo Institute of Technology) — collaborator affiliations not independently verified

items.claim: Scale-up of the superconducting-flux-qubit work to a 3D programmable spin glass on more than 5,000 qubits, measuring quantum critical dynamics in a regime where classical simulation of the many-body quantum dynamics is intractable. Optional for the chapter, but the natural citation if it wants to argue that Kibble-Zurek physics has become a benchmark for quantum simulators rather than merely a phenomenon being tested.
items.people: Andrew D. King, Jack Raymond, Trevor Lanting, Richard Harris, Alex Zucca, and 22 further co-authors (27 total)
items.affiliation: D-Wave Quantum Systems, with Boston University collaborators (not independently verified)

items.claim: Recent superfluid test: universal Kibble-Zurek scaling in a homogeneous, strongly interacting atomic Fermi superfluid, probed with two distinct control parameters (temperature and interaction strength) whose microscopic condensate-formation physics differs by two orders of magnitude in timescale, yet which yield a consistent scaling exponent of about 0.68. The two-pathway design is the strongest available evidence for universality specifically. The 0.68 value comes from a search summary of the abstract rather than the article text, so confirm before quoting a number.

items.affiliation: Seoul National University (not independently verified; Crossref lists the fourth author as 'Y. Shin')

items.claim: Earlier Fermi-superfluid result from the same lead group, reporting Kibble-Zurek universality in a strongly interacting Fermi superfluid — here the observable IS defect density, with the scaling exponent relating defect density to quench rate determined by the underlying symmetries. Pair with the 2024 paper if the chapter wants both the first Fermi-superfluid observation and its two-pathway confirmation.
