items.affiliation: Seoul National University (not independently verified; Crossref lists the third author as 'Y. Shin')

openQuestions: The Zurek 1985 Nature letter proposes the experiment and the random-phase-domain picture but does not state the quench-rate power law in the form the chapter probably uses. The most explicit early statement is usually attributed to Zurek, 'Cosmic strings in laboratory superfluids and the topological remnants of other phase transitions,' Acta Physica Polonica B 24, 1301 (1993). I did NOT verify that reference and am not asserting it. If the chapter's sentence is 'Zurek derived the scaling law,' either verify the 1993 Acta Phys. Pol. B citation or cite Zurek 1996 Physics Reports instead, which I did verify.

Does the chapter state the scaling law as a defect-density relation or a correlation-length relation? These are the same physics but different citations. If it says 'defect density scales as a power of quench rate,' the supporting experiments are Ulm 2013, Pyka 2013, Ko 2019, King 2022. If it says 'correlation length scales as a power of quench rate,' the supporting experiments are Navon 2015 and Keesling 2019. Citing Keesling under a defect-density claim is the specific error the brief was written to prevent.

In the Keesling paper the fit is presented against inverse detuning sweep rate, and the OCR of the printed formula reads as a positive exponent on (s/s0). I have stated the result conservatively as 'mu = 0.50(3) from a power-law fit of correlation length against inverse sweep rate,' which is unambiguous and matches Figure 2c. If the chapter reproduces the formula with an explicit sign, check the sign convention against the published text.

Author affiliations for roughly half these entries are stated from general knowledge, not from a fetched source, because IOP, Nature, APS, and Science article pages are bot-blocked. Only the Keesling affiliations were read directly. If the chapter names institutions for Kibble, Zurek, the helium-3 groups, the trapped-ion groups, or the D-Wave collaborators, those should be confirmed against the papers themselves before print.

Two numeric values in this set came from search-result summaries rather than article text and are marked 'probable': the Monaco 2002 exponent (sigma = 0.27 +/- 0.05 against a predicted 0.25) and the Lee 2024 exponent (about 0.68). Do not print either number without checking the source.

How does the chapter want to handle the superfluid helium-4 episode? The 1994 Hendry result is widely cited as an early confirmation, but the same group's 1998 experiment found no vortices. A chapter that lists helium-4 among the confirmations without the 1998 caveat would be repeating a common secondary-literature error.

Should the chapter cite a QKZM review alongside the three 2005 primary papers? Jacek Dziarmaga, 'Dynamics of a quantum phase transition and relaxation to a steady state,' Advances in Physics 59(6), 1063-1189 (2010), DOI 10.1080/00018732.2010.514702, is Crossref-verified and would serve, but I omitted it from the item list as a review rather than a primary source.

The brief describes the Rydberg work as 'from the Lukin and Greiner groups at Harvard and MIT.' Read literally that could imply Greiner has an MIT affiliation. Per the paper, Lukin and Greiner are both at Harvard; MIT enters through Vladan Vuletic. Recommend phrasing it as a Harvard-MIT collaboration led from the Lukin and Greiner groups at Harvard with Vuletic at MIT.

verdicts.claim: SUMMARY / del Campo & Zurek 2014 scaling law: 'the frozen-out correlation length scales as a power of the quench time with exponent nu/(1+nu*z), and defect density as the inverse d-th power of that.'
verdicts.correction: THIS IS THE MOST SERIOUS ERROR IN THE DOSSIER AND MUST NOT REACH PRINT. The correlation-length half is right; the defect-density half is wrong. Verified against the full text of del Campo & Zurek, arXiv:1310.1600 (= Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 29, 1430018), which gives:  xi_hat = xi_0 (tau_Q/tau_0)^(nu/(1+z*nu))  and  n ~ (1/xi_0^(D-d)) * (tau_0/tau_Q)^((D-d)*nu/(1+z*nu)). The paper defines D as the dimension of SPACE and d as the dimension of the DEFECT (d=1 for vortex lines in a 3D superfluid; d=0 for point defects). Defect density therefore scales as the inverse (D-d)-th power of the frozen correlation length -- the inverse CODIMENSION power -- not the inverse d-th power. The dossier's version is not a typo but a sign/symbol swap that inverts the physics: for vortex lines in 3D it would give n ~ 1/xi_hat instead of the correct n ~ 1/xi_hat^2. Correct text for the chapter: 'The frozen-out correlation length scales as the quench time to the power nu/(1+nu*z), and the defect density as the inverse (D-d) power of that length, where D is the dimension of space and d the dimension of the defect.'

verdicts.claim: Direct quotation from Keesling et al. 2019: "While the QKZM is a coarse-grained description that predicts the mean density of defects, the shape of the correlation function gives further access to microscopic details of the system."
verdicts.correction: MISQUOTE presented inside quotation marks. Verified against the full text (arXiv:1809.05540v2, the accepted version). The actual sentence reads: "While the quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism is a coarse-grained description predicting the mean density of defects, the shape of the correlation function gives further access to microscopic details of the system." The dossier substitutes the abbreviation 'QKZM' for 'the quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism' and 'that predicts' for 'predicting'. The substance is unchanged, but a book published under a real author's name cannot print an altered string inside quotation marks. Use the exact wording above, or paraphrase without quotation marks.

verdicts.claim: Direct quotation from Keesling et al. 2019: the authors claim this as "the first experimental verification of the QKZM in an isolated quantum system that defies a mean-field description."
verdicts.correction: Same misquote pattern. The actual sentence is: "These results offer the first experimental verification of the quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism in an isolated quantum system that defies a mean-field description." Again 'QKZM' is the dossier's abbreviation, not the authors'. Quote it in full or paraphrase.

verdicts.claim: Keesling et al. 2019, Nature 568, 207-211 -- 15 named authors in the stated order; mu = 0.50(3) from an exponential fit to the modulus of the Rydberg density-density correlation function G(r) versus inverse detuning sweep rate; defect density NOT the reported observable; chiral clock mu ~ 0.38 (Z3) and ~ 0.25 (Z4); 51-atom rubidium-87 array.
verdicts.correction: Every element verified. Crossref and Nature metadata confirm Nature 568(7751), 207-211, April 2019, DOI 10.1038/s41586-019-1070-1, title 'Quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism and critical dynamics on a programmable Rydberg simulator'. The 15-author list and order match arXiv:1809.05540v2 exactly. Full text confirms mu = 0.50(3) for the Z2 transition, extraction of correlation length by fitting an exponential decay to the modulus of the correlation function, mu ~ 0.38 (Z3) and mu ~ 0.25 (Z4), and that defect density was not the reported observable. The dossier's central precision point is correct and well founded. ONE SPELLING FIX: the fourteenth author is Vladan Vuletic with an acute accent -- Vuletić -- per Nature's own author metadata. The dossier carefully flags diacritics for Bauerle, Placais, Rossnagel, Degunther, Mehlstaubler and Gomez-Ruiz but silently drops this one.

verdicts.claim: Keesling et al. affiliations: Harvard (Keesling, Omran, Levine, Bernien, Choi, Samajdar, Sachdev, Greiner, Lukin); Pichler jointly Harvard + ITAMP; Vuletic at MIT Physics and RLE; Schwartz at Laboratoire Kastler Brossel, ENS/CNRS/Sorbonne/College de France; Silvi and Zoller at IQOQI Austrian Academy of Sciences + Center for Quantum Physics, University of Innsbruck; Endres at Caltech.
verdicts.correction: Independently re-verified against Nature's citation_author_institution metadata for DOI 10.1038/s41586-019-1070-1. Every assignment matches, including Pichler's dual Harvard/ITAMP listing and Silvi/Zoller's dual IQOQI/University of Innsbruck listing. The dossier's recommended phrasing -- a Harvard-MIT collaboration led from the Lukin and Greiner groups at Harvard, with Vuletić at MIT -- is correct; Greiner has no MIT affiliation on this paper.

verdicts.claim: Preprint of the Rydberg paper: arXiv:1809.05540 [quant-ph], submitted 14 September 2018, revised 1 April 2019, same author list as the Nature version.
verdicts.correction: arXiv API confirms submission 2018-09-14T18:00:04Z, title identical to the journal version, 15 authors in identical order. The URL https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.05540 resolves to that exact work.

verdicts.claim: Kibble 1976, J. Phys. A 9(8), 1387-1398 -- type of defect determined by homotopy groups of the manifold of degenerate vacua; domain-wall theories likely excluded by unacceptable gravitational effects; a cosmic network of strings may well have formed.
verdicts.correction: Crossref and INSPIRE-HEP both confirm 'Topology of cosmic domains and strings', T. W. B. Kibble, J. Phys. A: Math. Gen. 9(8), 1387-1398 (1976), DOI 10.1088/0305-4470/9/8/029. The abstract matches the claim nearly word for word: 'It is shown that the formation of domain wall, strings or monopoles depends on the homotopy groups of the manifold of degenerate vacua... while theories generating domain walls can probably be eliminated (because of their unacceptable gravitational effects), a cosmic network of strings may well have been formed.' Kibble's Imperial College London affiliation could not be read from the 1976 source (IOP blocks automated access), but Nature's metadata for the 1996 Ruutu paper independently lists him at 'Blackett Laboratory, Imperial College, London' -- use that if you need a sourced institution.

verdicts.claim: Kibble 1980, Physics Reports 67(1), 183-199 -- 'the source of the causal-horizon argument for the initial density of defects... This is where the density estimate (as opposed to the topological classification) originates on the cosmology side.'
verdicts.correction: The citation is exact -- INSPIRE-HEP and Crossref confirm 'Some implications of a cosmological phase transition', T. W. B. Kibble, Phys. Rep. 67(1), 183-199 (1980), DOI 10.1016/0370-1573(80)90091-5. But the ORIGINALITY claim overstates. Two problems. (1) The paper's own abstract describes it as a set of Les Houches winter-school lectures whose 'aim is mainly pedagogical, with special emphasis on unsolved problems' -- not the introduction of a new density estimate. (2) del Campo & Zurek 2014, the dossier's own preferred modern source, credits the field to 'the seminal papers of Tom Kibble [1,2]' -- citing the 1976 and 1980 papers JOINTLY, not the 1980 one alone, for the causal argument. Recommended text: 'Kibble's causality argument -- that domains cannot be correlated over distances larger than the causal horizon at the transition, which sets a lower bound on defect separation -- is developed across his 1976 and 1980 papers.' Cite both.

verdicts.claim: Zurek 1985, Nature 317(6037), 505-508 -- proposes the cosmic string / superfluid vortex analogy and a cryogenic pressure-quench experiment; the condensate phase is chosen randomly in domains of characteristic size d, so the phase mismatch around an annulus of circumference C scales as (C/d)^(1/2).
verdicts.correction: Fully verified, including the formula, from Nature's own abstract metadata for DOI 10.1038/317505a0: '...the phase of the Bose condensate wavefunction -- the 4He analogue of the broken symmetry of the field-theoretic vacuum -- will be chosen randomly in domains of some characteristic size d. When the quench is performed in an annulus of circumference C the typical value of the phase mismatch around the loop will be ~(C/d)1/2.' Title: 'Cosmological experiments in superfluid helium?'. Pages 505-508 confirmed (citation_lastpage=508); note that some secondary sources give 505-507 and are wrong. BONUS RESOLUTION: Zurek's affiliation is confirmed from the article metadata as 'Theoretical Astrophysics, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos' -- the dossier can drop its 'not independently verified' hedge.

verdicts.claim: Zurek 1996, Physics Reports 276, 177-221 -- the standard primary source for the Kibble-Zurek scaling law in its usual form.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms 'Cosmological experiments in condensed matter systems', W. H. Zurek, Phys. Rep. 276(4), 177-221 (November 1996), DOI 10.1016/S0370-1573(96)00009-9. Add the issue number (4) if your style requires it. The dossier's advice -- cite this rather than the 1985 Nature letter when stating the quench-rate power law -- is sound.

verdicts.claim: OPEN QUESTION, now resolved: Zurek, 'Cosmic strings in laboratory superfluids and the topological remnants of other phase transitions,' Acta Physica Polonica B 24, 1301 (1993) -- flagged in the dossier as unverified and not asserted.
verdicts.correction: This reference is real and I verified it via INSPIRE-HEP. Exact citation: W. H. Zurek, 'Cosmic strings in laboratory superfluids and the topological remnants of other phase transitions,' Acta Physica Polonica B 24, 1301-1311 (1993). Note the page range ends at 1311, which the dossier did not have. The journal's own archive is at https://www.actaphys.uj.edu.pl/ -- there is no DOI for this volume, so cite it without one. You may now use it if the chapter's sentence is 'Zurek derived the scaling law'; Zurek 1996 Phys. Rep. remains the safer, DOI-bearing alternative.

verdicts.claim: Laguna & Zurek 1997, PRL 78, 2519-2522 -- 'First numerical demonstration of the quench-rate scaling law for kink density.'
verdicts.correction: Bibliography exact: 'Density of Kinks after a Quench: When Symmetry Breaks, How Big are the Pieces?', Pablo Laguna and Wojciech Hubert Zurek, Phys. Rev. Lett. 78(13), 2519-2522 (31 March 1997), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2519. But drop the word 'first'. The paper makes no priority claim; its own abstract calls it 'a limited (1D) test of the more general theory of domain-size evolution.' It also states a concrete result the dossier omits and the chapter would benefit from: numerical Landau-Ginzburg evolution gives a kink density 'proportional to the fourth root of its rate.' Recommended text: 'A 1D numerical study of Landau-Ginzburg dynamics found the kink density proportional to the fourth root of the quench rate, and the authors present it as a limited test of the general domain-size theory.'

verdicts.claim: del Campo & Zurek 2014, Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 29(8), art. 1430018 -- the best single modern citation for the scaling law, covering classical and quantum cases.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms 'Universality of phase transition dynamics: Topological defects from symmetry breaking', Adolfo del Campo and Wojciech H. Zurek, Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 29(08), 1430018 (30 March 2014), DOI 10.1142/S0217751X1430018X. Preprint arXiv:1310.1600. The characterization is accurate EXCEPT for the defect-density exponent, corrected in the first entry above. One useful addition: this review restricts itself to 'the experiments that test the scaling of the number of topological defects with the quench rate' and states plainly that 'He-4 remains a confounding exception' -- which is independent, authoritative support for the dossier's helium-4 caveat.

verdicts.claim: Kibble 2007, Physics Today 60(9), 47-52 -- accessible retrospective by Kibble on how early-universe speculation led to laboratory experiments.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms 'Phase-transition dynamics in the lab and the universe', Tom Kibble, Physics Today 60(9), 47-52 (1 September 2007), DOI 10.1063/1.2784684. The AIP article page blocks automated access, so the description of the article's content is plausible and matches the known framing but was not read from the source; the bibliographic record is solid.

verdicts.claim: Damski 2005, PRL 95, art. 035701 -- reframes Landau-Zener transitions as the simplest quantum model supporting Kibble-Zurek topological defect production.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms Bogdan Damski, 'The Simplest Quantum Model Supporting the Kibble-Zurek Mechanism of Topological Defect Production: Landau-Zener Transitions from a New Perspective', Phys. Rev. Lett. 95(3), 035701 (13 July 2005), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.035701. Preprint cond-mat/0411004, whose abstract confirms the claim: 'dynamics of the Landau-Zener model can be accurately described in terms of the Kibble-Zurek theory... The simplest quantum model exhibiting the Kibble-Zurek mechanism is presented.'

verdicts.claim: Zurek, Dorner & Zoller 2005, PRL 95, art. 105701 -- companion paper establishing the QKZM; near a quantum critical point the relevant timescale is set by the inverse gap, and faster-than-gap driving freezes the growth of correlated regions. 'This is the paper the Rydberg experiment cites as the QKZM foundation.'
verdicts.correction: Bibliography exact: 'Dynamics of a Quantum Phase Transition', Wojciech H. Zurek, Uwe Dorner, Peter Zoller, Phys. Rev. Lett. 95(10), 105701 (1 September 2005), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.105701, preprint cond-mat/0503511. Two adjustments. (1) The physics paraphrase is defensible but not what the abstract emphasizes; the abstract presents TWO approaches -- one retracing the standard thermodynamic argument in a quantum setting, one 'purely quantum, based on the Landau-Zener formula for transition probabilities in avoided level crossings' -- and shows they 'yield compatible results for the scaling of the defect density with the quench rate.' If you describe the paper, describe that. (2) Delete the singular claim that this is 'the paper the Rydberg experiment cites as the QKZM foundation': Keesling et al. cite the 2005 quantum-extension literature collectively, not this paper uniquely. Say 'one of the papers the Rydberg experiment cites' or drop the clause.

verdicts.claim: Dziarmaga 2005, PRL 95, art. 245701 -- exact solution of the quantum Ising model under a linear quench, giving kink density scaling analytically.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms Jacek Dziarmaga, 'Dynamics of a Quantum Phase Transition: Exact Solution of the Quantum Ising Model', Phys. Rev. Lett. 95(24), 245701 (9 December 2005), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.245701, preprint cond-mat/0509490. The abstract confirms the analytic result and supplies a number worth quoting: 'Average density of defects excited in this way scales like a square root of the transition rate. This scaling is the same as the scaling obtained when the standard Kibble-Zurek mechanism... is applied to the quantum phase transition in the Ising model.'

verdicts.claim: Chuang, Durrer, Turok & Yurke 1991, Science 251(4999), 1336-1342 -- earliest laboratory test of the defect-formation picture; supports the 'one-scale' model for cosmic string evolution; observes textures decaying into monopole-antimonopole pairs; first 'cosmology in the lab' experiment in this lineage.
verdicts.correction: Bibliography and author order exact: Isaac Chuang, Ruth Durrer, Neil Turok, Bernard Yurke, 'Cosmology in the Laboratory: Defect Dynamics in Liquid Crystals', Science 251(4999), 1336-1342 (15 March 1991), DOI 10.1126/science.251.4999.1336. The one-scale and texture-decay claims are confirmed verbatim from the abstract. FIX THE FRAMING: this is a test of defect DYNAMICS and EVOLUTION, not of defect FORMATION. The abstract is explicit -- 'the direct study of the scaling solution for a network of strings', 'a model for the evolution of monopoles and texture' -- and it never measures a Kibble-Zurek quench-rate scaling. Calling it 'the earliest laboratory test of the defect-formation picture' will mislead a reader into thinking the KZ scaling law was tested in 1991; it was not. Recommended text: 'The earliest cosmology-in-the-lab experiment in this lineage, testing defect dynamics -- the one-scale model for string network evolution and the decay of textures into monopole-antimonopole pairs -- rather than the quench-rate formation law.'

verdicts.claim: Hendry, Lawson, Lee, McClintock & Williams 1994, Nature 368, 315-317 -- pressure-quenched helium-4 vortex generation as a cosmic-string analogue; not reproduced by the same group's 1998 experiment.
verdicts.correction: Crossref and Nature confirm 'Generation of defects in superfluid 4He as an analogue of the formation of cosmic strings', Nature 368(6469), 315-317 (March 1994), DOI 10.1038/368315a0, five authors in the stated order. Affiliations, read from Nature's metadata, are now sourced: Hendry, Lawson, Lee and McClintock at the School of Physics and Materials, Lancaster University; Williams at the Department of Physics, University of Exeter -- so 'Lancaster University and University of Exeter' is right. The abstract confirms the mechanism ('the superfluid transition of liquid 4He induced by fast adiabatic expansion through the critical density... We observe copious production of quantized vortices'). The dossier's caveat is not merely defensible but is endorsed by del Campo & Zurek 2014, which calls He-4 'a confounding exception.' Do not cite this paper as a confirmation without the 1998 companion.

verdicts.claim: Dodd, Hendry, Lawson, McClintock & Williams 1998, PRL 81, 3703-3706 -- fast mechanical expansions of liquid helium-4 through the lambda transition produced no observable vortices.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms 'Nonappearance of Vortices in Fast Mechanical Expansions of Liquid 4He through the Lambda Transition', Phys. Rev. Lett. 81(17), 3703-3706 (26 October 1998), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.81.3703, five authors in the stated order. Note for the chapter's wording: the dossier calls it 'the retraction-in-effect', which is fine as editorial framing but should not be phrased so that a reader thinks a formal retraction was issued. It was a later, improved experiment by the same group reporting a null result, not a retraction.

verdicts.claim: Bauerle, Bunkov, Fisher, Godfrin & Pickett 1996, Nature 382, 332-334 -- Grenoble/Lancaster helium-3 confirmation via neutron-induced local heating and recooling. Bauerle is properly Bauerle with an umlaut.
verdicts.correction: Crossref and Nature confirm 'Laboratory simulation of cosmic string formation in the early Universe using superfluid 3He', Nature 382(6589), 332-334 (July 1996), DOI 10.1038/382332a0, five authors in the stated order, Bäuerle with the umlaut as flagged. Affiliations now sourced from Nature metadata: Bäuerle, Bunkov, Fisher and Godfrin all at Centre de Recherches sur les Tres Basses Temperatures, CNRS, Grenoble; Pickett at the School of Physics and Chemistry, Lancaster University -- so 'Grenoble/Lancaster collaboration' is exactly right. The abstract adds a detail worth having: the vortex density was inferred from the DEFICIT IN ENERGY RELEASED as neutron-heated normal regions passed back into the superfluid, and 'agrees very well with the predictions of Zurek's modification of the original Kibble mechanism.'

verdicts.claim: Ruutu, Eltsov, Gill, Kibble, Krusius, Makhlin, Placais, Volovik & Xu 1996, Nature 382, 334-336 -- companion helium-3 confirmation with Kibble himself as co-author. Placais is properly Placais with a cedilla.
verdicts.correction: Crossref and Nature confirm 'Vortex formation in neutron-irradiated superfluid 3He as an analogue of cosmological defect formation', Nature 382(6589), 334-336 (July 1996), DOI 10.1038/382334a0, nine authors in the stated order, Plaçais with the cedilla as flagged. Affiliations now sourced: Ruutu, Eltsov, Krusius, Makhlin, Volovik and Xu at the Low Temperature Laboratory, Helsinki University of Technology (Espoo); Gill and Kibble at the Blackett Laboratory, Imperial College London (Gill also T-6, Los Alamos); Plaçais at LPMC, Ecole Normale Superieure, Paris. The dossier's 'Helsinki University of Technology, with Kibble at Imperial College London' is correct but incomplete -- Plaçais is at ENS Paris, not Helsinki. The abstract supports the strength of the claim: results 'provide clear confirmation' and 'give quantitative support to the Kibble-Zurek mechanism.' Note also that the preprint circulated under a different title, 'Big bang simulation in superfluid 3He-B -- Vortex nucleation in neutron-irradiated superflow'; cite the Nature title.

verdicts.claim: Monaco, Mygind & Rivers 2002, PRL 89, art. 080603 -- annular Josephson junction fluxon trapping, measured Zurek-Kibble exponent sigma = 0.27 +/- 0.05 against a predicted 0.25. Flagged 'probable', numbers from a search snippet.
verdicts.correction: BOTH NUMBERS NOW CONFIRMED FROM THE SOURCE, so the 'probable' flag can be cleared. Crossref confirms 'Zurek-Kibble Domain Structures: The Dynamics of Spontaneous Vortex Formation in Annular Josephson Tunnel Junctions', R. Monaco, J. Mygind, R. J. Rivers, Phys. Rev. Lett. 89(8), 080603 (6 August 2002), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.89.080603. The preprint is arXiv:cond-mat/0112321, whose abstract states: 'Using symmetric and long Josephson Tunnel Junctions, for which the predicted index is sigma = 0.25, we find sigma = 0.27 +/- 0.05. Further, there is agreement with the ZK prediction for the overall normalisation.' One wording note: the junctions are described as 'symmetric and long', and the dossier's characterization of the quench as through 'the normal-superconducting transition' is correct for the mechanism but is not the abstract's language.

verdicts.claim: Ulm et al. 2013, Nature Communications 4, art. 2290 -- laser-cooled ion string, linear-to-zigzag structural transition, kink creation rate follows the Kibble-Zurek power law.
verdicts.correction: Bibliography and the eleven-author list are exact: 'Observation of the Kibble-Zurek scaling law for defect formation in ion crystals', Nat. Commun. 4, 2290 (7 August 2013), DOI 10.1038/ncomms3290, with Roßnagel and Degünther carrying the diacritics as flagged. But the description is too vague for a book that is making a point about precision. The abstract specifies: the crystal is SIXTEEN laser-cooled trapped ions; the measured scaling is defect formation proportional to the traversal rate to the power 2.68 +/- 0.06; and this 'supports the prediction of 8/3 = 2.67 FOR FINITE INHOMOGENEOUS SYSTEMS.' That is the inhomogeneous KZM exponent, not the homogeneous Kibble-Zurek exponent, and the authors themselves stress the result 'demonstrates that the scaling laws also apply in the mesoscopic regime.' Recommended text: 'In a crystal of 16 laser-cooled trapped ions driven through the linear-to-zigzag structural transition, defect formation scaled with the traversal rate to the power 2.68 +/- 0.06, matching the 8/3 prediction of the inhomogeneous Kibble-Zurek mechanism for finite systems.'

verdicts.claim: Pyka et al. 2013, Nature Communications 4, art. 2291 -- companion trapped-ion paper with Zurek and del Campo as co-authors, reporting enhanced power-law scaling consistent with numerical simulations.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms 'Topological defect formation and spontaneous symmetry breaking in ion Coulomb crystals', Nat. Commun. 4, 2291 (7 August 2013), DOI 10.1038/ncomms3291, twelve authors in the stated order including W. H. Zurek and A. del Campo, with Mehlstäubler carrying the umlaut as flagged. Published the same day as Ulm et al. (article numbers 2290 and 2291), so 'published simultaneously' is accurate. The abstract confirms the result: defects created 'by a controlled quench of the confining potential', and the authors 'observe an enhanced power law scaling in accordance with numerical simulations and recent predictions.'

verdicts.claim: Cui et al. 2020, Communications Physics 3, art. 44 -- single trapped ion as a momentum-space quantum simulator; kink-pair number follows a Poisson binomial distribution in which all cumulants scale with a universal power law in quench time.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms 'Experimentally testing quantum critical dynamics beyond the Kibble-Zurek mechanism', Commun. Phys. 3, 44 (6 March 2020), DOI 10.1038/s42005-020-0306-6, six authors in the stated order, Gómez-Ruiz with the accent as flagged; preprint arXiv:1903.02145 (6 March 2019). The abstract confirms every element: 'using a single trapped ion as a quantum simulator in momentum space. The number of kink pairs after the transition follows a Poisson binomial distribution, in which all cumulants scale with a universal power-law as a function of the quench time.' One honesty note the chapter should carry if it leans on this paper: the authors verified the scaling 'for the first cumulants' only, and 'report deviations due to noise-induced dephasing of the trapped ion.'

verdicts.claim: Weiler et al. 2008, Nature 455, 948-951 -- spontaneous vortices in BEC formation, interpreted as Kibble-Zurek defect formation; the first clear BEC-based observation.
verdicts.correction: Bibliography exact: 'Spontaneous vortices in the formation of Bose-Einstein condensates', Nature 455(7215), 948-951 (October 2008), DOI 10.1038/nature07334, six authors in the stated order. The priority claim is also supported -- the preprint (arXiv:0807.3323) states 'our results encompass the first experimental observations and statistical characterisation of spontaneous vortex formation in the condensation transition.' THE CAUTION THE DOSSIER SHOULD HAVE FLAGGED, given that this is precisely the error class the brief exists to prevent: Weiler et al. observed and statistically characterized spontaneous vortices but did NOT measure a power-law scaling of defect number against quench rate, and neither the published nor the preprint abstract mentions Kibble-Zurek by name. This paper belongs in the 'do defects form at all' column, not the 'defect density scales as a power of quench rate' column. del Campo & Zurek 2014 sorts the literature exactly that way. Cite it for observation, never for the scaling law.

verdicts.claim: Lamporesi et al. 2013, Nature Physics 9, 656-660 -- spontaneous creation of Kibble-Zurek solitons in an elongated BEC, with defect number scaling with the quench rate. Trento group.
verdicts.correction: Bibliography exact: 'Spontaneous creation of Kibble-Zurek solitons in a Bose-Einstein condensate', Nature Physics 9(10), 656-660 (October 2013), DOI 10.1038/nphys2734, five authors in the stated order. One precision fix: the abstract says 'We measure the power-law dependence of defect number on the QUENCH TIME', not the quench rate. In a chapter whose whole subject is a power law in tau_Q, quench time and quench rate are reciprocals and the exponent changes sign between them; keep the paper's own variable. The abstract also adds a finding worth a clause: 'lower atomic densities enhance defect formation.'

verdicts.claim: Navon, Gaunt, Smith & Hadzibabic 2015, Science 347(6218), 167-170 -- box-trapped homogeneous Bose gas thermally quenched through the BEC transition; homodyne matter-wave interferometry measured first-order correlation functions, verifying the homogeneous-system power-law scaling of the COHERENCE LENGTH with quench rate.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms 'Critical dynamics of spontaneous symmetry breaking in a homogeneous Bose gas', Science 347(6218), 167-170 (9 January 2015), DOI 10.1126/science.1258676, four authors in the stated order, Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge. The preprint (arXiv:1410.8487) matches the dossier almost word for word: 'Using homodyne matter-wave interferometry to measure first-order correlation functions, we verify the central quantitative prediction of the Kibble-Zurek theory, namely the homogeneous-system power-law scaling of the coherence length with the quench rate.' Two additions the chapter could use: they 'directly confirm its underlying hypothesis, the freezing of the correlation length near the transition due to critical slowing down', and they support z = 3/2 as the dynamical critical exponent for this universality class, which includes the lambda transition of liquid He-4. The dossier's placement of this paper alongside Keesling as a correlation-length observable is correct.

verdicts.claim: King et al. 2022, Nature Physics 18, 1324-1328 -- coherent evolution through a QPT in a 1D transverse-field Ising chain using up to 2,000 superconducting flux qubits; observed QKZM with theoretically predicted kink statistics plus positive kink-kink correlations, independent of system temperature, in quantitative agreement with closed-system analytical solutions.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms 'Coherent quantum annealing in a programmable 2,000 qubit Ising chain', Nature Physics 18(11), 1324-1328 (November 2022), DOI 10.1038/s41567-022-01741-6, and all 24 authors appear in exactly the order the dossier lists them. Preprint arXiv:2202.05847 (11 February 2022). The abstract confirms the claim nearly verbatim: 'In large systems we observe the quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism with theoretically predicted kink statistics, as well as characteristic positive kink-kink correlations, independent of system temperature... results are in quantitative agreement with analytical solutions to the closed-system quantum model.' Worth adding for balance, since the chapter is being careful about non-confirmatory evidence: 'For slower anneals we observe anti-Kibble-Zurek scaling in a crossover to the open quantum regime.'

verdicts.claim: King et al. 2023, Nature 617, 61-66 -- 3D programmable spin glass on more than 5,000 qubits, measuring quantum critical dynamics where classical simulation of the many-body quantum dynamics is intractable. '27 total' authors.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms 'Quantum critical dynamics in a 5,000-qubit programmable spin glass', Nature 617(7959), 61-66 (4 May 2023), DOI 10.1038/s41586-023-05867-2. The author count is exactly 27, the five named leading authors and their order are correct, and the Boston University collaborator the dossier alludes to is Anders W. Sandvik (second-to-last author). Preprint arXiv:2207.13800 (27 July 2022). The abstract confirms 'we measure dynamics in 3D spin glasses on thousands of qubits, where simulation of many-body quantum dynamics is intractable.' If the chapter uses this to argue KZ physics has become a quantum-simulator benchmark, note the paper's own framing is a claim of 'a scaling advantage in reducing energy as a function of annealing time' for quantum over thermal annealing -- a contested optimization claim, so keep the chapter's sentence about critical dynamics and stay out of the advantage debate.

verdicts.claim: Lee, Kim, Kim & Shin 2024, Nature Physics 20, 1570-1574 -- homogeneous strongly interacting atomic Fermi superfluid probed with two control parameters (temperature and interaction strength) differing by two orders of magnitude in condensate-formation timescale, yielding a consistent exponent of about 0.68. Flagged 'probable'.
verdicts.correction: THE 0.68 VALUE IS NOW CONFIRMED FROM THE SOURCE, so the 'probable' flag can be cleared. Crossref confirms 'Universal Kibble-Zurek scaling in an atomic Fermi superfluid', Nature Physics 20(10), 1570-1574 (October 2024), DOI 10.1038/s41567-024-02592-z. The preprint (arXiv:2310.05437, 9 October 2023) states: 'The microscopic physics of condensate formation is markedly different for the two quench parameters, signaled by their two orders of magnitude difference in the condensate formation timescale. However, regardless of the thermodynamic direction in which the system passes through a phase transition, the Kibble-Zurek exponent is identically observed to be about 0.68.' Author-name note the dossier half-caught: Crossref abbreviates the fourth author to 'Y. Shin', but arXiv gives the full form 'Yong-il Shin', so the dossier's spelling is right and the hedge can go.

verdicts.claim: Ko, Park & Shin 2019, Nature Physics 15, 1227-1231 -- first Fermi-superfluid Kibble-Zurek result; the observable IS defect density, with the exponent determined by the underlying symmetries.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms 'Kibble-Zurek universality in a strongly interacting Fermi superfluid', Nature Physics 15(12), 1227-1231 (December 2019), DOI 10.1038/s41567-019-0650-1, three authors in the stated order (Crossref abbreviates the third to 'Y. Shin'; the preprint arXiv:1902.06922 does the same, so use 'Yong-il Shin' only if you can source the full form). The defect-density point is confirmed by the abstract: 'the Kibble-Zurek mechanism for the creation of topological defects unveils this universality through a characteristic power-law exponent, which captures the dependence of the DEFECT DENSITY on the quench rate... the quench formation of vortices reveals a constant scaling exponent arising from the U(1) gauge symmetry of the system.' One caveat to carry: 'For rapid quenches, destructive vortex collisions lead to the saturation of their densities' -- the power law does not hold at the fast end.

verdicts.claim: Overall bibliographic integrity: no citation in the dossier is hallucinated or garbled.
verdicts.correction: I checked all 27 DOIs directly against the Crossref REST API and independently cross-checked titles, author lists and author ORDER against arXiv, INSPIRE-HEP, Semantic Scholar and (for the Nature papers) Nature's own citation metadata. Every DOI resolves to the exact work described. Every volume, issue, page range and article number matches. Every author list and ordering matches, including the 15-author Keesling list, the 24-author King 2022 list and the 27-author King 2023 count. All flagged diacritics (Bäuerle, Plaçais, Roßnagel, Degünther, Mehlstäubler, Gómez-Ruiz) are correct; one unflagged diacritic (Vuletić) needs adding. The overall MAJOR verdict rests entirely on non-bibliographic problems: the wrong defect-density exponent (inverse d instead of inverse D-d), two altered strings presented as verbatim quotations from Keesling et al., and three descriptions that overstate what a paper showed (Laguna-Zurek 'first', Chuang formation-vs-dynamics, Weiler as scaling evidence).

superconductivity-ml.domain: Machine learning applied to superconductivity and the superconducting transition
superconductivity-ml.summary: The superconducting transition is the textbook case of a continuous (second-order) phase transition with a well-defined order parameter: Ginzburg-Landau theory (1950) posits a complex order parameter psi that goes continuously to zero at Tc, and BCS theory (Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer, Physical Review 1957) supplies the microscopic content — a phonon-mediated pairing instability whose gap Delta(T) is the order parameter and closes continuously at Tc. Machine learning entered this field mainly through one empirical resource, the NIMS SuperCon database, whose provenance is unusually consequential: it grew out of a Japanese national project launched in 1987 after the 1986 cuprate discovery, was distributed for years through the MatNavi web interface, had that interface decommissioned in 2021, and now circulates as re-edited MDR datasheets plus derived products (the UCI/Hamidieh feature table, 3DSC with inferred crystal structures, and the literature-mined SuperCon2). The canonical ML paper is Stanev, Oses, Kusne, Rodriguez, Paglione, Curtarolo and Takeuchi (npj Computational Materials 2018), which classified materials above/below 10 K at roughly 92% out-of-sample accuracy from composition alone and proposed more than 30 candidate oxides from the ICSD. The documented weakness of this whole line of work is that random train/test splits measure interpolation inside dense, heavily sampled families (cuprates, iron-based, A15/alloy) rather than the extrapolation that discovery requires — Meredig and co-authors made this precise in 2018 with leave-one-cluster-out cross-validation, and composition-only models additionally cannot distinguish polymorphs. Very few ML Tc predictions have been experimentally confirmed; the clearest genuine case is the closed-loop JHU-APL work of Pogue and colleagues (npj Computational Materials 2023), which found one new superconductor in the Zr-In-Ni system. By contrast, the celebrated hydride predictions that were confirmed — H3S by Duan and colleagues (2014), LaH10 by Liu, Naumov, Hoffmann, Ashcroft and Hemley and by Peng and colleagues (2017) — came from crystal-structure search plus Migdal-Eliashberg electron-phonon theory, not from data-driven ML; ML entered hydride work later as a surrogate to triage structure-search candidates (Shipley, Hutcheon, Needs and Pickard 2021; Cerqueira, Sanna and Marques 2024). The hydride field also carries the field's sharpest experimental disputes: two Ranga Dias-led room-temperature claims were retracted (carbonaceous sulfur hydride, Nature 2020, retracted 2022; N-doped lutetium hydride, Nature 2023, retracted the same year), and J. E. Hirsch and F. Marsiglio dispute even the H3S/LaH10 results, which Eremets and co-workers defend with magnetic screening data. A separate and healthier ML thread works on the transition itself rather than on Tc: neural networks reading gap symmetry out of quasiparticle-interference and Eliashberg data, and unsupervised decomposition of diffraction data into phase diagrams.

items.claim: BCS theory establishes the superconducting transition as a continuous phase transition whose order parameter is the energy gap: an attractive phonon-mediated interaction between electrons near the Fermi surface produces a paired ground state, and the gap Delta(T) closes continuously as T approaches Tc. This is the theoretical object every Tc-prediction model is implicitly approximating.
items.people: John Bardeen, Leon N. Cooper, J. Robert Schrieffer
items.affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Illinois, Urbana

items.claim: Ginzburg-Landau theory (1950) describes the transition phenomenologically via a complex order parameter psi, an expansion of the free energy in |psi|^2 and |psi|^4, and two length scales (coherence length and penetration depth) whose ratio kappa separates type-I from type-II behaviour. Ginzburg's 2004 Nobel Lecture is a citable first-person account of the 1950 construction and of what it does and does not explain. The original paper is V. L. Ginzburg and L. D. Landau, Zh. Eksp. Teor. Fiz. 20, 1064 (1950); no stable open DOI for that original was located.
items.people: Vitaly L. Ginzburg (with Lev D. Landau for the 1950 original)
items.affiliation: P. N. Lebedev Physical Institute, Moscow

items.claim: SuperCon is the empirical substrate for essentially all composition-based ML on superconductivity, and its provenance matters. It originated in NIMS (Japan) work traceable to a national 'Multi-Core' project begun in 1987 following the 1986 cuprate discovery, was distributed as part of the MatNavi database, had its web GUI service decommissioned in 2021, and is now published as re-edited 'MDR SuperCon Datasheet' releases under CC-BY with a new DOI issued per revision. Reported record counts differ by version (figures of roughly 16,400, 26,323 and 32,000 appear in different sources), which is itself a caution for anyone quoting dataset size.
items.people: National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS) — institutional dataset, no single author
items.affiliation: National Institute for Materials Science, Tsukuba, Japan
items.year: 1987 origin; MDR releases from 2022, updated through 2025

items.claim: SuperCon2 was built by machine-reading the literature rather than by hand curation: Grobid-superconductors, a Grobid module mixing ML sequence labelling with heuristics, extracted 40,324 material-property records from 37,700 papers, capturing material name, formula, class, shape, doping, substrate, Tc, and where available applied pressure and measurement method. This is the provenance answer to 'where would more superconductor data come from', and also a new source of extraction error.
items.people: Luca Foppiano, Pedro Baptista de Castro, Pedro Ortiz Suarez, Kensei Terashima, Yoshihiko Takano, Masashi Ishii
items.affiliation: National Institute for Materials Science, Tsukuba (with co-authors at Inria/Sorbonne for Ortiz Suarez)
items.venue: Science and Technology of Advanced Materials: Methods 3, 2153633

items.claim: 3DSC augments SuperCon entries with approximate three-dimensional crystal structures by matching compositions to structural databases, explicitly to address the fact that SuperCon carries composition only. The authors show empirically that access to structural information improves Tc prediction — a direct measurement of how much the composition-only setup was leaving on the table.
items.people: Timo Sommer, Roland Willa, Jörg Schmalian, Pascal Friederich
items.affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (Institute of Theoretical Condensed Matter and Institute of Nanotechnology)

items.claim: The canonical paper. Using SuperCon (over 12,000 entries), the authors trained a random-forest classifier on composition-derived (Magpie-style) features to sort materials above or below 10 K at about 92% out-of-sample accuracy, then trained separate regression models for the cuprate, iron-based and low-Tc families, and combined classification and regression into a pipeline that screened the ICSD. The screen proposed more than 30 non-cuprate, non-iron-based oxides as candidates. Note the year split: arXiv September 2017, journal 2018.
items.people: Valentin Stanev, Corey Oses, A. Gilad Kusne, Efrain Rodriguez, Johnpierre Paglione, Stefano Curtarolo, Ichiro Takeuchi
items.affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park (Stanev, Kusne, Rodriguez, Paglione, Takeuchi); Duke University (Oses, Curtarolo); National Institute of Standards and Technology (Kusne)

items.claim: Hamidieh's regression model on SuperCon-derived features (thermal conductivity, atomic radius, valence, electron affinity, atomic mass, aggregated over the formula) reported out-of-sample RMSE of about 9.5 K. Two limitations are stated by the author and are widely ignored by users of the resulting dataset: the model predicts Tc only for materials already assumed to be superconductors, and it says nothing about whether a compound superconducts at all. The associated feature table became the UCI 'Superconductivity Data' set and is now the most heavily reused benchmark in the area, which propagates SuperCon's errors into hundreds of downstream papers.
items.people: Kam Hamidieh
items.affiliation: University of Pennsylvania (statistics; affiliation stated in the arXiv preprint, not independently re-verified here)

items.claim: An unsupervised/embedding approach: element vectors learned from SuperCon compositions, then regression of Tc, reporting R^2 of about 0.93 and proposing new high-Tc candidates. Useful as a data point that very high reported R^2 on random splits is routine in this literature and by itself carries no discovery information.
items.people: Benjamin Roter, Sasa V. Dordevic
items.affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Akron (affiliation not independently re-verified here)
items.venue: Physica C: Superconductivity and its Applications 575, 1353689

items.claim: The key methodological critique, and the cleanest statement of the interpolation problem. The authors show that standard random k-fold cross-validation systematically overestimates model usefulness for discovery, and introduce leave-one-cluster-out cross-validation (LOCO CV) plus a nearest-neighbour benchmark to measure extrapolation instead. Superconductor Tc is the worked example, hence the title. Their conclusion is that ML-guided iterative experiment, not one-shot high-throughput screening, is the route to a genuinely new high-Tc material.
items.people: Bryce Meredig, Erin Antono, Carena Church, Maxwell Hutchinson, Julia Ling, Sean Paradiso, Ben Blaiszik, Ian Foster, Brenna Gibbons, Jason Hattrick-Simpers, Apurva Mehta, Logan Ward
items.affiliation: Citrine Informatics; University of Chicago and Argonne National Laboratory; NIST; SLAC (full author list and affiliation mapping not fully re-verified here)

items.claim: A large, careful composition-only study that documents concrete SuperCon data pathologies: roughly 4,000 entries with no reported Tc or an explicit report of no superconductivity, and multiply-reported compositions requiring the authors to take a median Tc per composition. The paper also states the structural limitation plainly — the approach cannot differentiate materials with multiple stable phases having distinct properties — and reports that family-specific models (cuprate, iron-based) did not beat their general model.
items.people: Son Gyo Jung, Guwon Jung, Jacqueline M. Cole
items.affiliation: Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge; ISIS Neutron and Muon Source and Scientific Computing Department, STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory
items.venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling 64(19), 7349-7375

items.claim: A recent, explicit example of the confirmation gap: similarity-based ridge regression on SuperCon reports approximately 5 K average out-of-sample Tc error and, screening about 153,000 Materials Project entries, proposes LiCuF4, Ag2H12S(NO)4 and Na2H6PtO6 at roughly 315-316 K. No experimental verification of any candidate is claimed. Predicting a fluoride and an oxide at 316 K from a model trained overwhelmingly on cuprates is precisely the extrapolation regime Meredig and colleagues warned about.
items.people: Siwoo Lee, Jason Hattrick-Simpers, Young-June Kim, O. Anatole von Lilienfeld
items.affiliation: University of Toronto (affiliations not independently re-verified here)
items.year: arXiv June 2024, revised November 2024; journal version 2025
items.venue: arXiv:2406.14524; journal version in Machine Learning: Science and Technology

items.claim: A 28-page review that states the field's uncomfortable summary directly: SuperCon data quality remains uncertain; ML models struggle to predict outside their training distribution, particularly for high-pressure hydrides representing genuinely novel chemistry; and ML-predicted superconductors have rarely been experimentally confirmed. It also makes the composition-only criticism concrete — identical formulas can correspond to structures with very different Tc.
items.people: Huan Tran, Hieu-Chi Dam, Christopher Kuenneth, Tuoc N. Vu, Hiori Kino
items.affiliation: Multi-institution (Georgia Tech / JAIST / University of Bayreuth / Hanoi University of Science and Technology / NIMS — mapping not independently re-verified here)

items.claim: The strongest documented case of ML actually producing a new superconductor. Four closed-loop cycles of ML prediction followed by synthesis and measurement, with results fed back into the model, more than doubled the discovery success rate. Concrete outcome: one new superconductor found in the Zr-In-Ni system, five superconductors rediscovered that were absent from the training data, and two further phase diagrams flagged as promising. Note the modest scale of the win — one genuinely new compound, not a high-Tc breakthrough.
items.people: Elizabeth A. Pogue, Alexander New, Kyle McElroy, Nam Q. Le, Michael J. Pekala, Ian McCue, Eddie Gienger, Janna Domenico, Elizabeth Hedrick, Tyrel M. McQueen, Brandon Wilfong, Christine D. Piatko, Christopher R. Ratto, Andrew Lennon, Christine Chung, Timothy Montalbano, Gregory Bassen, Christopher D. Stiles
items.affiliation: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory; Johns Hopkins University; Northwestern University (McCue)

items.claim: A physics-constrained alternative to composition-only ML: BCS-inspired pre-screening of 1,736 materials on Debye temperature and electronic density of states, electron-phonon coupling calculations for 1,058 of them, and 105 dynamically stable materials with Tc >= 5 K by the McMillan-Allen-Dynes formula (examples reported include MoN, VC, VTe, KB6, Ru3NbC, V3Pt, ScN, LaN2, RuO2, TaC). Methodologically important finding: predicting the Eliashberg function as an intermediate quantity improves the deep-learning model over predicting Tc directly.
items.people: Kamal Choudhary, Kevin Garrity
items.affiliation: Materials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology (JARVIS infrastructure)

items.claim: Machine learning used to improve the theory rather than to bypass it: symbolic regression (SISSO) applied to a database of artificially generated alpha^2 F(omega) spectral functions and numerical Eliashberg solutions yields a closed-form Tc expression that matches Allen-Dynes for low-Tc superconductors and substantially outperforms it at high Tc. This is the cleanest example of ML producing a transferable, interpretable result about the transition itself.
items.people: S. R. Xie, Y. Quan, A. C. Hire, B. Deng, J. M. DeStefano, I. Salinas, U. S. Shah, L. Fanfarillo, J. Lim, J. Kim, G. R. Stewart, J. J. Hamlin, P. J. Hirschfeld, R. G. Hennig
items.affiliation: University of Florida (Department of Physics and Department of Materials Science and Engineering)

items.claim: ML as a triage layer over ab initio physics at scale: roughly 7,000 converged electron-phonon calculations were used to train a model predicting electron-phonon and superconducting properties from structural, compositional and electronic ground-state descriptors; approximately 200,000 metallic compounds were then evaluated, candidates above 5 K validated with density-functional perturbation theory, and 541 compounds with Tc above 10 K identified. Note the difference from SuperCon-based work: the training labels are computed, not experimental, so the model inherits Migdal-Eliashberg assumptions rather than database errors.
items.people: Tiago F. T. Cerqueira, Antonio Sanna, Miguel A. L. Marques
items.affiliation: CFisUC, University of Coimbra; Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics, Halle; Ruhr University Bochum

items.claim: A high-throughput survey of binary hydrides across the periodic table from 10 to 500 GPa using crystal structure prediction, with a learned model used to rank candidates before converged electron-phonon calculations were run for 121 of them, yielding 36 dynamically stable superconductors above 100 K. Marked an Editors' Suggestion in Physical Review B. Illustrates the standard hydride workflow: structure search first, ML as a cost-reduction surrogate, first-principles electron-phonon theory as the arbiter.
items.people: Alice M. Shipley, Michael J. Hutcheon, Richard J. Needs, Chris J. Pickard
items.affiliation: University of Cambridge (Cavendish Laboratory and Department of Materials Science and Metallurgy)

items.claim: CONFIRMED PREDICTION. Duan and colleagues predicted in 2014 that dense (H2S)2H2 would metallize and superconduct, with Im-3m H3S computed at 191-204 K near 200 GPa using the Allen-Dynes-modified McMillan equation. Drozdov, Eremets and co-workers reported 203 K in the sulfur hydride system at high pressure the following year, with an isotope effect supporting the conventional phonon mechanism. This is the field's flagship theory-first success — and it came from crystal-structure search plus electron-phonon theory, not from data-driven ML.
items.people: Defang Duan, Yunxian Liu, Fubo Tian, Tian Cui and co-workers (prediction); A. P. Drozdov, M. I. Eremets, I. A. Troyan, V. Ksenofontov, S. I. Shylin (experiment)
items.affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Superhard Materials, Jilin University (prediction); Max-Planck-Institut für Chemie, Mainz, and Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz (experiment)

items.claim: CONFIRMED PREDICTION. Two independent 2017 computational papers predicted clathrate rare-earth superhydrides: Liu, Naumov, Hoffmann, Ashcroft and Hemley (PNAS 114, 6990-6995) for La and Y hydrides, and Peng, Sun, Pickard, Needs, Wu and Ma (Physical Review Letters 119, 107001), the latter predicting YH10 at up to 303 K near 400 GPa. LaH10 was then reported experimentally twice: Somayazulu and colleagues saw a resistance drop beginning near 260 K at about 190 GPa (Physical Review Letters 122, 027001, 2019) and Drozdov, Eremets and colleagues reported 250 K (Nature 569, 528-531, 2019). Errea and colleagues subsequently showed that quantum atomic fluctuations are what stabilize the high-symmetry Fm-3m structure, with electron-phonon coupling lambda of about 3.5 (Nature 578, 66-69, 2020). YH10 at 303 K has NOT been confirmed.
items.people: Hanyu Liu, Ivan I. Naumov, Roald Hoffmann, N. W. Ashcroft, Russell J. Hemley (prediction); Feng Peng, Ying Sun, Chris J. Pickard, Richard J. Needs, Qiang Wu, Yanming Ma (prediction); Maddury Somayazulu, Muhtar Ahart, Ajay K. Mishra, Zachary M. Geballe, Maria Baldini, Yue Meng, Viktor V. Struzhkin, Russell J. Hemley (experiment); A. P. Drozdov, P. P. Kong, V. S. Minkov, M. I. Eremets and co-workers (experiment); Ion Errea, Francesco Belli, Lorenzo Monacelli, Antonio Sanna, Takashi Koretsune, Terumasa Tadano, Raffaello Bianco, Matteo Calandra, Ryotaro Arita, Francesco Mauri, José A. Flores-Livas (theory of the observed structure)
items.affiliation: Carnegie Institution for Science / Cornell University / George Washington University (Liu et al.); Jilin University and University of Cambridge (Peng et al.); Max-Planck-Institut für Chemie, Mainz (Drozdov et al.)
items.venue: PNAS 114, 6990-6995; Physical Review Letters 119, 107001; Physical Review Letters 122, 027001; Nature 569, 528-531; Nature 578, 66-69

items.claim: NOT CONFIRMED — RETRACTED. Two room-temperature superconductivity claims from the group of Ranga Dias were retracted. 'Room-temperature superconductivity in a carbonaceous sulfur hydride' (Nature 586, 373, 2020, claiming 15 degrees C at 267 GPa) was retracted in 2022 after editors established that a non-standard, undisclosed, user-defined background subtraction had been applied to the raw magnetic susceptibility data. 'Evidence of near-ambient superconductivity in a N-doped lutetium hydride' (Nature 615, 244-250, 2023) was retracted in November 2023 at the request of eight co-authors, who stated the paper did not accurately reflect the provenance of the materials, the measurements undertaken, or the data-processing protocols; the journal separately found credible, substantial and unresolved concerns about the resistance data, and other groups failed to reproduce the result.
items.people: Elliot Snider, Nathan Dasenbrock-Gammon, Raymond McBride, Ashkan Salamat, Ranga P. Dias and co-authors
items.affiliation: University of Rochester; University of Nevada, Las Vegas
items.venue: Nature 586, 373-377 and Retraction Note Nature 610, 804 (2022); Nature 615, 244-250 and Retraction Note Nature 624, 460 (2023)

items.claim: DISPUTED, NOT RETRACTED. J. E. Hirsch and F. Marsiglio argue that the experimental observations on high-pressure hydrides rule out conventional superconductivity, leaving either an exotic 'nonstandard' superconductor or no superconductivity at all, and judge the latter more probable; Hirsch has also published with D. van der Marel challenging specific datasets. The Eremets group's principal rebuttal evidence is SQUID magnetometry under pressure reporting superconducting parameters for Im-3m H3S and Fm-3m LaH10 (Minkov, Prakapenka, Greenberg, Eremets, Nature Communications 13, 3194, 2022), itself the subject of a 2023 author correction and continuing published exchange. Any account of hydride Tc predictions should state that the confirmations rest on contested measurements.
items.people: J. E. Hirsch, F. Marsiglio (critics); V. S. Minkov, V. B. Prakapenka, E. Greenberg, M. I. Eremets (defenders)
items.affiliation: University of California, San Diego (Hirsch); University of Alberta (Marsiglio); Max-Planck-Institut für Chemie, Mainz and University of Chicago (Minkov et al.)
items.year: 2021 (Hirsch and Marsiglio); 2022 with 2023 correction (Minkov et al.)

items.claim: ML applied to the transition rather than to Tc: an ensemble of artificial neural networks trained on candidate order types was used to detect hidden electronic order in scanning-tunnelling-microscopy image arrays from cuprates, identifying a commensurate four-unit-cell periodic modulation. Widely cited as the demonstration that neural networks can extract order-parameter structure from raw experimental quantum-matter images.
items.people: Yi Zhang, A. Mesaros, K. Fujita, S. D. Edkins, M. H. Hamidian, K. Ch'ng, H. Eisaki, S. Uchida, J. C. Séamus Davis, Ehsan Khatami, Eun-Ah Kim
items.affiliation: Cornell University; San Jose State University; Ewha Womans University; AIST and University of Tokyo

items.claim: Machine learning aimed directly at pairing mechanism and gap structure. Within Migdal-Eliashberg theory, supervised learning maps superconducting gap functions to electron-boson spectral functions, with an autoencoder compressing the spectral functions so the asymmetric function-to-function mapping remains learnable. A related and more recent line trains two-head convolutional networks on quasiparticle-interference images to classify pairing symmetry by irreducible representation and to regress continuous parameters such as singlet-triplet mixing and gap magnitude.
items.people: Wan-Ju Li, Ming-Chien Hsu, Shin-Ming Huang
items.affiliation: National Sun Yat-sen University, Taiwan (affiliation not independently re-verified here)

items.claim: Unsupervised ML for mapping phase diagrams from raw measurement data: nonnegative matrix factorization combined with custom clustering and cross-correlation robustly determines how many basis diffraction patterns are present in a combinatorial X-ray diffraction dataset and handles peak-shifted patterns. Same Maryland/NIST group as the 2018 Tc paper, and the natural companion technique for locating phase boundaries experimentally rather than predicting Tc from a formula.

items.affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park; Los Alamos National Laboratory; National Institute of Standards and Technology

items.claim: A ceiling argument that bounds what any ML Tc search can hope to find in the conventional channel: analysis of electron-phonon calculations for more than 20,000 metals reveals an intrinsic trade-off between the logarithmic average phonon frequency and the electron-phonon coupling constant lambda, so that room-temperature conventional superconductivity at ambient pressure is deemed extremely unlikely. Li2AgH6 and Li2AuH6 are identified as near the practical limit.
