Fisher's bibliography confirms the a/b labeling: 1965a = Surface Tension, 3892-97; 1965b = Equation of State, 3898-3905. The dossier's warning that textbooks conflate the two is well-founded and the disambiguation is correct.

verdicts.claim: Essam and Fisher (1963), J. Chem. Phys. 38(4), 802-812, doi:10.1063/1.1733766 — proposed alpha' + 2 beta + gamma' = 2 as an equality and introduced the standard alpha/beta/gamma/delta notation.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms title 'Pade Approximant Studies of the Lattice Gas and Ising Ferromagnet below the Critical Point', authors in order John W. Essam then Michael E. Fisher, JCP 38(4), 802-812, 15 Feb 1963. Fisher (1998) fn. 50 verified verbatim: 'the second relation was advanced in Essam and Fisher (1963) where the now generally accepted notation for the thermodynamic critical exponents was also introduced,' and adds that the initial proposal was written alpha' + 2beta + gamma' = 2 with primes. Fn. 85 confirms the droplet-model origin. Affiliation, previously unverified, is now confirmed for both authors: Wheatstone Physics Laboratory, King's College, London W.C.2, England.

verdicts.claim: Rushbrooke (1963), 'On the Thermodynamics of the Critical Region for the Ising Problem', J. Chem. Phys. 39(3), 842-843, doi:10.1063/1.1734338; affiliation given as 'Newcastle upon Tyne, UK'.
verdicts.correction: Bibliography is right; the affiliation is wrong. Crossref's record for this paper carries the author entry {"given":"G. S.","family":"Rushbrooke","affiliation":[{"name":"Chemistry Department, University of Oregon, Eugene, Oregon"}]} — this two-page note was published from Oregon, not Newcastle. Rushbrooke's career home was Newcastle, which is presumably how the error crept in; if the book prints an affiliation for this paper it must say University of Oregon. Everything else checks: title, sole author, JCP 39(3), 842-843, 1 Aug 1963. Fisher (1998) fn. 50 verbatim: 'Moved by the suggested thermodynamic exponent equality, Rushbrooke (1963) quickly showed that for magnetic systems (with H -> -H symmetry) the positivity of specific heats implied by the Second Law of Thermodynamics could be used to prove rigorously the inequality alpha' + 2beta + gamma' >= 2. His proof was soon extended to fluid systems (Fisher 1964), see Eq. (2.20).'

verdicts.claim: Griffiths (1965), 'Thermodynamic Inequality Near the Critical Point for Ferromagnets and Fluids', Phys. Rev. Lett. 14(16), 623-624, doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.14.623; longer treatment J. Chem. Phys. 43(6), 1958-1968, doi:10.1063/1.1697060; Buckingham & Gunton, Phys. Rev. 178, 848 (1969) for correlation-exponent inequalities.
verdicts.correction: All three references verified. PRL: Crossref confirms title, sole author Robert B. Griffiths, 14(16), 623-624, 19 April 1965. The JCP companion, which the dossier flagged as needing verification before printing, now resolves cleanly on Crossref: 'Ferromagnets and Simple Fluids near the Critical Point: Some Thermodynamic Inequalities', J. Chem. Phys. 43(6), 1958-1968, 15 Sept 1965, doi:10.1063/1.1697060, affiliation 'Physics Department, Carnegie Institute of Technology, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania' — which also confirms the previously unverified affiliation guess for Griffiths. Buckingham & Gunton confirmed from Fisher's 1998 bibliography: 1969, 'Correlations at the Critical Point of the Ising Model,' Phys. Rev. 178, 848-853, and fn. 50 credits them specifically 'for correlation exponents.' Caveat: APS returns 403 to this environment, so I could not read the PRL abstract itself; the specific form alpha' + beta(1+delta) >= 2 and the convexity derivation are standard and consistent with Fisher's fn. 50 ('Other valuable exponent inequalities... were proved by Griffiths (1965, 1972) for thermodynamic exponents') but were not read off the paper.

verdicts.claim: Fisher (1964), 'Correlation Functions and the Critical Region of Simple Fluids', J. Math. Phys. 5(7), 944-962, doi:10.1063/1.1704197 — Eq. (5.7) for gamma = (2-eta)nu, Eq. (2.20) extending Rushbrooke to fluids; rigorous inequality in Fisher (1969), Trieste IAEA volume, pp. 19-46.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms title, sole author Michael E. Fisher, J. Math. Phys. 5(7), 944-962, July 1964, affiliation 'The Rockefeller Institute, New York, New York'. Fisher (1998) fn. 50 verified verbatim: 'See Fisher (1959; 1962; 1964, see Eq. (5.7); 1967b) for the first relation here' (i.e. gamma = (2-eta)nu), Eq. (2.20) for the fluid extension, and 'the inequality gamma <= (2-eta)nu was proven rigorously in (Fisher, 1969).' The Fisher (1969) entry in his own bibliography reads exactly as the dossier gives it: 'Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena,' in Contemporary Physics, Vol 1, Proc. International Symposium, Trieste, 7-28 June 1968 (IAEA, Vienna), pp. 19-46 — no DOI, correctly flagged.

verdicts.claim: Josephson (1967), 'Inequality for the specific heat: I. Derivation', Proc. Phys. Soc. 92(2), 269-275, doi:10.1088/0370-1328/92/2/301, and 'II. Application to critical phenomena', 276-284, doi:10.1088/0370-1328/92/2/302 — the rigorous hyperscaling inequality nu d >= 2 - alpha.
verdicts.correction: Both Crossref records match exactly, including the two subtitles, the page splits 269-275 / 276-284, volume 92 issue 2, 1967, sole author B. D. Josephson. The IOP page for Part II gives the affiliation as 'Royal Society Mond Laboratory, Cambridge University', confirming the dossier's unverified 'University of Cambridge', and its abstract confirms the application: 'Using plausible assumptions about the correlations in the neighbourhood of the critical point,' relations connecting critical exponents are derived. One note: Josephson does not appear anywhere in Fisher's 1998 bibliography, so the Josephson attribution for the inequality is standard-literature attribution, not Fisher's; the dossier does not claim otherwise, and Fisher's fn. 88 credit of the EQUALITY to Kadanoff/Widom(1965a)/Stell is separately verified.

verdicts.claim: Wegner (1972), 'Corrections to Scaling Laws', Phys. Rev. B 5(11), 4529-4536, doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.5.4529 — nonlinear scaling fields as analytic functions of the physical fields, corrections to scaling, origin of logarithms; Wilson cited 'Wegner (1972a, 1976)' for the formal theory near fixed points; Wegner (1976) chapter in Domb & Green Vol. 6, pp. 7-124.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms title, sole author Franz J. Wegner, PRB 5(11), 4529-4536, 1 June 1972; the published byline gives Department of Physics, Brown University, Providence (the 'on leave from Kernforschungsanlage Juelich' clause is plausible and matches Wegner's biography but I did not read it off the title page). The abstract confirms the content: higher-order contributions absorbed by redefined fields that are 'normally analytic functions of the physical fields,' corrections to power laws derived from the exact scaling law, plus an explanation of logarithmic terms in the free energy. Fisher's bibliography confirms both halves of the pairing: 'Wegner, F. J., 1972a, Corrections to Scaling Laws, Phys. Rev. B 5, 4529-4536' and 'Wegner, F. J., 1976, The Critical State, General Aspects, in Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena, ed. Domb and Green (Academic, London), Vol. 6, pp. 7-124' — exactly as the dossier gives them. One imprecision: the dossier sources Wilson's four-part division to 'Fisher (1998) fn. 33-37'. The Wegner citation is in Fisher's MAIN TEXT at that passage — 'he especially cites Wegner (1972a, 1976), as did I, above' — with fn. 37 pointing to Wilson (1975), p. 796, col. 1. Cite the passage, not the footnotes.

verdicts.claim: Fisher (1974), 'The renormalization group in the theory of critical behavior', Rev. Mod. Phys. 46(4), 597-616, doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.46.597, with erratum RMP 47, 543 (1975) — and Fisher (1998) points back to THIS 1974 review in fn. 87 for 'the special character of the hyperscaling relations' and in fn. 91 for the account of apparent hyperscaling violations 'with hindsight enlightened by RG theory'.
verdicts.correction: This is the garbled citation. The RMP article and its erratum are real and correctly described (Crossref: Michael E. Fisher, RMP 46(4), 597-616, 1 Oct 1974; erratum, RMP 47, issue 2, p. 543, 1 April 1975 — note the dossier omits the issue number, it is 47(2)). But footnotes 87 and 91 do NOT point to it. Read verbatim from the full text: '87 See (Fisher, 1974a) where the special character of the hyperscaling relations is stressed' and '91 As expounded systematically in (Fisher, 1974a) with hindsight enlightened by RG theory.' Fisher's own bibliography defines 1974a and 1974b as DIFFERENT papers: 'Fisher, M. E., 1974a, General Scaling Theory for Critical Points, Proceedings of the Nobel Symp. XXIV, Aspenasgarden, Lerum, Sweden, June 1973, in Collective Properties of Physical Systems, edited by B. Lundqvist and S. Lundqvist (Academic, New York), pp. 16-37' versus 'Fisher, M. E., 1974b, The Renormalization Group in the Theory of Critical Phenomena, Rev. Mod. Phys. 46, 597-616.' So fns. 87 and 91 cite the Nobel Symposium XXIV article, not the RMP review. (Fn. 138, which does cite the RMP, correctly writes 'Fisher (1974b)'.) Two consequences for the book: do not cite RMP 46, 597 as Fisher's source for the special character of hyperscaling or for the 3D-Ising hyperscaling-violation postmortem — cite Fisher 1974a, the Nobel Symposium article, or drop the footnote attribution. Second, smaller point: the published RMP title is 'The renormalization group in the theory of critical BEHAVIOR' per Crossref and per the erratum's own title; Fisher's 1998 bibliography renders it '...critical PHENOMENA'. Use the Crossref form.

verdicts.claim: Fisher (1998), 'Renormalization group theory: Its basis and formulation in statistical physics', Rev. Mod. Phys. 70(2), 653-681 — Eq. (50) gives 2-alpha = d/lambda_1, Delta = lambda_2/lambda_1, phi_j = lambda_j/lambda_1, nu = 1/lambda_1; eigenoperators Q_k with Lambda_k(b) = b^(lambda_k) forced by the semigroup property; relevance/marginality/irrelevance by sign; first and last of Eq. (50) give hyperscaling.
verdicts.correction: Every element verified against the full text. Crossref: RMP 70(2), 653-681, April 1998; the paper's own byline gives 'Institute for Physical Science and Technology, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland 20742', exactly as the dossier states. Eq. (49) is the generalized free-energy scaling form f_s(t,h,...,g_j,...) ~ |t|^(2-alpha) F(h/|t|^Delta, ..., g_j/|t|^(phi_j), ...). Eq. (50) reads exactly as claimed, immediately followed by 'the sign of a given lambda_j... determines the relevance (for lambda_j>0), marginality (for lambda_j=0), or irrelevance (for lambda_j<0)' and 'the first and last of the equations (50) yield the hyperscaling relation Eq. (32)' where Eq. (32) is d nu = 2 - alpha. The eigenoperator passage confirms 'eigenoperators, say Q_k (which will be partial Hamiltonians)' and 'by the semigroup property the eigenvalues must be related by Lambda_k(b) = b^(lambda_k).' The first-person epsilon-expansion account, the 'd appeared simply as an explicit parameter' line, 'I suggested that maybe one could treat the dimensional deviation, epsilon = 4-d, as a small, nonintegral parameter', 'the recursion relations proved to be exact to leading order in epsilon (so that if one replaced b=2 by a general value, the expected universal results were indeed independent of b)', 'the first general formula for a nonclassical exponent', and 'a major barrier to progress had been overcome' are all present verbatim. Also verified: Eq. (32) 'holds exactly for the d=2 Ising model' and hyperscaling breaks down above d=4 via a 'dangerous irrelevant variable' (fn. 93).

verdicts.claim: Wilson (1983), 'The renormalization group and critical phenomena', Rev. Mod. Phys. 55(3), 583-600 — Nobel lecture delivered 8 December 1982.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms title, sole author Kenneth G. Wilson, RMP 55(3), 583-600, 1 July 1983. The Nobel Foundation's own PDF is headed 'THE RENORMALIZATION GROUP AND CRITICAL PHENOMENA, Nobel lecture, 8 December 1982', with Wilson at the Laboratory of Nuclear Studies, Cornell University — confirming both the date and the affiliation. Its structure (basic ideas plus epsilon expansion; history prior to 1971; developments since) matches the dossier's use of it, and Fisher (1998) does repeatedly cite Wilson (1983) for his own account of the path from Gell-Mann-Low through Kadanoff to the recursion formula.

verdicts.claim: Tauber, 'Renormalization Group: Applications in Statistical Physics', arXiv:1112.1375 (6 Dec 2011), Nucl. Phys. B Proc. Suppl. 228C, 7-34 (2012) — Eqs. (44)-(45) recursion relations, (48)-(49) differential flow, (50) thermal recursion, (51) nu = 1/2 + eps/12 and eta = O(eps^2), (65)-(66) Z-factors with (n+2)/6 and (n+8)/6, (76) u* = 6 eps/(n+8), (77) eta, (78) 1/nu = 2 - [(n+2)/(n+8)] eps.
verdicts.correction: I read the source text and every equation number checks out. (44): r' = b^2[r + (u/2)S_d integral_{Lambda/b}^{Lambda} p^(d-1)dp/(r+p^2)]. (45): u' = b^(4-d)u[1 - (3u/2)S_d integral p^(d-1)dp/(r+p^2)^2]. (48)-(49): the differential flow, with (49) = du/dl = (4-d)u - (3/2)u^2 S_d Lambda^(d-4). (50): dtau/dl = tau[2 - (u/2)S_d Lambda^(d-4)]. (51): nu = 1/2 + eps/12 + O(eps^2), eta = 0 + O(eps^2), with 1/nu = 2 - eps/3 identified just above it. (65) Z_tau = 1 - [(n+2)/6]u_R/eps, (66) Z_u = 1 - [(n+8)/6]u_R/eps, (76) u*_H = 6eps/(n+8), (77) eta = (n+2)eps^2/[2(n+8)^2], (78) 1/nu = 2 - [(n+2)/(n+8)]eps, with Tauber's own remark that (78) reduces to (51) at n=1. Journal reference confirmed on Crossref: Nucl. Phys. B Proc. Suppl. 228, pp. 7-34, July 2012, doi:10.1016/j.nuclphysbps.2012.06.002; affiliation 'Department of Physics, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA 24061-0435, USA' as printed. Two small fixes needed in the dossier's PROSE, not the citation. (a) The summary writes the fixed point as 'u* S_d Lambda^(4-d) = (2/3) epsilon', which contradicts its own flow equation; Tauber's text reads u*_I S_d = (2/3)(4-d)Lambda^(4-d), i.e. u* S_d Lambda^(d-4) = (2/3)eps. The dossier's item entry states this correctly; the summary paragraph has the exponent sign flipped. (b) That fixed-point value is stated in running text after Eq. (49), not as Eq. (48) — the summary's 'Tauber Eq. 48' mislabels it. Arithmetic spot-checked: nu = 1/2 + [(n+2)/(4(n+8))]eps follows from (78), and 4(n+8)/(n+2) = 12 at n=1.

verdicts.claim: Pelissetto and Vicari, 'Critical Phenomena and Renormalization-Group Theory', Physics Reports 368(6), 549-727 (2002); arXiv:cond-mat/0012164 (v1 Dec 2000, v6 3 May 2002) — cite for reference exponent values and for the epsilon expansion being asymptotic, not convergent.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms title, authors in order Andrea Pelissetto then Ettore Vicari, Phys. Rep. 368(6), 549-727, October 2002, doi:10.1016/S0370-1573(02)00219-3. The arXiv v6 title page is stamped 'arXiv:cond-mat/0012164v6 [cond-mat.stat-mech] 3 May 2002' and dated April 2002 'To appear in Physics Reports', matching the dossier's version history. Affiliations, previously unverified, are confirmed from the title page and match the dossier's parenthetical guesses: Pelissetto at Dipartimento di Fisica and INFN Sezione di Roma I, Universita di Roma 'La Sapienza'; Vicari at Dipartimento di Fisica and INFN Sezione di Pisa, Universita di Pisa. The divergence claim is supported in the text: 'FT perturbative expansions are divergent. Thus, in order to obtain accurate results, an appropriate resummation is required. This can be done by exploiting their Borel summability, that has been proved for the fixed-dimension expansion... and has been conjectured for the epsilon expansion.'

verdicts.claim: Guida and Zinn-Justin (1998), 'Critical exponents of the N-vector model', J. Phys. A: Math. Gen. 31(40), 8103-8121, doi:10.1088/0305-4470/31/40/006 — Borel-type resummation of both fixed-dimension and epsilon-expansion series.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms title, authors in order R. Guida then J. Zinn-Justin, J. Phys. A 31(40), 8103-8121, 9 Oct 1998. The preprint is arXiv:cond-mat/9803240 (submitted 19 March 1998, revised 31 August 1998), journal-ref 'J.Phys.A31:8103-8121,1998', and it carries report number SPhT-t97/40 — SPhT being the Service de Physique Theorique at CEA Saclay, which confirms the dossier's previously unverified 'Saclay'. The abstract confirms the method: the seven-loop Murray-Nickel extension of the 3D phi^4 RG functions is resummed, alongside the epsilon-expansion series.

verdicts.claim: Kos, Poland, Simmons-Duffin and Vichi (2016), 'Precision Islands in the Ising and O(N) Models', JHEP 2016(8), 036; arXiv:1603.04436 — Delta_sigma = 0.5181489(10), Delta_epsilon = 1.412625(10), lambda_sse = 1.0518537(41), lambda_eee = 1.532435(19); the dossier's own conversion gives nu = 0.629971 and eta = 0.0362978.
verdicts.correction: Crossref confirms all four authors in that order, JHEP volume 2016, issue 8, article 36, August 2016, doi:10.1007/JHEP08(2016)036. The arXiv abstract prints the quadruple verbatim: '(Delta_sigma, Delta_epsilon, lambda_sigma sigma epsilon, lambda_epsilon epsilon epsilon) = (0.5181489(10), 1.412625(10), 1.0518537(41), 1.532435(19))'. The dossier's caveat is correct and important: the abstract quotes scaling dimensions, not exponents. I independently recomputed the conversions and they are right: nu = 1/(3 - 1.412625) = 1/1.587375 = 0.6299717, and eta = 2(0.5181489) - 1 = 0.0362978. The comparison claim also checks: the raw one-loop nu = 1/2 + 1/12 = 0.58333 at eps=1 is 7.4% below 0.62997, so 'about 7 percent low' is accurate. If the book prints nu with an uncertainty it must propagate it, exactly as the dossier's open question says.

ising-ml-bridge.domain: Machine-learning identification of phases from Monte Carlo configurations: the specific published protocols, and what feature the classifiers actually use
ising-ml-bridge.summary: The canonical supervised protocol is Carrasquilla & Melko (Nature Physics 13, 431-434, 2017). Input: raw Monte Carlo spin configurations sigma_i = +/-1 fed as N = L^2 inputs, no preprocessing, no knowledge of lattice or Hamiltonian. Architecture: one fully-connected hidden layer of 100 sigmoid units plus a two-unit softmax output; cross-entropy loss with L2 regularization; Adam optimizer; TensorFlow. Labels: binary "low-temperature" vs "high-temperature", assigned by whether the sampling temperature is below or above the exactly known Onsager T_c - so on the training lattice the network is told T_c, not discovering it. Accuracy 94% at L=10, 99% at L=40; antiferromagnetic couplings work equally well. T_c is extracted on an UNSEEN lattice: the square-lattice-trained net is fed triangular-lattice Ising configurations and T_c is read from the crossing of the two test-set-averaged output neurons. Because the two softmax outputs sum to one, that crossing is exactly where each equals 1/2 - the "output crosses one-half" criterion, stated verbatim in Ch'ng, Carrasquilla, Melko & Khatami (PRX 7, 031038, 2017) and formalized as <q>_{T*} = 1/2 by Kim & Kim (PRE 98, 022138, 2018). arXiv v1 gives the single-size (L=30) crossing estimate T_c/J = 3.63581 vs exact 4/ln3 = 3.640957; the published version adds finite-size scaling up to L=60 with data collapse of the output against t*L^(1/nu), yielding T_c = 2.266(2), nu = 1.0(2) on the square lattice and T_c = 3.65(1) on the triangular lattice. Beyond the Ising model they tested two systems with no conventional order parameter: square ice (a Coulomb phase), where a plain 100-unit fully connected net separates T=0 ground states from high-T states at 99% accuracy purely from higher-order correlations; and the two-dimensional Ising lattice gauge theory, whose ground-state manifold is that of the toric code, where the fully connected net fails outright at 50% (chance) and only a CNN succeeds (100%). The genuinely surprising result there is negative: control experiments in the supplement show the CNN keys only on satisfied local plaquette constraints, not on topological order. Van Nieuwenburg, Liu & Huber's confusion scheme sweeps a proposed critical point c', relabels all data by it, retrains, and plots total performance P(c'), which traces a universal W with its middle peak at the true c and analytic form P(c') = 1 - min(c-c', c'-a)/(c-a) on the left branch; on structureless data the middle peak vanishes and the W degenerates to a V. On the direct question of whether these classifiers read magnetization or energy, the sharpest published answers are Wetzel & Scherzer (PRB 96, 184410) - a receptive-field-restricted "correlation probing" network proves the decision function is a function of the magnetization at 1x1, of the nearest-neighbour bond average (energy per site) at 1x2, and gains nothing from 1x2 up to the full 28x28 field - Suchsland & Wessel (PRB 97, 174435), who show the "network learns the magnetization" picture is an artifact of Wolff cluster sampling and breaks once extended domain walls enter the low-T training set, and Kashiwa, Kikuchi & Tomiya (PTEP 2019, 083A04), who see fully connected first layers track magnetization while convolutional ones track internal energy.

items.claim: THE CORE SUPERVISED PROTOCOL. Fully connected feed-forward net implemented in TensorFlow: input layer = raw Monte Carlo spin configuration (sigma_i = +/-1, N = L^2 values, no preprocessing), one hidden layer of 100 sigmoid neurons, and a two-unit output layer; cross-entropy cost with an L2 regularization term; trained with Adam. Training data: Monte Carlo configurations over a broad range of temperatures above and below T_c on the square-lattice ferromagnetic Ising model H = -J sum_<ij> sigma_i^z sigma_j^z, J = 1. LABELS ARE BINARY AND SUPERVISED BY THE KNOWN T_c: each configuration is tagged 'low-temperature' or 'high-temperature' according to whether its sampling temperature lies below or above the Onsager value T_c/J = 2/ln(1+sqrt2). The network correctly classifies 94% of an uncorrelated test set at N = L^2 = 10^2, rising to 99% at L = 40. Identical success with antiferromagnetic couplings H = +J sum sigma_i sigma_j, i.e. for an order parameter with ordering wavevector q = (pi/a, pi/a). The paper does NOT claim to discover T_c on the training lattice.
items.people: Juan Carrasquilla; Roger G. Melko
items.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, Waterloo (Carrasquilla); Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo and Perimeter Institute (Melko)
items.year: 2017 journal; arXiv v1 5 May 2016; received 27 June 2016, accepted 11 January 2017, published online 13 February 2017, issue date May 2017

items.claim: HOW T_c IS EXTRACTED, AND THE ONE-HALF CROSSING. Carrasquilla and Melko extract a critical temperature not on the lattice they trained on but on an unseen one: the square-lattice-trained network is fed Monte Carlo configurations of the TRIANGULAR-lattice ferromagnetic Ising model (L = 30), with no information about the Hamiltonian, the lattice structure, or even the locality of interactions. The two output neurons are averaged over the test set at each temperature and plotted against T; T_c is estimated from their crossing point, giving T_c/J = 3.63581 against the exact 4/ln3 = 3.640957 (arXiv v1 value, single size). Because the two softmax outputs are complementary and sum to one, the crossing is precisely the point where each output equals 0.5 - this is the origin of the 'output crosses one-half' criterion; the arXiv text says 'crossing point of the low- and high-temperature outputs' rather than writing 0.5 explicitly. The analytically constructed three-perceptron toy network, given the same task with no knowledge of either critical temperature, returns T_c/J = 3.63403, under 1% from the exact value.
items.people: Juan Carrasquilla; Roger G. Melko
items.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; University of Waterloo

items.claim: FINITE-SIZE SCALING IN THE PUBLISHED VERSION (NOT IN arXiv v1). The Nature Physics version adds a finite-size-scaling analysis absent from the arXiv preprint: system sizes up to L = 60, with the averaged output F^T for the ferromagnetic class shown to collapse when plotted against the scaling variable t*L^(1/nu), t the reduced temperature. The collapse yields T_c = 2.266 +/- 0.002 and nu = 1.0 +/- 0.2, consistent with the exact 2/ln(1+sqrt2) = 2.269 and the exact 2D Ising nu = 1; the triangular-lattice estimate quoted from the same 100-unit network is T_c = 3.65(1). USE WITH CARE: I could not read the paywalled published text directly. These numbers are quoted verbatim by two independent later papers that had the published version in hand - Chertenkov, Burovski & Shchur, PRE 108, L032102 (2023), which states the L <= 60 data collapse and the values 2.266 +/- 0.002 and nu = 1.0 +/- 0.2, and Kim & Kim, PRE 98, 022138 (2018), which quotes 'T_c = 2.266(2) with nu = 1.0(2)' and 'T_c = 3.65(1)' as the 100-unit network results of Carrasquilla2017.
items.people: Juan Carrasquilla; Roger G. Melko (values as reported by Vladislav Chertenkov, Evgeni Burovski, Lev Shchur; and by Dongkyu Kim, Dong-Hee Kim)
items.affiliation: Perimeter Institute / University of Waterloo
items.venue: Nature Physics 13, 431-434 (2017); confirmed in Phys. Rev. E 108, L032102 (2023) and Phys. Rev. E 98, 022138 (2018)

items.claim: WHAT THE ISING NETWORK IS READING, IN THE ORIGINAL PAPER ITSELF. Carrasquilla and Melko construct an analytic toy replacement for the hidden layer: three Heaviside perceptrons with weight matrix W = (1/(N(1+eps))) * [[1..1],[-1..-1],[1..1]] and bias b = (eps/(1+eps))*(-1,-1,1)^T, so that Wx + b = (1/(1+eps)) * (m(x)-eps, -m(x)-eps, m(x)+eps) where m(x) = (1/N) sum_i sigma_i is exactly the magnetization; eps in (0,1) is a magnetization threshold. Two perceptrons fire on polarized states, the third on 'polarized-up or unpolarized'. They then train a real 3-sigmoid network numerically and show that during training the components of W_t x + b_t become approximately linear functions of m(x), concluding 'These results clearly support our claim about the neural network's ability to encode and learn the magnetization in the hidden layer.' Their own summary sentence: neural networks 'encode information about conventional ordered phases by learning the order parameter of the phase'. A t-SNE embedding of the training set shows two low-T (up/down) lobes and one high-T region separated by a hyperplane.
items.people: Juan Carrasquilla; Roger G. Melko
items.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; University of Waterloo
items.venue: Nature Physics 13, 431-434 (2017), supplementary material (Appendices A-B of arXiv:1605.01735)

items.claim: THE COULOMB PHASE TEST. Two-dimensional square ice, H = J sum_v Q_v^2 with vertex charge Q_v = sum_{i in v} sigma_i^z and Ising spins on the bonds. The two classes are T = 0 ground states (an extensively degenerate Coulomb phase, power-law spin-spin correlations, no bulk magnetization or any local order parameter) versus high-temperature states (exponentially decaying correlations). Trained on raw configurations with the same standard fully connected 100-hidden-unit network, at N = 2 x 16 x 16 spins it separates the two classes with 99% accuracy, with no information about the underlying lattice. The authors' reading: 'the learning capabilities of neural networks go beyond the simple ability to encode order parameters, extending to the detection of subtle differences in higher-order correlation functions.' This is the surprise - a plain shallow classifier separating states that differ only in the functional form of their correlations.
items.people: Juan Carrasquilla; Roger G. Melko
items.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; University of Waterloo

items.claim: THE TORIC-CODE / ISING GAUGE THEORY TEST, AND THE NEGATIVE RESULT. Two-dimensional Ising lattice gauge theory H = -J sum_p prod_{i in p} sigma_i^z, spins on the bonds of a square lattice, ground-state manifold the same as the toric code, exponentially decaying spin-spin correlations. The standard fully connected network FAILS: it cannot exceed 50% accuracy, 'equivalent to simply guessing'. A convolutional network succeeds: 64 filters of size 2x2 convolved on each of the two sublattices, unit stride, no padding, periodic boundary conditions, ReLU, then a 64-unit fully connected ReLU layer with dropout, then a two-output softmax; trained on configurations at T = 0 and T = infinity it reaches 100% accuracy on a 1x10^4-configuration test set. The surprise is what the supplement then shows: (i) flipping one spin every m = 2 (m = 8) plaquettes preserves the topological order but violates local constraints, and accuracy collapses to 50% (55%); (ii) cutting ground states into 4 pieces and restitching pieces from different states destroys the extended closed-loop structure and the topological degeneracy while preserving local constraints almost everywhere - and the CNN still classifies these as ground states with high confidence. Conclusion: 'local constraints are the only features that the CNN relies on'. An analytic toy CNN with 16 2x2 filters per sublattice that literally enumerates the 8 satisfied and 8 unsatisfied plaquette configurations also reaches 100%. So the network is not detecting topological order; it is detecting the Hamiltonian's local energetic constraints.
items.people: Juan Carrasquilla; Roger G. Melko
items.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; University of Waterloo
items.venue: Nature Physics 13, 431-434 (2017), main text and Appendix C

items.claim: LEARNING BY CONFUSION - THE EXACT SCHEME. Data lie in a parameter range (a,b) containing an unknown critical point c. Propose a trial critical point c', label everything below c' as 0 and everything above as 1, train a fresh network N_{c'} on that deliberately-part-wrong labelling, then evaluate its total performance P(c') on the entire data set. Sweeping c' from a to b produces the universal W-SHAPE: P = 1 at c' = a and c' = b (the net assigns one label to everything and is right by construction), P = 1 again at c' = c (the correct labelling), and two minima in between where the net learns the majority label and scores P(c') = 1 - min(c-c', c'-a)/(c-a) for a < c' < c. The middle peak always sits at the correct c; asymmetric placement of c distorts the depths of the two minima but not the peak position. CONTROL: trained on unstructured random data against a fictitious tuning parameter the middle peak disappears and the W becomes a V, so the peak is evidence of real structure. Systems: (1) Kitaev chain, input = the largest 10 entanglement-spectrum eigenvalues for L = 20 with L_A = L_B = 10, transition recovered at mu = -2t; (2) two-dimensional classical Ising, network with L^2 input and L^2 hidden neurons and 2 outputs trained on L x L configurations - the peak deviates from T_c for L = 10 by finite-size effects and sits exactly at k_B T_c ~ 2.27 J for L = 20; (3) many-body localization in a random-field Heisenberg chain, L = 12, 64 entanglement-spectrum levels, 10^5 disorder realizations per field strength, giving h_c ~ 3J. A separate 'blanking' test shows a supervised net trained with a window of width up to w = 3t blanked out around the transition still locates it.
items.people: Evert P. L. van Nieuwenburg; Ye-Hua Liu; Sebastian D. Huber
items.affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zurich

items.claim: UNSUPERVISED BASELINE: PCA FINDS THE MAGNETIZATION. Wang collects 100 uncorrelated Wolff-sampled square-lattice Ising configurations at each of T/J = 1.6, 1.7, ..., 2.9 into an M x N matrix X with M = 1400, and solves X^T X w_l = lambda_l w_l. Exactly ONE dominant explained-variance ratio appears, and the weight vector of the first principal component is flat across all lattice sites - i.e. the first principal component IS the uniform magnetization (1/N) sum_i sigma_i. Projecting onto the first two components separates the samples into three clusters (two ordered, one paramagnetic) that sharpen as N goes 20^2, 40^2, 80^2. For the conserved-order-parameter Ising model (same Hamiltonian, sum_i sigma_i identically zero, so magnetization is useless) there are FOUR leading components with weights cos(theta_i), cos(phi_i), sin(theta_i), sin(phi_i), and the nonlinear combination sum_{l=1..4} y_l^2 is proportional to a structure factor S detecting domain-wall orientational order - a quantity Wang states was unknown to him before the learner found it. He explicitly flags the limitation: PCA is linear, so topological order, duality, Wilson loops and string order remain out of reach.
items.people: Lei Wang
items.affiliation: Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing

items.claim: THE CRITICAL EXAMINATION - PRECISELY WHAT FAILED AND WHERE. Hu, Singh and Scalettar apply PCA (and an autoencoder) to the square-lattice Ising ferromagnet, triangular-lattice Ising antiferromagnet, Blume-Capel model, a biquadratic-exchange spin-one Ising (BSI) model, and the 2D XY model. SUCCESSES: PCA locates transition temperatures with reasonable accuracy; strong first-order transitions are distinguishable from second-order ones by the evolution of the principal-component distribution; a crossover is distinguishable from a true transition; principal components map onto Fourier modes and order parameters and their size dependence yields critical exponents; in the frustrated triangular antiferromagnet the components point to incipient orders. FAILURES, MODEL BY MODEL: (a) BSI model - feeding raw {S_i} produces NO dominant principal component and a complete mixture of all temperatures in the projection, because the order lives in the checkerboard arrangement of S_i^2 (the 'charge') while PCA averages the S_i = +/-1 variables to zero; feeding {S_i^2} restores a dominant component. (b) 2D XY model - feeding raw local vorticity (plaquette winding number +1, 0, -1) again gives no dominant component, because equal numbers of vortices and antivortices cancel; feeding ABSOLUTE vorticity (1 if a vortex or antivortex is present, 0 otherwise) recovers a dominant component, but the signal 'appears more like a crossover than a true phase transition', and the authors write that seeing the vortex-antivortex unbinding transition 'may be difficult in PCA or any machine learning technique'. They also establish that the BSI model has no phase transition and a macroscopic ground-state degeneracy. Overall lesson: the answer depends on which representation (bare spins vs bond, triangle, plaquette or vorticity variables) is fed in, and one is not recoverable from the other.
items.people: Wenjian Hu; Rajiv R. P. Singh; Richard T. Scalettar
items.affiliation: Department of Physics (and Department of Computer Science), University of California, Davis

items.claim: PCA TO VARIATIONAL AUTOENCODERS ON THE ISING MODEL. Wetzel samples the 2D Ising model on L = 28 (N = 784) with periodic boundaries, 50,000 configurations for the ferromagnet over T in [0,5] (10,000 for the antiferromagnet), and the 3D XY model on L = 14 (N = 2744). He compares four unsupervised methods with a single latent variable each: PCA, kernel PCA, a plain autoencoder, and a variational autoencoder (one fully connected 256-neuron hidden layer in encoder and in decoder). Result: the latent parameter of all four correlates cleanly with the magnetization, i.e. the learned latent variable IS the known order parameter; PCA is the most accurate, the VAE close behind, the plain autoencoder inaccurate (which is his stated motivation for the variational version). Separately he shows the mean-squared-error reconstruction loss, averaged at fixed temperature, changes character at T_c and proposes it as a 'universal identifier for phase transitions' requiring no order parameter. The latent representations cluster, allowing phases to be identified without prior knowledge of their existence or of the Hamiltonian.
items.people: Sebastian Johann Wetzel
items.affiliation: Institut fuer Theoretische Physik, Universitaet Heidelberg

items.claim: THE SHARPEST PUBLISHED ANSWER TO 'MAGNETIZATION OR ENERGY?'. Wetzel and Scherzer build a 'correlation probing neural network': a fully convolutional localization subnetwork whose output neurons have a FIXED receptive field, an averaging layer that destroys all spatial information, and a fully connected prediction subnetwork. Restricting the receptive field restricts which spin correlations the decision function can possibly contain. Trained on 2D Ising configurations sampled below T = 1.6 and above T = 2.9 (L = 28): (i) at receptive field 1x1 the decision function is provably D(S) = F((1/N) sum_i sigma_i), since sigma_i^2 = 1 kills all higher Taylor terms; its latent prediction xi is PERFECTLY correlated with |m| and NOT correlated with the average product of neighbouring spins, and its P = 0.5 crossing gives only T = 2.5 +/- 0.5. (ii) At receptive field 1x2 the latent prediction is perfectly correlated with the average nearest-neighbour product - the expected energy per site - and NOT with the norm of the average spin; crossing gives T = 2.25 +/- 0.25, and the loss drops sharply relative to 1x1. (iii) Enlarging the receptive field from 1x2 all the way to the full 28x28 (equivalent to an unrestricted CNN) produces NO further drop in training or validation loss. Conclusion stated in the abstract: 'the neural network predicts the phase by the magnetization and the expected energy per spin' - and nothing beyond nearest-neighbour correlations is used. The same pipeline applied to SU(2) lattice gauge theory reconstructs the Polyakov loop as the decision function.
items.people: Sebastian Johann Wetzel; Manuel Scherzer
items.affiliation: Institut fuer Theoretische Physik, Universitaet Heidelberg

items.claim: THE MAGNETIZATION STORY DEPENDS ON THE MONTE CARLO UPDATE. Suchsland and Wessel note that the Carrasquilla-Melko low-temperature training set was generated with the Wolff cluster algorithm, which yields strongly polarized low-T configurations containing NO extended domain walls (EDW) - and that this is what makes the 'network learns the magnetization' picture hold. Once a significant fraction of EDW configurations is included in the low-T set (as happens naturally with local spin updates), a fully connected network's hidden-layer activations show 'no clear overall relation' to the magnetization except at large |m|, and instead exhibit 'traces of a linear relation between the activations and the configurational energy'; the network 'performs the classification task based on a combined representation of the energy and the magnetization'. They further show a shallow CNN with N_k = 8 fixed 2x2 ReLU filters (a layout modelled on Carrasquilla-Melko) handles EDW configurations efficiently precisely because its filters can pick up local contributions to BOTH the magnetization and the local configurational energy. They also combine learning-by-confusion with a simple threshold-value classifier as a diagnostic for what a network has learned, and contrast bare-spin against vortex-preprocessed inputs for the 2D XY model.
items.people: Philippe Suchsland; Stefan Wessel
items.affiliation: Institut fuer Theoretische Festkoerperphysik, JARA-FIT and JARA-HPC, RWTH Aachen University

items.claim: MAGNETIZATION IN FULLY CONNECTED LAYERS, INTERNAL ENERGY IN CONVOLUTIONAL ONES. Kashiwa, Kikuchi and Tomiya train networks on 2D Ising and Potts configurations labelled by TEMPERATURE (20 target couplings K = 0.05, 0.10, ..., 1.0 at L = 16), never telling the network which phase a configuration is in, and then dissect the trained weights. For a fully connected network (hidden layer reduced from 80 to 5 and then 3 units) the first-layer outputs x_a = w_ai sigma_i + b_a are cleanly correlated with the magnetization per site of the input configuration, and the second-layer weights change structure at the exact critical coupling K_c = 0.4407. For a convolutional network (filters of size 2,2,4 with 64, 32, 3 channels, giving N_h = 3 hidden units) the picture flips: 'We clearly see the transition in what the neural network has learned. The first-layer outputs are now proportional to the internal energy rather than the magnetization of input configurations.' Their explanation: the internal energy varies far more strongly with temperature than |m| away from T_c, so a network optimizing temperature prediction prefers it - which is also why the CNN attains roughly twice the temperature-prediction accuracy of the fully connected net.
items.people: Kouji Kashiwa; Yuta Kikuchi; Akio Tomiya
items.affiliation: Fukuoka Institute of Technology (Kashiwa); RIKEN BNL Research Center, Brookhaven National Laboratory (Kikuchi, Tomiya)

items.claim: THE SMALLEST NETWORK, AND THE EXPLICIT ONE-HALF DEFINITION. Kim and Kim reduce the hidden layer to TWO neurons with weights fixed by Z_2 symmetry so that the hidden arguments are +/-(y - mu) with y = (1/N) sum_i s_i, and the output is q = [1 + tanh(Lambda z)]/2 with only two trainable parameters Lambda and mu. They define the pseudotransition temperature explicitly by <q>_{T*} = 1/2, the averaged output crossing one half. Solving the training problem analytically they find that the learned parameters encode the SCALING DIMENSION of the order parameter: Lambda_L ~ L^{2 Delta_sigma} and mu_L - ln3 ~ L^{-2 Delta_sigma} with Delta_sigma = beta/nu. Numerically, extrapolating T*_L for the square lattice gives T*_infinity = 2.267(1) with nu = 0.94(2) - matching the 100-unit network's 2.266(2) with nu = 1.0(2); the same square-lattice-trained network gives T_c ~ 3.637 on the triangular lattice (vs 3.65(1) from the 100-unit net) and a clean collapse at the exact 4/ln3 with nu = 1. This is the mechanism behind the transferability across lattices: same universality class, same scaling dimension. Applied instead to the 3D Ising model, the 2D-trained network's output curves develop NO crossing at all and converge to a wrong T*_infinity ~ 4.4695; using the correct 3D Delta_sigma = 0.51815 and nu = 0.63 recovers T_c = 4.51152(1).
items.people: Dongkyu Kim; Dong-Hee Kim
items.affiliation: Department of Physics and Photon Science, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST), Gwangju, Korea

items.claim: THE ONE-HALF CRITERION STATED IN WORDS, AND FITTING PROCEDURE. The companion paper to Carrasquilla-Melko, by the same group plus Ch'ng and Khatami, is the place where the criterion is written out plainly: 'The predicted critical temperatures ... are taken as temperatures at which the network is maximally confused, i.e., when the average output crosses 0.5', and 'the network is maximally confused (average is 0.5) at the transition temperatures'. Practical detail worth quoting in a book: because the averaged output is noisy, they fit a third-degree polynomial to the data near the 0.5 crossing to locate it. The physical setting is a three-dimensional convolutional network trained on determinantal-quantum-Monte-Carlo auxiliary-field configurations of the 3D Hubbard model (spatial 4^3 or 8^3 sites, 200 imaginary-time slices, 32/16/8 feature maps, dropout 0.5, softmax readout), which reproduces the Neel phase boundary at half filling and is then TRANSFER-LEARNED into the sign-problematic doped region, predicting magnetic order out to at least 5% doping.
items.people: Kelvin Ch'ng; Juan Carrasquilla; Roger G. Melko; Ehsan Khatami
items.affiliation: San Jose State University (Ch'ng, Khatami); Perimeter Institute and University of Waterloo (Carrasquilla, Melko)

items.claim: INTERPRETABLE KERNEL METHODS - THE DECISION FUNCTION IS m^2, AND THE GAUGE THEORY NEEDS DEGREE FOUR. Ponte and Melko replace neural networks with support vector machines using polynomial kernels K(sigma,sigma') = (sigma . sigma' + c_0)^k, so the decision function can be written down explicitly. For the 2D Ising model at T from 1.6 to 2.9: the linear kernel k = 1 fails outright (a linear boundary cannot separate three clusters, and its learned coefficients are structureless random numbers), while the quadratic kernel k = 2 reaches about 97% mean test accuracy at L = 40 with only a few dozen training samples, and its decision function d(sigma), plotted against temperature, coincides with the squared magnetization per spin m^2 = (sum_a sigma_a / N)^2 after fixing an overall scale and offset. For the conserved-order-parameter Ising model the quadratic SVM's coefficient map reproduces Wang's analytic structure factor. For the 2D Ising gauge theory at T = 0 versus T = infinity: EVERY polynomial kernel of degree less than 4 gives about 50% accuracy - pure guessing - while degree 4 converges to 100%, showing the classifier must literally reconstruct the four-spin plaquette term of the Hamiltonian to evaluate whether the local constraints are satisfied. Larger L needs more training samples to find that decision function.
items.people: Pedro Ponte; Roger G. Melko
items.affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo, and Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics

items.claim: THE KOSTERLITZ-THOULESS CASE: THE NETWORK CHEATS WITH THE MAGNETIZATION. Beach, Golubeva and Melko ask whether a network can classify phases from TOPOLOGICAL DEFECTS rather than a bulk order parameter, using the 2D classical XY model. Findings: a single-layer network does NOT correctly classify the phases of the XY model; a convolutional network classifies easily, but it does so 'by learning the global magnetization' - a finite-size pseudo-order-parameter, not the vortices; 'significant feature engineering of the raw spin states is required to convincingly claim that features of the vortex configurations are responsible for learning the transition temperature'. They then design a deep network that can learn vortices without feature engineering, and find that detecting vortices does not necessarily give the best classification accuracy, especially for lattices below roughly 1000 spins. This is the sharpest single demonstration that high classification accuracy is not evidence that the network has found the physically correct mechanism.
items.people: Matthew J. S. Beach; Anna Golubeva; Roger G. Melko
items.affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo; Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics (Melko)

items.claim: THE ONE-HALF CROSSING IS NOT A RELIABLE ESTIMATOR IN GENERAL. Chertenkov, Burovski and Shchur redo the supervised classification for two models in two universality classes - the 2D Ising model and the 2D Baxter-Wu model - across six architectures: a fully connected network, a CNN, and ResNet-10/18/34/50. They confirm the Carrasquilla-Melko phenomenology (output near 1 at low T, near 0 at high T, transition region narrowing with L) but find that the equal-prediction point F^T = 1/2 is systematically shifted into the paramagnetic phase for the fully connected network at all lattice sizes for both models, and shifted non-systematically for the ResNets (for ResNet-50 on the Ising model, L = 96, 144, 216 shift one way and L = 48, 72 the other). Their explicit conclusion: 'F^T = 1/2 is not a reliable finite-size estimate of the critical temperature T_c, in general'; it happens to work for a CNN on Ising data, which is the Carrasquilla-Melko case. They propose instead the VARIANCE of the network output function, whose peak sits in the critical region and whose peak WIDTH obeys finite-size scaling governed by nu, and extract T_c to within one standard error using a Ferdinand-Fisher fit (e.g. FCNN 2.2691(4), CNN 2.2687(4) for Ising).
items.people: Vladislav Chertenkov; Evgeni Burovski; Lev Shchur
items.affiliation: Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics, Chernogolovka; HSE University, Moscow

items.claim: WHAT THESE NETWORKS CONVERGE TO, ANALYTICALLY. Arnold and Schaefer derive closed-form expressions for the OPTIMAL output of three widely used neural-network methods for detecting phase transitions - including the Carrasquilla-Melko supervised scheme and the van Nieuwenburg learning-by-confusion scheme - in the limit of infinite model capacity, i.e. what a sufficiently large, well-trained network is approximating. The optimal predictions depend explicitly on the underlying data distributions, which is what reveals 'the inner workings of the considered methods'. Practically, evaluating the analytic expressions locates phase transitions directly from experimentally accessible data with no network training at all, and is faster. Validated numerically on topological, quantum, and many-body-localization transitions. This is the paper to cite when a book wants to say what the classifier is 'really' computing rather than what it happens to have learned.
items.people: Julian Arnold; Frank Schaefer
items.affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Basel; CSAIL and Department of Mathematics, MIT (Schaefer)

items.claim: THE OTHER CONTEMPORANEOUS CNN PAPER, OFTEN OMITTED. Tanaka and Tomiya trained a CNN on 2D Ising configurations labelled by DISCRETIZED INVERSE TEMPERATURE (not by phase), showed it finds the feature of the phase transition with no a priori information about it, defined a new order parameter constructed from the CNN itself that yields a well-approximated critical inverse temperature consistent with the exact value, and found empirically that the ReLU activation in the convolution layer is important for detecting the transition. This is the paper Kashiwa, Kikuchi and Tomiya later dissect; it establishes the temperature-regression variant of the protocol alongside the Carrasquilla-Melko phase-classification variant.
items.people: Akinori Tanaka; Akio Tomiya
items.affiliation: RIKEN (Tanaka); Central China Normal University / RIKEN BNL (Tomiya)

items.claim: THE PROTOCOL RUN ON REAL EXPERIMENTAL DATA. Rem, Kaeming, Tarnowski, Asteria, Flaeschner, Becker, Sengstock and Weitenberg applied artificial neural networks to single-shot momentum-space density images from ultracold-atom experiments rather than to Monte Carlo configurations, mapping out the two-dimensional topological phase diagram of the Haldane model and characterizing the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition in an inhomogeneous Bose-Hubbard system. Useful as the endpoint of the chapter's arc: the same supervised-classification idea, with experimental images as the raw configurations.
items.people: Benno S. Rem; Niklas Kaeming; Matthias Tarnowski; Luca Asteria; Nick Flaeschner; Christoph Becker; Klaus Sengstock; Christof Weitenberg
items.affiliation: Institut fuer Laserphysik / Institute for Quantum Physics, Universitaet Hamburg

openQuestions: The finite-size-scaling numbers T_c = 2.266(2), nu = 1.0(2), T_c(triangular) = 3.65(1) and the L <= 60 sweep appear ONLY in the paywalled Nature Physics version of Carrasquilla & Melko, not in arXiv:1605.01735v1. I verified them through two independent later papers that quote them (Chertenkov/Burovski/Shchur PRE 108 L032102 and Kim & Kim PRE 98 022138) but did not read the published text. Before printing them, get the published PDF and confirm the exact figure/panel and the exact scaling variable used (t*L^(1/nu) with t = (T - T_c)/T, per Chertenkov et al.).

Carrasquilla & Melko never write '0.5' in the arXiv text - they write 'the crossing point of the low- and high-temperature outputs'. The equality of that crossing with output = 1/2 follows because the two softmax outputs are complementary. If the book states the one-half criterion as their criterion, either derive it in a clause or attribute the explicit phrasing to Ch'ng/Carrasquilla/Melko/Khatami PRX 7, 031038 and to Kim & Kim's <q>_{T*} = 1/2. Do not attribute the literal phrase to the 2017 Nature Physics paper without checking the published Methods.

The paper tests square ice (Coulomb phase) and the two-dimensional Ising LATTICE GAUGE THEORY, not the toric code itself. The toric code enters only as the statement that the gauge theory's ground-state manifold is the same and, in the conclusion, that toric-code ground states can be represented by a CNN akin to theirs. Phrase this precisely; calling the tested system 'the toric code' is a common but sloppy shorthand.

There is no triangular-lattice ANTIFERROMAGNETIC Ising section in Carrasquilla & Melko - the triangular lattice they use is the FERROMAGNET, and the antiferromagnetic test is on the square lattice (q = (pi/a, pi/a)). The triangular antiferromagnet is Hu, Singh & Scalettar. Reviews frequently conflate these.

On 'is the classifier reading magnetization or energy', the literature does not give one answer, it gives an architecture- and sampling-dependent answer: fully connected + Wolff-sampled data -> magnetization (Carrasquilla & Melko; Suchsland & Wessel Sec. II); fully connected + extended domain walls in the training set -> combined energy and magnetization (Suchsland & Wessel Sec. III); convolutional + temperature regression -> internal energy (Kashiwa/Kikuchi/Tomiya); receptive-field analysis -> magnetization at 1x1, energy per site at 1x2, nothing beyond (Wetzel & Scherzer). A book chapter should state this as a dependency, not pick one.

I did not find a published paper that runs the specific null test a skeptical reader will want: train the Carrasquilla-Melko network, then compare its output curve directly against |m| and against E on the SAME configurations, and show whether a plain threshold on |m| locates T_c as well as the network does. Wetzel & Scherzer's 1x1 vs 1x2 comparison is the closest thing (and answers it indirectly: the 1x1 magnetization-only net is measurably worse, T = 2.5 +/- 0.5 vs 2.25 +/- 0.25). If the chapter wants to make this claim crisply it may need to be run in the demo app rather than cited.
